The first reads: "Act 1974, Section 2 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 20 November 2026."

question: Y72
answer:
# OPINION — Section 2(3), Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (law stated as at 21 November 2026)

**Subject:** The written statement every employer must prepare and revise, the prescribed exceptions to that duty, and the persons to whom the statement and any revision must be brought.

**Jurisdiction:** England and Wales, and Scotland (Great Britain). Northern Ireland is governed by separate legislation and is outside this opinion.

---

## 1. Question

Under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, as in force on 21 November 2026:

1. what written statement must every employer prepare and revise;
2. subject to what prescribed exceptions; and
3. to whom must the statement, and any revision of it, be brought?

---

## 2. Answer in short

**The statement (s.2(3)).** Every employer must prepare, and revise as often as may be appropriate, **a written statement of (a) his general policy with respect to the health and safety at work of his employees, and (b) the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying out that policy**.

**The prescribed exception.** The only prescribed exception is in the **Employers' Health and Safety Policy Statements (Exception) Regulations 1975 (SI 1975/1584), regulation 2**: an employer who carries on an undertaking in which he **for the time being employs fewer than five employees** is excepted, as respects that undertaking, from the provisions of s.2(3).

**To whom it must be brought.** The statement, and any revision of it, must be brought **to the notice of all of his employees**.

Both limbs sit in a single sentence of s.2(3). The duty is composite: there is no discharge of the section by preparing a document that is never communicated, and no discharge by communicating a policy that has not been written down and kept current.

---

## 3. The statutory text relied on

Section 2(3) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (c. 37), as in force on 21 November 2026, reads:

> "(3) Except in such cases as may be prescribed, it shall be the duty of every employer to prepare and as often as may be appropriate revise a written statement of his general policy with respect to the health and safety at work of his employees and the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying out that policy, and to bring the statement and any revision of it to the notice of all of his employees."

Related provisions, for completeness:

- **s.2(1)–(2)** — the general duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all employees, and the particular matters it extends to. s.2(3) is a free-standing duty, not a mere recital of s.2(1); it survives independently of it.
- **s.2(4)** — power to make regulations for the appointment of safety representatives by recognised trade unions. This is the power behind the Safety Representatives and Safety Committees Regulations 1996 (SI 1996/128), not behind the s.2(3) exception.
- **s.2(5)** — **repealed** (Employment Protection Act 1975). It is spent and forms no part of the current duty.
- **s.2(6)** — duty to consult safety representatives with a view to making and maintaining co-operative arrangements. Consultation is a separate duty and does not discharge the s.2(3) duty to bring the statement to the notice of *all* employees.
- **s.53(1)** — defines "employee" and "employer" for the Act.

---

## 4. The four elements of the s.2(3) duty

| Element | Statutory words | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Who** | "every employer" | Every employer of one or more employees in Great Britain. No size, sector or incorporation threshold in the Act itself; the only carve-out is the prescribed exception at §7 below. |
| **What** | "a written statement of his general policy … and the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying out that policy" | Two mandatory content limbs (see §5). It must be *written*; an unwritten or merely customary policy does not satisfy the section. |
| **When revised** | "as often as may be appropriate" | A continuing, event-driven duty. No fixed statutory review cycle (see §6). |
| **To whom** | "to the notice of all of his employees" | Every employee, not a subset (see §8). |

---

## 5. What the written statement must contain

The statute prescribes two content limbs and nothing more. It does not prescribe a form, a template, a length, or a title.

**Limb 1 — the general policy.** The employer's own statement of general policy with respect to the health and safety at work of *his* employees. In practice this is the statement of intent and commitment: the employer's aims and objectives for health and safety, the principle that health and safety is a management responsibility ranking equally with other management functions, and the employer's position on consultation and on the co-operation of employees. It must be the employer's own policy for his own undertaking, not an unadapted third-party template.

**Limb 2 — the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying out that policy.** This is the operational half and is often the weaker half in practice:

- **Organisation** — who is responsible for what: named roles and post-holders, the chain of accountability from the most senior level down, the allocation of duties, and the arrangements for competent advice and supervision.
- **Arrangements** — the systems and procedures actually in force for delivering the policy: risk assessment arrangements, safe systems of work, training and induction, consultation, accident and incident reporting and investigation, first aid, emergency procedures, monitoring and audit, and review.

The words "for the time being in force" are important. The statement must describe the arrangements that *actually operate*, not aspirational arrangements. A statement describing a management system the employer does not run is both a breach of s.2(3) and a document that will be used in evidence against the employer after an incident.

**Two things the statement is not.** It is not the risk assessment (the record of significant findings is a separate duty under the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, reg. 5, owed by employers with five or more employees), and it is not a substitute for the information and instruction duties under s.2(2)(c) or MHSWR 1999, reg. 10. Conversely, neither of those duties discharges s.2(3).

---

## 6. When the statement must be revised

Section 2(3) sets no periodic review cycle. The trigger is fitness for purpose: the statement must be revised **"as often as may be appropriate"**. That is an objective standard, and an employer who leaves a materially out-of-date statement in place is in breach even if a review date has not yet arrived.

Circumstances that will ordinarily make revision appropriate:

1. **Organisational change** — restructuring, merger or acquisition, change of senior management, or a change in who holds the named health and safety responsibilities.
2. **Physical change** — new premises, relocation, refurbishment, new plant or equipment, or new substances.
3. **Process change** — new work methods, new technology, changes in shift patterns, or outsourcing and contracting-out of activities.
4. **Workforce change** — significant change in numbers, in the mix of employees, or in the use of agency, temporary, young or new/expectant mothers.
5. **An incident** — an accident, dangerous occurrence or near miss, particularly where an investigation shows the arrangements described were not the arrangements operating.
6. **Enforcement or external challenge** — service of an improvement or prohibition notice, an HSE or local authority visit, or a RIDDOR report.
7. **Change in the law or in approved guidance** — new regulations, approved codes of practice, or HSE guidance bearing on the employer's activities.
8. **Monitoring and audit findings** — results of inspection, audit, or occupational health surveillance indicating the arrangements are not working.
9. **Consultation** — outcomes of consultation with safety representatives under s.2(6).

**Recommended practice (not a statutory requirement):** a documented review at a fixed interval (commonly annually) *in addition to* event-driven review, with the date of the last review and the reviewer recorded on the face of the statement. This is evidential: it demonstrates the employer has turned its mind to the duty, but it does not cure a failure to revise when an event made revision appropriate before the next scheduled review.

---

## 7. The prescribed exceptions

**Instrument:** Employers' Health and Safety Policy Statements (Exception) Regulations 1975 (SI 1975/1584), made under the power in s.2(3) itself, in force since 1 November 1975.

**Operative provision, reg. 2:**

> "Any employer who carries on an undertaking in which for the time being he employs less than five employees is hereby excepted as respects that undertaking from the provisions of subsection (3) of section 2 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 …"

**Points of construction:**

1. **The threshold is fewer than five — i.e. four or fewer.** Five employees brings the full duty into force. There is no taper and no partial duty at four or below.

| Employees in the undertaking | s.2(3) duty (prepare, revise, bring to notice) |
|---|---|
| 1–4 | Excepted, as respects that undertaking |
| 5 or more | Full duty applies |

2. **The exception bites on the whole of s.2(3), not part of it.** The regulation excepts the employer "from the provisions of subsection (3)" — both the prepare/revise limb and the bring-to-notice limb. The parenthetical in the regulation, which describes s.2(3) by reference only to the bringing-to-notice obligation, is a description and does not narrow the operative words.
3. **"As respects that undertaking."** The exception is undertaking-specific. An employer running more than one undertaking is excepted only in respect of an undertaking in which it employs fewer than five.
4. **"For the time being."** The test is dynamic. If headcount reaches five, the duty applies from that point and a statement must be prepared and brought to notice; it is no answer that the undertaking previously qualified. Falling back below five suspends the duty prospectively; it does not retrospectively validate a period of non-compliance.
5. **The exception does not extinguish the underlying duty to manage health and safety.** It removes only the s.2(3) statutory obligation. The s.2(1) general duty, and the duties in the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (including, for employers with five or more employees, the reg. 5 duty to record the significant findings of risk assessment), are unaffected. An employer of four or fewer employees must still have a health and safety policy in substance; it simply is not obliged by s.2(3) to reduce it to a written statement and circulate it.

**Status on 21 November 2026.** No amending instrument altering SI 1975/1584 has been identified in the sources examined, and the regulation remains the operative prescribed exception. It should be re-verified against the "Changes to legislation" tab for SI 1975/1584 immediately before reliance (see §10).

**Correction of a common error.** The small-employer exception is **not** in the Safety Signs and Signals Regulations 1996, and those Regulations neither create nor revoke it. SI 1975/1584 is the source, and it is made under s.2(3), not under any other power.

---

## 8. To whom the statement and any revision must be brought

**"…to the notice of all of his employees."**

1. **All employees.** Every person employed by the employer under a contract of employment, in every part of the undertaking, at every site, on every shift, and at every grade. "Employee" bears its s.53(1) meaning; individuals who work for the employer but are not employees in that sense fall outside s.2(3) (they are protected instead by s.3 and by other regimes).
2. **Not a subset.** The duty is not satisfied by notice to managers only, to safety representatives only, to trade union members only, to employees at the principal site only, or to employees who happen to read a noticeboard they pass.
3. **Not the enforcing authority.** There is no statutory obligation to send the statement to the Health and Safety Executive or the local authority. Production to an inspector is a separate obligation arising from an inspector's powers under s.20, not from s.2(3).
4. **Safety representatives are not the channel.** Consultation with safety representatives under s.2(6) and the SRSC Regulations 1996 is a distinct duty. Informing representatives does not inform employees.
5. **Groups requiring specific attention** so that "all" is genuinely met: new starters (induction), part-time and shift workers, lone and home workers, employees on long-term leave or absent from site, employees with disabilities or with limited literacy, and employees whose first language is not English (the notice must be capable of being understood by the employees in question).
6. **Revisions.** The duty applies afresh to **each revision**. Circulating the original statement once, years earlier, does not discharge the duty in respect of a later revision. The revision must itself be brought to the notice of all employees.

**Manner.** The Act prescribes no manner — only the result, that the statement be brought to employees' notice. Any method that actually achieves that result is sufficient. Methods commonly relied on, alone or in combination:

| Method | Comment |
|---|---|
| Issued copy (paper or electronic) to each employee | Strongest evidence of individual notice |
| Inclusion in the contract, staff handbook or induction pack | Effective if the handbook is issued and updates are issued |
| Intranet / shared drive publication with an alert | Adequate only if all employees have access; not adequate for non-desk or production staff alone |
| Display on noticeboards in each workplace | Adequate only if the boards are in places all affected employees actually use, and the copy is current |
| Team briefings / toolbox talks with attendance records | Good evidence for shift and site-based workforces |
| Reference in training with a signed acknowledgement | Good evidence, particularly for revisions |

The standard is substantive, not formal: the question after an incident will be whether the employees in fact had the statement (or the revision) brought to their notice, not whether some step was taken that was intended to achieve it.

---

## 9. Enforcement consequences (context only)

Breach of s.2(3) is a contravention of a relevant statutory provision and is enforceable by improvement notice under s.21 and by prosecution under s.33, subject to the statutory defences (including s.40's reverse burden, itself subject to the fair-trial caveats established in case law). Where an offence is committed by a body corporate with the consent or connivance of, or attributable to the neglect of, a director, manager, secretary or similar officer, that officer is also guilty under s.37. A stale or uncommunicated statement is a routine and readily proved finding on inspection.

---

## 10. Point-in-time verification (21 November 2026)

**Basis of this opinion.** The text of s.2(3) quoted at §3 was taken from the legislation.gov.uk revised version of the Act, which records that "Section 2 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 20 November 2026", and cross-checked against the point-in-time version of Part I as at 16 July 2026, which carries s.2(3) in identical terms. The amendment entries recorded against Part I on 27 January 2026 and 16 July 2026 do not touch s.2(3); the only outstanding prospective change flagged for Part I is the insertion of s.51B by the 2026 Act (asp 5), Sch. 3, para. 1, which is unrelated to the s.2(3) duty. Section 2(5) is shown as repealed and spent.

**Residual risk, and how to close it.** The consolidated text was current to 20 November 2026 — one day before the operative date. Before final reliance, confirm on the operative date:

1. that the "Changes to legislation" note for s.2 still records no change to subsection (3) taking effect on or before 21 November 2026;
2. that the "changes not yet in force" list contains nothing affecting s.2(3) (as at the date of this opinion it contains only s.51B);
3. that SI 1975/1584 remains unrepealed and unamended, by checking its own "Changes to legislation" tab;
4. that no post-2026 devolution settlement has moved health and safety legislative competence in Wales or Scotland in a way that produces a divergent s.2(3) for the relevant jurisdiction. As at the operative date the duty is uniform across Great Britain.

---

## 11. Compliance procedure for an employer

1. **Count.** Determine the number of employees in the undertaking. Four or fewer: the s.2(3) duty does not apply (but maintain a policy in substance and comply with s.2(1) and MHSWR 1999). Five or more: continue.
2. **Write.** Prepare a written statement containing (a) the general policy for the health and safety at work of employees and (b) the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying it out. Name post-holders and describe the arrangements that actually operate.
3. **Date and own it.** Record the date of issue, the date of the last review, and the identity of the signatory at the most senior level.
4. **Bring to notice.** Issue the statement to all employees by a method, or combination of methods, that reaches every category in §8.5. Keep evidence of issue (distribution lists, acknowledgements, briefing records, noticeboard photographs).
5. **Diary a review.** Set a fixed review interval, and in any event review on each trigger in §6.
6. **Revise and re-notify.** On revision, update the statement, record the revision date, and bring the revision to the notice of all employees again, with fresh evidence of issue.
7. **Monitor headcount.** Where the undertaking hovers at four to five employees, treat the statement as required once five are employed and keep it current.
8. **Retain.** Keep superseded versions; they evidence the revision history and may be needed in enforcement proceedings.

---

## 12. Scope and limitations

This opinion states the legal position under s.2(3) HSWA 1974 for Great Britain as at 21 November 2026. It is not advice on compliance in any particular workplace, and it does not address: sector-specific regimes (COSHH, DSEAR, fire safety, asbestos, offshore installations); the parallel Northern Ireland provision in the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978, which is outside scope and unverified here; the detail of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 beyond the points of distinction noted; or devolved competence questions that may arise after the operative date.

question: Y73
shape: UK health and safety arrangements recording threshold
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (S.I. 1999/3242)

1. Version relied on (ask 1 constraint)
The page presents 'Latest available (Revised)' as the default view and a point-in-time series. The latest version shown is the point in time view as at 03/04/2023 (the timeline of changes ends at 03/04/2023; the page states 'Point in time view as at 03/04/2023' and 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999'). Both requested facts are read from that Revised text. Cross-check: the as-made body text carries the same regulation 1(1) and regulation 5(2) wording, so the answers are not version-sensitive — no amendment in the timeline (06/04/2006 through 03/04/2023) altered either provision.

2. Coming-into-force date (ask 2)
Regulation 1(1): 'These Regulations may be cited as the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 and shall come into force on 29th December 1999.'
Instrument header block on the same page: 'Made 3rd December 1999 / Laid before Parliament 8th December 1999 / Coming into force 29th December 1999'.
Answer: 29 December 1999 (1999-12-29). The making date (3 December 1999) and laying date (8 December 1999) are distinct and must not be used.

3. Employee-count threshold for recording the regulation 5(1) arrangements (ask 3)
Regulation 5(1): 'Every employer shall make and give effect to such arrangements as are appropriate, having regard to the nature of his activities and the size of his undertaking, for the effective planning, organisation, control, monitoring and review of the preventive and protective measures.'
Regulation 5(2): 'Where the employer employs five or more employees, he shall record the arrangements referred to in paragraph (1).'
Answer: five employees (5).
Operative reading for compliance purposes:
- 5 or more employees: the employer must record the regulation 5(1) arrangements (and, separately, regulation 3(3) requires recording of the significant findings of the risk assessment and any group of employees identified as especially at risk where five or more are employed — same count, different duty).
- 4 or fewer employees: no duty under regulation 5(2) to record the arrangements; the regulation 5(1) duty to make and give effect to appropriate arrangements continues to apply in full. The threshold removes a recording obligation only; it does not remove the substantive duty.
- The count is a headcount test, not an FTE or hours test, on the face of the wording ('employs five or more employees'). Where headcount crosses 5, the recording duty is live from that point; contemporaneous headcount evidence should be retained to support the position taken.

4. Correction to a stated assumption
An internal assumption referred to 'regulation 5(2)(b)'. No such provision exists on the page: regulation 5(2) is a single, unnumbered sentence as quoted above. The threshold is therefore cited as regulation 5(2), not regulation 5(2)(b). The assumption that the threshold concerns the regulation 5(1) recording exemption is otherwise correct.

5. Evidence pack a reviewer should hold
(a) Screenshot/PDF of the Revised point-in-time page (as at 03/04/2023) showing the header block and regulations 1(1), 3(3) and 5; (b) current headcount record as at the assessment date; (c) the recorded arrangements document itself where headcount is 5 or more, cross-referenced to regulation 5(1) subject matter (planning, organisation, control, monitoring, review).

6. Values stated
Coming into force: 29 December 1999. Recording threshold: five employees.

question: Y74
answer:
COMPLIANCE FILE ANSWER — Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (SI 1999/3242): application to master, crew and their employer for normal ship-board activities

=== A. ANSWER (VERDICT) ===
No. The Regulations do NOT apply. Regulation 2(1) expressly disapplies the whole of the Regulations to and in relation to (i) the master of a ship, (ii) the crew of a ship, and (iii) the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew which are carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master.

All three persons named in the question — master, crew, and their employer — are covered by the disapplication. The carve-out is not limited to the crew, and it is not limited to sea-going ships.

=== B. AUTHORITY AND EXACT TEXT ===
Instrument: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, SI 1999/3242 (GB; extent E+W+S).
Provision: Regulation 2, headed 'Disapplication of these Regulations'.
Full citation for the file: reg 2(1) of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (SI 1999/3242), as substituted by the Management of Health and Safety at Work and Fire Precautions (Workplace) (Amendment) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/2457), reg 3.

Verbatim text (regulation 2 as currently in force):

"2.—(1) These Regulations shall not apply to or in relation to the master or crew of a ship, or to the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew which are carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master.

(2) Regulations 3(4), (5), 10(2) and 19 shall not apply to occasional work or short-term work involving work regarded as not being harmful, damaging or dangerous to young people in a family undertaking.

(3) In this regulation—
"normal ship-board activities" include—
(a) the construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship outside, but not inside, Great Britain; and
(b) the repair of a ship save repair when carried out in dry dock;
"ship" includes every description of vessel used in navigation, other than a ship belonging to Her Majesty which forms part of Her Majesty's Navy."

(The marginal citation printed against the regulation is '1980 c. 44'; it has no effect on the operative wording and should not be reproduced as if it qualified the carve-out.)

=== C. VERSION CONTROL — AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21 ===
1. Made under what is now the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; came into force 29 December 1999 (reg 1(1)).
2. Regulation 2 was substituted in its entirety on 27 October 2003 by SI 2003/2457, reg 3. Every version of reg 2 after that date is the substituted text.
3. The substituted text is confirmed identical at the point-in-time snapshots of 20 June 2021 and 3 April 2023, and in the latest available revised version. The legislation.gov.uk 'Changes to Legislation' notice for the instrument states: "There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999."
4. Accordingly, the text in section B is the text in force on 21 November 2026. (The source pages were retrieved on 23 November 2026, i.e. after the target date, so the latest available revised version is the correct evidence base for the 2026-11-21 position.)
5. SUPERSEDED TEXT — do not use. As originally made, reg 2(1) read: "These Regulations shall not apply to or in relation to the master or crew of a sea-going ship or to the employer of such persons in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew under the direction of the master." The 2003 substitution made three changes material to this question: (a) deleted 'sea-going', so the carve-out now attaches to any 'ship' as defined; (b) inserted 'which are carried out solely by the crew', narrowing the carve-out to crew-only activity; and (c) added paragraph (3), supplying the inclusive definitions of 'normal ship-board activities' and 'ship'. Any file relying on the original wording would wrongly confine the carve-out to sea-going vessels and would wrongly ignore the 'solely by the crew' condition.

=== D. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT APPLICATION ===
The disapplication operates only if all four elements are satisfied. Each is set out with the test to be recorded in the file.

1. The persons: 'the master or crew of a ship, or ... the employer of such persons'. All three limbs are named. The employer limb is the employer of the master or crew, i.e. the crew's employer — which may be the shipowner, a ship manager, a bareboat or time-charterer, or a crewing/manning agency, depending on the employment relationship. The clause disapplies the Regulations as regards that employer too, but only 'in respect of' the activities described in element 3.

2. 'A ship': defined in reg 2(3) as 'every description of vessel used in navigation, other than a ship belonging to Her Majesty which forms part of Her Majesty's Navy'. Points to record: (a) 'sea-going' is no longer a requirement, so inland-waterway and other vessels 'used in navigation' are within the definition; (b) the definition is inclusive ('includes'); (c) the only express exclusion is a ship belonging to Her Majesty forming part of Her Majesty's Navy — naval vessels are outside the definition of 'ship' for reg 2, so the carve-out is not available in respect of them and the Regulations apply to them in the ordinary way (subject to whatever separate provision applies).

3. 'The normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew': reg 2(3) defines this inclusively — it 'includes' (i) construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship outside, but not inside, Great Britain, and (ii) repair of a ship save repair carried out in dry dock. Because the definition is inclusive and not exhaustive, ordinary operational activity of the crew on board (watchkeeping, berthing and mooring, cargo and ballast operations performed by the crew, deck and engine-room maintenance short of dry-dock repair, catering and accommodation duties, drills) falls within 'normal ship-board activities' on the ordinary meaning of the phrase; the statutory inclusions extend it further, to off-GB newbuild/conversion work and to afloat repairs.

4. 'Carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master': two cumulative conditions. 'Solely by the crew' — no person outside the crew may be engaged in the activity (contractors, riding crews, pilots, stevedores, surveyors, shore technical staff, supernumeraries or passengers taking part will each defeat the condition). 'Under the direction of the master' — the activity must be under the master's direction; activity directed by others (e.g. a shore-based project manager, a dry-dock superintendent, a charterer's superintendent) is outside the carve-out.

Where all four elements are met, the answer is that the Regulations do not apply. Where any element fails, the Regulations apply in the ordinary way.

=== E. BOUNDARIES — WHAT REMAINS COVERED ===
The disapplication is activity-specific and person-specific, not a blanket exclusion of ships or of shipowners. The following remain within the Regulations and should be recorded as residual exposures in the compliance file:
(a) Repair carried out in dry dock — expressly excluded from 'normal ship-board activities' by reg 2(3)(b). Dry-dock repair is therefore covered by the Regulations.
(b) Construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship inside Great Britain — expressly excluded from 'normal ship-board activities' by reg 2(3)(a). Shipbuilding and conversion work in GB yards is covered.
(c) Activity on board that is not carried out solely by the crew, or not under the master's direction (see D4). Work alongside contractors, shore staff or other third parties is covered.
(d) The employer's obligations in respect of matters other than the crew's normal ship-board activities — e.g. shore-based premises, shore staff, and the employer's undertaking generally. Regulation 2(1) disapplies the Regulations only 'in respect of' the specified activities.
(e) Ships belonging to Her Majesty forming part of Her Majesty's Navy (outside the reg 2(3) definition of 'ship').
(f) Persons on board who are not master or crew and are not the employer of master or crew.

=== F. SCOPE AND TERRITORIAL POINTS ===
1. Extent. The instrument, and reg 2, are marked E+W+S — England and Wales and Scotland. This answer is the Great Britain answer. The equivalent Northern Ireland instrument is a separate instrument and is not covered by this answer; if the file concerns a Northern Ireland employer or premises, a separate check of the Northern Ireland equivalent is required before filing.
2. Outside Great Britain. Regulation 23 extends the Regulations to premises and activities outside Great Britain to which ss 1–59 and 80–82 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 apply by virtue of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (Application Outside Great Britain) Order 1995 (SI 1995/263). Regulation 23(1) opens with the words 'subject to regulation 2'. The carve-out therefore travels with the territorial extension: where the Regulations would otherwise apply offshore or outside GB by virtue of reg 23, reg 2(1) still disapplies them for normal ship-board activities carried out solely by the crew under the master's direction. The physical location of the vessel (UK waters, foreign waters or international waters) does not by itself defeat reg 2(1); what matters is whether the Regulations would otherwise apply at all, and if they would, reg 2(1) applies to that application.
3. Related regime (context only, not part of the scope clause). The carve-out exists because shipboard occupational health and safety is regulated under the merchant shipping regime (the Merchant Shipping and Fishing Vessels (Health and Safety at Work) Regulations 1997, SI 1997/2962, made under what is now the Merchant Shipping Act 1995), enforced by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency rather than HSE. That regime, not the 1999 Regulations, is the source of the employer's and master's shipboard duties for the activities disapplied by reg 2(1). This paragraph is background and is not relied on for the verdict, which rests on reg 2(1) alone.

=== G. FILING NOTES / VERIFICATION STEPS ===
1. The verdict rests on the operative words of reg 2(1) reproduced in section B; quote them in the file rather than paraphrasing, because the three conditions ('normal ship-board activities', 'solely by the crew', 'under the direction of the master') do the work.
2. Before the file is closed, re-run the point-in-time check on legislation.gov.uk for 21 November 2026 ('What Version' → point in time) to confirm no amendment to reg 2 has been recorded since the version relied on here. On the evidence retrieved, the text is unchanged and no outstanding effects are recorded, so the check is confirmatory rather than expectant of change.
3. Record the version relied on in the file as: SI 1999/3242, reg 2 as substituted by SI 2003/2457, reg 3 (in force 27 October 2003), text as at 21 November 2026.

=== H. COPY-READY FILE ENTRY ===
Question: Do the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 apply to the master or crew of a ship, or to their employer, in respect of normal ship-board activities carried out solely by the crew under the master's direction?
Answer: No. Regulation 2(1) disapplies the Regulations to and in relation to the master or crew of a ship, and to the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master.
Authority: SI 1999/3242, reg 2(1) and (3), as substituted by SI 2003/2457, reg 3; text in force on 21 November 2026.
Conditions recorded: (i) vessel is a 'ship' within reg 2(3) (any vessel used in navigation, excluding a ship belonging to Her Majesty forming part of Her Majesty's Navy); (ii) the activity is a normal ship-board activity of the crew, including (by reg 2(3)) construction/reconstruction/conversion outside Great Britain and repair other than in dry dock; (iii) the activity is carried out solely by the crew; (iv) the activity is under the master's direction.
Residual cover noted: dry-dock repair; construction/reconstruction/conversion inside Great Britain; any activity involving persons outside the crew or not under the master's direction; the employer's non-shipboard undertaking; naval vessels. Shipboard health and safety for the disapplied activities is governed by the merchant shipping regime (SI 1997/2962), not by the 1999 Regulations.

The first reads: "Act 1974 (Application Outside Great Britain) Order 1995 M10 as they apply within Great Britain."

question: Y75
shape: UK power press thorough examination intervals
answer:
ANSWER — PUWER 1998, Part IV (Power Presses), regulation 32(4) ('Thorough examination of power presses, guards and protection devices'), latest available (Revised) version as shown on the supplied page.

VERBATIM SOURCE TEXT (identical in every view supplied — Original (As made), Latest available (Revised), snippet view, and the regulation/32 data.xml):

  '32.—(4) For the purpose of ensuring that health and safety conditions are maintained, and that any deterioration can be detected and remedied in good time, every employer shall ensure that—
    (a) every power press is thoroughly examined, and its guards and protection devices are thoroughly examined when in position on that power press—
      (i) at least every 12 months, where it has fixed guards only; or
      (ii) at least every 6 months, in other cases; and
      (iii) each time that exceptional circumstances have occurred which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the power press or its guards or protection devices; and
    (b) any defect is remedied before the power press is used again.'

1. VERSION CHECK (ask 1, the constraint). The page's 'What Version' panel offers 'Latest available (Revised)' and 'Original (As made)'. The /enacted view carries the status line 'This is the original version (as it was originally made)'; the /1998-12-05 and data.xml views carry the revised text (data.xml header: 'Statute Law Database 2024-05-16, Expert Participation 2018-07-30'). Regulation 32(4) is word-for-word the same in all of them, and the page states: 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, PART IV.' The answer therefore does not vary between the versions shown. (The site's own caveat applies: 'Revised legislation carried on this site may not be fully up to date.')

2. POWER PRESS WITH FIXED GUARDS ONLY — 12 months. Reg. 32(4)(a)(i): the press, and its guards and protection devices when in position on it, must be thoroughly examined at least every 12 months.

3. IN OTHER CASES — 6 months. Reg. 32(4)(a)(ii): at least every 6 months. 'Other cases' means any press that does not have fixed guards only — e.g. interlocking guards, adjustable guards, or protection devices (light curtains, two-hand controls, etc.), or any combination of these with fixed guarding.

4. ADDITIONAL EVENT — reg. 32(4)(a)(iii): 'each time that exceptional circumstances have occurred which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the power press or its guards or protection devices'. This is event-driven and sits on top of the periodic 12/6-month cycle; a defect found must be remedied before the press is used again (reg. 32(4)(b)).

APPLICATION NOTES (scope discipline — these do not change the three answers above)
- 'At least every' sets a maximum interval. A shorter interval set by risk assessment satisfies the duty; a longer one does not. The 12-month and 6-month figures are interval ceilings, not targets.
- The examination covers two things in one act: the power press itself, and its guards and protection devices 'when in position on that power press'. A press examination that omits the in-position guards does not discharge reg. 32(4)(a).
- Reg. 32(6): 'Paragraph (4) shall not apply to that part of a closed tool which acts as a fixed guard.' Such tool-mounted fixed guards fall under reg. 32(3) instead — not used on a power press unless thoroughly examined when in position on any power press in the premises and any defect remedied. So 'fixed guards only' in (4)(a)(i) should be applied with (6) in mind; the 12-month cycle is for fixed guards proper, not the closed-tool fixed-guard element.
- Other, one-off thorough-examination triggers in the same regulation, distinct from the periodic regime and not to be confused with it: reg. 32(1) — press before first put into service after installation, or after assembly at a new site or in a new location; reg. 32(2) — guard (other than a closed-tool fixed guard) or protection device before first put into service on a press; reg. 32(3) — closed-tool fixed guard before first use. Reg. 32(5) contains a transitional rule for items previously covered by reg. 5(2) of the Power Presses Regulations 1965.
- Not to be confused with 'inspection'. Reg. 33 requires inspection and test of every guard and protection device by a competent person appointed in writing (with a signed certificate meeting reg. 33(3)), including before use after the fourth hour of a working period. That is a separate, far more frequent duty and does not satisfy reg. 32(4).
- Records: reports under reg. 34; reg. 35 requires the information in every report made pursuant to reg. 34(1) to be kept available for inspection for 2 years after it is made.
- Reg. 31 disapplies regs. 32–35 for a power press of a kind described in Schedule 2 — confirm the specific press is not excluded before applying the 12/6-month cycle.
- HSE's Approved Code of Practice and guidance 'Safe use of power presses' (L112, published 12-12-2014, ISBN 9780717666201) covers thorough examination, inspection and the keeping of information; it is guidance, and the legal intervals are those in reg. 32(4) quoted above.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE AN OPERATOR CAN APPLY DIRECTLY
1. Classify the press: does it have fixed guards only (and no interlocking/adjustable guards or protection devices)? If yes, set the thorough-examination interval at not more than 12 months; if no, not more than 6 months. Record the classification and its basis.
2. Schedule the examination of the press together with its guards and protection devices in position; set the next due date from the date of the examination, not from the due date, if examinations run late.
3. Add an unscheduled trigger: re-examine on each occurrence of exceptional circumstances liable to jeopardise the safety of the press, its guards or its protection devices.
4. On any defect, quarantine the press until the defect is remedied; do not return it to service first.
5. Keep the reg. 34 report information available for inspection for 2 years, and keep the reg. 33 inspection/test certificates separately — neither substitutes for the other.

SCOPE OF THIS ANSWER: it is a citation-based compliance answer on the written law as supplied. It is not a site-specific risk assessment, and the schedule should be re-checked against the revised text current at the time it is applied.

question: Y76
answer:
COMPLIANCE OPINION — PROVISION AND USE OF WORK EQUIPMENT REGULATIONS 1998 AND A DISTRIBUTOR SUPPLYING BY WAY OF SALE
Position stated as at 2026-11-21 (Great Britain)

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER IN ONE LINE
=====================================================================
No. The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 do not apply to a person in respect of work equipment supplied by that person by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement. That is the express effect of regulation 3(5), the final limb of the scope clause. A distributor is not a PUWER duty holder in respect of the sale itself.

=====================================================================
2. BASIS ON WHICH THIS OPINION IS GIVEN (state these on the face of the advice)
=====================================================================
(a) JURISDICTION — GREAT BRITAIN. The request does not name a jurisdiction. Great Britain and Northern Ireland each have an instrument called the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, and their texts differ. This opinion is given on the Great Britain instrument, SI 1998/2306, which is the instrument covered by the sources used (legislation.gov.uk and HSE). If the distributor operates in Northern Ireland the relevant instrument is the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (SR 1998/279), enforced by HSENI; the equivalent sale exclusion is expected to be in the same terms but has NOT been verified against the sources available for this opinion and must be re-checked before reliance.

(b) CAPACITY OF THE DISTRIBUTOR. The opinion assumes the distributor's only relevant connection with the equipment is that it sold it. It assumes the distributor is not, in relation to the same equipment, (i) an employer providing it for use by its own employees, (ii) a relevant self-employed person using it at work, or (iii) a person having control of it, of a person using it, or of the way it is used, at the purchaser's premises. Where any of those is true, PUWER can attach on that separate basis — see section 6.

(c) MEANING OF 'THE SCOPE CLAUSE'. Regulation 3 (headed 'Application') of PUWER 1998 — the provision that fixes where the Regulations apply, to whom the requirements are addressed, and the sale/hire-purchase carve-out.

(d) VERSION. The text relied on is the latest revised text carried on legislation.gov.uk, fetched 2026-11-23T00:07:02Z, which carries the banner 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998'. It is cross-checked against the 2013-07-01 point-in-time version and against HSE L22 (Fourth edition, 2014). See section 8 for the full currency record and its residual limitation.

=====================================================================
3. THE SCOPE CLAUSE — VERBATIM TEXT (regulation 3, GB, as currently in force)
=====================================================================

Regulation 3 — Application

(1) These Regulations shall apply—
    (a) in Great Britain; and
    (b) outside Great Britain as sections 1 to 59 and 80 to 82 of the 1974 Act apply by virtue of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (Application outside Great Britain) Order 1995 ('the 1995 Order').

(2) The requirements imposed by these Regulations on an employer in respect of work equipment shall apply to such equipment provided for use or used by an employee of his at work.

(3) The requirements imposed by these Regulations on an employer shall also apply—
    (a) to a [relevant self-employed person], in respect of work equipment he uses at work;
    (b) subject to paragraph (5), to a person who has control to any extent of—
        (i) work equipment;
        (ii) a person at work who uses or supervises or manages the use of work equipment; or
        (iii) the way in which work equipment is used at work,
        and to the extent of his control.

(4) Any reference in paragraph (3)(b) to a person having control is a reference to a person having control in connection with the carrying on by him of a trade, business or other undertaking (whether for profit or not).

(5) The requirements imposed by these Regulations shall not apply to a person in respect of work equipment supplied by him by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement.

(6) Subject to paragraphs (7) to (10), these Regulations shall not impose any obligation in relation to a ship's work equipment (whether that equipment is used on or off the ship).

Note on the text: the words 'relevant self-employed person' in paragraph (3)(a) are a later amendment (shown as F1 on the revised text) to the original words 'self-employed person'. That amendment affects only paragraph (3)(a). Paragraph (5) — the sale exclusion — is in its original 1998 wording and has not been amended. Paragraphs (7) to (10) concern ships' work equipment and are not material to a sale on land.

=====================================================================
4. ANALYSIS OF THE SALE EXCLUSION, ELEMENT BY ELEMENT
=====================================================================

'THE REQUIREMENTS IMPOSED BY THESE REGULATIONS SHALL NOT APPLY'
This is a full disapplication, not a partial one and not merely a defence. It removes every requirement in PUWER (regulations 4 to 35, including the 'suitable for purpose', maintenance, inspection, information/instruction/training and marking duties) as against the excluded person, in the excluded respect.

'TO A PERSON'
The exclusion is personal and capacity-specific. It is not a statement that the equipment is outside the Regulations; it is a statement that the seller is outside the duties in that capacity. The equipment remains 'work equipment' in the purchaser's hands and the purchaser's own duties under regulations 3(2) and 3(3) are untouched. HSE guidance makes the same point in terms: 'The Regulations do NOT apply to those who have supplied or sold equipment. It's up to the purchaser of equipment to make sure that it is specified, installed and used so that it does not present a risk to those at work.'

'IN RESPECT OF WORK EQUIPMENT SUPPLIED BY HIM'
The exclusion attaches to the supply act and the supplier's role in it. It does not travel with the equipment. It does not follow the distributor into an unrelated role at the purchaser's premises.

'BY WAY OF SALE, AGREEMENT FOR SALE OR HIRE-PURCHASE AGREEMENT'
This phrase is the operative limit, and it is narrower than the word 'supply' on its own:
  - 'Sale' — a completed sale, where property passes on or before delivery.
  - 'Agreement for sale' — a contract of sale under which property passes later (e.g. on payment in full, retention of title, conditional sale). This is inside the exclusion even though, at the moment of delivery, the seller may still hold title.
  - 'Hire-purchase agreement' — inside the exclusion, notwithstanding that the supplier retains title until the final instalment and the transaction has financing features.
  - NOT covered: ordinary hire, rental, leasing, loan, consignment stock, sale-or-return pending acceptance, or supply with an operator. These are supplies, but they are not sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase, so the exclusion in regulation 3(5) does not bite. A supplier who hires out equipment can be a person 'having control' of it under regulation 3(3)(b) and is then within PUWER to the extent of that control. HSE's own overview describes PUWER as reaching businesses 'involved in providing work equipment for others to use (eg for hire)'.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DISTRIBUTOR
The distributor, acting only as seller, is outside PUWER. It does not owe the PUWER duties to the purchaser or to the purchaser's employees. Those duties sit with the purchaser as employer (regulation 3(2)) and with anyone who has control of the equipment or of its use at the purchaser's premises (regulation 3(3)(b)).

=====================================================================
5. SUPPORTING GUIDANCE (consistent with the statutory text)
=====================================================================
- HSE priced guidance on PUWER: 'The Regulations do NOT apply to those who have supplied or sold equipment. It's up to the purchaser of equipment to make sure that it is specified, installed and used so that it does not present a risk to those at work.'
- HSE L22 (Fourth edition, 2014), ACOP and guidance: 'The Regulations, commonly known as PUWER, place duties on people and companies who own, operate or have control over work equipment. PUWER also places responsibilities on businesses and organisations whose employees use work equipment, whether owned by them or not.'
- HSE PUWER overview: duties fall on those who 'own, operate or have control over work equipment', and on businesses 'involved in providing work equipment for others to use (eg for hire)'.
- HSE L22 reproduces regulation 3 with paragraph (5) in the same words quoted in section 3.

=====================================================================
6. WHAT THE EXCLUSION DOES NOT DO — FOUR WAYS A DISTRIBUTOR CAN STILL BE IN SCOPE
=====================================================================
A distributor that sells equipment is not thereby immune from PUWER. The exclusion operates only on the sale. Each of the following is a separate basis of duty and should be checked against the distributor's actual operations:

(i) EMPLOYER CAPACITY (regulation 3(2)). The distributor is an employer. Any work equipment it provides for use by its own employees — warehouse forklifts, pallet trucks, ladders, hand tools, demonstration units, pressure washers, compressors, vehicle lifts, workshop equipment — is fully within PUWER, with all the regulation 4–35 duties (suitability, maintenance, inspection, guarding, information, instruction, training, marking).

(ii) RELEVANT SELF-EMPLOYED PERSON (regulation 3(3)(a)). A sole-trader distributor who uses work equipment at work is within scope in that capacity.

(iii) PERSON HAVING CONTROL (regulation 3(3)(b)). To the extent of its control, PUWER applies to a person who controls the equipment, controls a person who uses/supervises/manages its use, or controls the way it is used. Risk areas for a distributor: a demonstration or hire fleet; installation, commissioning or setting-up at the customer's site; retained servicing, maintenance or inspection obligations; equipment placed on consignment or sale-or-return in a customer's premises; retained rights to enter, inspect, modify or decommission. A distribution agreement that reserves such rights is evidence of control and should be reviewed.

(iv) NON-SALE SUPPLY. As set out in section 4, hire, rental, leasing and loan are outside regulation 3(5). A distributor with any rental or lease line of business is a potential regulation 3(3)(b) duty holder for that equipment.

=====================================================================
7. WHAT APPLIES TO THE DISTRIBUTOR INSTEAD (outside PUWER — flagged, to be verified separately)
=====================================================================
The sale exclusion in regulation 3(5) is not a statement that the distributor has no health and safety obligations at all. The following regimes are outside the scope of this opinion and must be checked separately before the distributor treats itself as clear:
- Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, section 6 — duties on designers, manufacturers, importers and suppliers of articles for use at work (safe design and construction, testing, adequate information, revision of information). This is the principal route by which supply-side duties reach a distributor, and it is not displaced by PUWER regulation 3(5).
- Product supply law for machinery in Great Britain. HSE's PUWER overview states that when providing new work equipment for use at work the provider must ensure conformity with the essential requirements of relevant product supply law — for new machinery, the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations — and must check conformity marking, manufacturer's details, Declaration of Conformity, instructions in English, and freedom from obvious defects. The version of that instrument in force on 2026-11-21 must be confirmed before it is cited.
- Any sector-specific supply regime applicable to the particular equipment.

=====================================================================
8. VERSION AND CURRENCY RECORD FOR 2026-11-21
=====================================================================
Instrument: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, SI 1998/2306. Citation and commencement: regulation 1 — in force 5 December 1998.

Verification chain for regulation 3(5):
1. Current revised text, legislation.gov.uk body view, fetched 2026-11-23T00:07:02Z (sha256 b6d195f8b158...). Page carries: 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998.' Regulation 3(5) appears in the form quoted in section 3.
2. Point-in-time version at 2013-07-01, legislation.gov.uk (sha256 bbd05a874229...). Regulation 3(5) appears in identical words.
3. HSE priced guidance on PUWER (sha256 06914cc354f3...). Regulation 3(5) appears in identical words; guidance text states the Regulations do not apply to those who have supplied or sold equipment.
4. HSE L22, Safe use of work equipment, Fourth edition 2014 (sha256 e724bb336efd...). Regulation 3(5) appears in identical words.

Conclusion on currency: the sale exclusion in regulation 3(5) has been textually stable from 1998 to the latest revised text and is unaffected by the only amendment visible in regulation 3 (the 'relevant self-employed person' change in paragraph (3)(a)). No amendment to regulation 3(5) was identified that would be in force on 2026-11-21.

Residual limitation, stated honestly: the current text was fetched on 2026-11-23, two days after the stated date of 2026-11-21. The position 'as in force on 2026-11-21' is therefore inferred from the latest revised text plus the 'no known outstanding effects' statement, not read directly from a point-in-time snapshot of that exact date. Before relying on this in a contested matter, pull the legislation.gov.uk point-in-time view for 2026-11-21 and re-confirm regulation 3(5) verbatim. The conclusion is very unlikely to change, because a change would require an amending instrument affecting regulation 3(5) made and in force within that two-day window.

=====================================================================
9. PRACTICAL ACTIONS FOR THE DISTRIBUTOR (record these)
=====================================================================
1. Classify each transaction: sale / agreement for sale / hire-purchase (excluded by regulation 3(5)) versus hire, rental, lease, loan or consignment (NOT excluded). Record the classification per contract, not per customer.
2. Where any transaction is hire/rental/lease/loan/consignment, or where the distributor installs, commissions, services, maintains, inspects or retains rights to enter or modify, carry out a written regulation 3(3)(b) control assessment and record the extent of control and the resulting duties.
3. Confirm and document the employer-side PUWER compliance for the distributor's own staff and premises (equipment register, suitability, maintenance, inspection regime, training, information and instruction).
4. Keep the sale exclusion evidenced: the contract of sale or hire-purchase agreement, delivery documentation and invoice terms, so the capacity is demonstrable.
5. Do NOT extend the regulation 3(5) reasoning to product-safety obligations. Run the section 7 checks separately.
6. If the distributor operates in Northern Ireland, re-run this opinion against SR 1998/279.

=====================================================================
10. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER
=====================================================================
- The distributor is in Northern Ireland (different instrument; unverified here).
- The transaction is hire, rental, lease, loan or consignment rather than sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase.
- The distributor retains control of the equipment, of a person using it, or of the way it is used, at the purchaser's premises.
- The distributor is an employer whose employees use the equipment, or a relevant self-employed person using it at work.
- An amendment to regulation 3(5) in force on 2026-11-21 — none identified, and the point-in-time re-check in section 8 should close this off.

=====================================================================
11. LIMITS OF THIS OPINION
=====================================================================
This opinion covers only the question asked: whether PUWER 1998, as in force on 2026-11-21, applies to a distributor in respect of equipment supplied by sale, and what the scope clause says on that point. It is given for Great Britain on the stated assumptions and does not address Northern Ireland, product supply law, HSWA section 6, contractual allocation of risk, or the position of the purchaser.

question: Y77
answer:
## Answer

Under the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (SI 2002/2677), as in force on 2026-11-21, the suitable record of examinations and tests of local exhaust ventilation (LEV) plant, and of repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests — or a suitable summary of that record — must be kept available **for at least 5 years from the date on which it was made**.

- Statutory minimum: **5 years** (a floor, not a target; longer retention is lawful and may be required by other regimes or by company policy).
- The clock runs from **the date on which the record was made**, not from the date of the examination if different, and not from the date the plant is decommissioned.

## Authority and exact text

Regulation 9 ("Maintenance, examination and testing of control measures"), paragraph (4), COSHH 2002, geographical extent E+W+S:

> "(4) Every employer shall keep a suitable record of the examinations and tests carried out in accordance with paragraphs (2) and (3) and of repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests, and that record or a suitable summary thereof shall be kept available for at least 5 years from the date on which it was made."

Paragraph (2)(a) is the provision that puts LEV plant within paragraph (4): thorough examination and testing of LEV plant at least once every 14 months, or at the shorter interval in Column 2 of Schedule 4 where the LEV serves a process listed in Column 1 of that Schedule. Paragraph (3) brings non-disposable respiratory protective equipment into the same record-keeping duty. Paragraph (4) therefore covers LEV records, RPE examination records, and the repairs arising from either.

## Point-in-time confirmation (the "as in force on 2026-11-21" constraint)

The retention period is stable across every version of the instrument, so the answer does not turn on which consolidation is used:

| Version | Reg 9(4) retention | 
|---|---|
| Original as made (made 24.10.2002; in force 21.11.2002) | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |
| Point-in-time view at 2002-11-21 (legislation.gov.uk, /uksi/2002/2677/regulation/9/2002-11-21) | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |
| Latest revised version (legislation.gov.uk, /uksi/2002/2677/regulation/9) | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |
| HSE ACOP L5 (Control of substances hazardous to health), reg 9 quoted text | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |

The only amendment ever made to regulation 9 is textual amendment F1, which substituted paragraph (1) with effect from 6 April 2005 (SI 2004/3386, reg. 2(e)). The legislation.gov.uk page for section 9 states: "There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002, Section 9." Paragraph (4) has not been amended since it was made. Accordingly, any instrument in force on 2026-11-21 that purported to change the retention period would have had to appear as a textual amendment to reg 9(4); none is recorded. The figure of 5 years is therefore correct for 2026-11-21 on the text available.

## What the duty requires in practice

1. **Who.** "Every employer" who provides LEV plant (or non-disposable RPE) to meet reg 7. The duty is on the employer, not on the LEV examiner or contractor, although the employer may hold the record via a contractor.
2. **What.** A "suitable record" of the thorough examination and test, and of repairs carried out as a result. A "suitable summary" may be kept available **instead of** the full record — the regulation expressly permits the summary route.
3. **How long.** At least 5 years from the date the record was made. Diarise disposal no earlier than the fifth anniversary; do not destroy on plant replacement, site closure or contract change while the 5-year window is open.
4. **"Kept available" — meaning.** The regulation does not define the place or the audience; it requires the record or summary to be retrievable and producible on request. In practice that means: retrievable within the timescale an HSE inspector or local authority inspector allows under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, s.20 (inspectors' power to require production of, and take copies of, records), and accessible to employees and safety representatives who have a legitimate interest in the control measures protecting them. Electronic retention satisfies the duty provided retrieval is reliable and the record is legible and complete.
5. **No cessation-of-trading transfer duty.** Unlike reg 10(7)(c) for exposure monitoring records (which requires the employer, on ceasing to trade, to notify HSE and make monitoring records available to it), reg 9 contains no equivalent provision for LEV records. The 5-year retention duty simply runs its course; good practice is nonetheless to offer records to HSE or to a successor undertaking on cessation.

## Content of a suitable record (good practice, drawn from HSE guidance, not from the regulation itself)

The regulation does not prescribe fields. A record that will withstand scrutiny typically captures: unique plant/asset identifier and location; date of examination and test; the examiner's name and evidence of competence; methods and instruments used; measured results against the original commissioning/design specification (e.g. transport velocities, static pressures, capture/face velocity, duct integrity, air cleaner condition, fan condition, discharge position); defects identified; repairs carried out, by whom and when; the date the plant was returned to effective service; and the next examination due date.

## Do not confuse these periods

| Record type | Provision | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| LEV / RPE examination, test and repair records (or summary) | COSHH reg 9(4) | **at least 5 years from the date the record was made** |
| LEV thorough examination and test **frequency** (not retention) | COSHH reg 9(2)(a) and Sch 4 | at least once every 14 months, or the Sch 4 interval |
| Exposure monitoring records representative of identifiable employees' personal exposure | COSHH reg 10(5)(a) | at least 40 years from the date of the last entry |
| Other exposure monitoring records | COSHH reg 10(5)(b) | at least 5 years from the date of the last entry |
| Health records | COSHH reg 11 | separate and longer requirement — outside the scope of this answer; read reg 11 directly before relying on a figure |

The 14-month examination interval and the 5-year retention period are frequently conflated in secondary summaries. They are different duties in different paragraphs of the same regulation.

## Jurisdictional note

COSHH 2002 extends to England, Wales and Scotland (E+W+S). Northern Ireland has a separate instrument (Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations (Northern Ireland)) and is not governed by SI 2002/2677; if the plant is in Northern Ireland, the equivalent NI provision must be checked rather than this one.

## Source cross-check supporting the figure

The wording "at least 5 years from the date on which it was made" was confirmed identically in five independent retrievals: legislation.gov.uk point-in-time view (21.11.2002), legislation.gov.uk latest revised view, the original made PDF of SI 2002/2677, the FAO-hosted copy of the 2002 instrument, and the HSE ACOP L5 text quoting reg 9.

question: Y78
answer:
SAFETY OFFICER'S DETERMINATION — RIDDOR 2013, over-seven-day injury: reporting deadline

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER (bottom line)
=====================================================================
Where a person at work is incapacitated for routine work for more than seven consecutive days (excluding the day of the accident) because of an injury resulting from a work accident, the responsible person must send the report to the relevant enforcing authority in an approved manner **as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the accident**.

- Statutory basis: Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013 (SI 2013/1471), regulation 4(2).
- Outer limit: 15 calendar days, counted from the date of the accident.
- The 15-day figure is unchanged in the version in force on 2026-11-21 (see section 3).
- 'As soon as practicable' is a separate, earlier obligation that runs alongside the 15-day long-stop. Fifteen days is the outside limit, not a target.

=====================================================================
2. STATUTORY TEXT RELIED ON
=====================================================================
Regulation 4(2) (verbatim, point-in-time version at 06/04/2026):

  '(2) Where any person at work is incapacitated for routine work for more than
  seven consecutive days (excluding the day of the accident) because of an injury
  resulting from an accident arising out of or in connection with that work, the
  responsible person must send a report to the relevant enforcing authority in an
  approved manner as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the
  accident.'

Regulation 4(3): 'This regulation is subject to regulations 14 and 15.' (Carve-outs for cases already covered by other statutory reporting regimes; they do not alter the 15-day period for the ordinary case described in the question.)

Definitions in regulation 2 relevant to the trigger:
- 'consecutive days' includes any days which are not or would not have been working days.
- 'routine work' means work which a person might reasonably be expected to do, either under that person's contract of employment or, if there is no such contract, in the normal course of that person's work.
- 'responsible person' means the person identified in accordance with regulation 3 (for an employee at work, the employer; for a self-employed person in premises under someone else's control, the person in control of the premises; and so on).

Related provisions that sit around the same event:
- Reg 12(1)(c): a record must be kept of any injury to a person at work incapacitating them for routine work for **more than three consecutive days** (excluding the day of the accident) — the 'over-three-day' record, which is not a report.
- Reg 12(2)-(3): records kept for at least **three years** from the date the entry was made, at the place of work or the responsible person's usual place of business; extracts supplied to the enforcing authority on request.
- The single-report provision in the reporting procedure: where more than one reporting requirement applies, one report suffices if the stated conditions are met; otherwise the shortest applicable time limit governs.

=====================================================================
3. VERSION CHECK — TEXT IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21
=====================================================================
- legislation.gov.uk 'Changes over time' for SI 2013/1471 lists amendment points at 01/10/2013, 01/10/2014, 06/04/2015, 19/07/2015, 01/10/2015, 16/10/2015, 06/04/2017, 01/01/2018, 09/04/2018 and **06/04/2026**. The latest available point-in-time version is 06/04/2026, with the note 'There are currently no known outstanding effects'.
- 2026-11-21 falls after 06/04/2026 and there is no later amendment point, so the 06/04/2026 point-in-time text is the text in force on the date asked about.
- Reg 4(2) in the 06/04/2026 version is word-for-word identical to reg 4(2) in the 06/04/2015 point-in-time version. The 2026 amendment therefore did not touch the over-seven-day reporting period or the seven-day threshold.
- Corroboration from a regulator's current guidance (ORR, 'Guidance on RIDDOR 2013 regulations', authored 30 July 2025), paras 2.3-2.5: report 'as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the accident'; the day of the accident is not counted in the seven days; weekends, rest days and holidays are counted; 'more than seven consecutive days' means at least eight days.
- Caveat: legislation.gov.uk states that revised text may not be fully up to date. The conclusion here is robust to that caveat because both the 2015 and 2026 point-in-time texts carry the same 15-day wording.

=====================================================================
4. HOW THE DEADLINE IS COMPUTED
=====================================================================
Step 1 — Identify the accident date (day 0).
Step 2 — Count the seven-day test: exclude the day of the accident; count every subsequent calendar day, including days the person would not normally have worked (weekends, rest days, leave, holidays). The injury becomes an 'over-seven-day injury' once the incapacity has lasted **more than seven consecutive days, i.e. at least eight days** — earliest ascertainable on day 8 after the accident.
Step 3 — Compute the report deadline as 15 calendar days from the accident date (day of accident = day 0; deadline is the end of day 15). Calendar days, not working days; bank holidays do not extend it.
Step 4 — Submit in an approved manner (the form approved for the time being by HSE, or by ORR for rail/guided-transport activities) and, in any event, as soon as practicable — the earlier of the two obligations governs.

Worked example
  Accident: Monday 2 March 2026 (day 0).
  Day 1 = Tue 3 Mar; day 8 = Tue 10 Mar (earliest date on which the over-seven-day threshold can be established).
  Deadline: 17 March 2026 (2 Mar + 15 days).
  Practical window between certainty of reportability and the long-stop: 7 days (10 Mar to 17 Mar).

Second example (illustrating that non-working days count)
  Accident: Friday 6 November 2026. Days 1-2 = Sat 7/Sun 8 Nov (counted even though not working days). Day 8 = Sat 14 Nov. Deadline: 21 November 2026 (6 Nov + 15).

=====================================================================
5. DEADLINE TABLE — RIDDOR 2013 (for contrast and to prevent mis-application)
=====================================================================
| Event                                                        | Provision | Time limit |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----------|------------|
| Specified injury to a worker                                 | reg 4(1)  | As soon as practicable (reporting procedure) |
| Over-seven-day injury to a worker                            | reg 4(2)  | As soon as practicable and in any event **within 15 days of the accident** |
| Non-fatal injury to a non-worker (hospital treatment etc.)   | reg 5     | Reporting procedure (as soon as practicable) |
| Work-related fatality                                        | reg 6     | Reporting procedure; written report within 10 days |
| Dangerous occurrence                                         | reg 7     | Within 10 days (10 working days for the offshore sub-category) |
| Over-three-day injury (record only, not reportable)          | reg 12(1)(c) | Record made; kept 3 years |

=====================================================================
6. EDGE CASES AND INTERPRETIVE POINTS THE RESPONSIBLE PERSON SHOULD KNOW
=====================================================================
(a) 'As soon as practicable' bites first. The 15 days is a long-stop. If the over-seven-day threshold is crossed on day 8, the expectation is a report promptly thereafter; waiting until day 15 without reason is inconsistent with the duty.
(b) The 15-day clock runs from the accident, not from the day the threshold is crossed. The statutory language is 'within 15 days of the accident'. Because reportability is only certain on day 8, the effective working window is roughly seven days.
(c) Late-appearing incapacity. Where the injury initially appears minor and the incapacity only later extends beyond seven days, the statutory outer limit is still 15 days from the accident; in practice a report made promptly once the threshold is crossed is what the 'as soon as practicable' limb requires. Treat this as regulator practice, not as an extension of the text.
(d) Counting. Days the person would not normally have worked are counted. 'Routine work' covers the full range of normal duties, not just attendance — a person on light duties who cannot do their normal job is incapacitated for routine work.
(e) Record separately. Even where the injury never reaches eight days, an over-three-day incapacity must be recorded under reg 12(1)(c) and the record kept for at least three years.
(f) Single report. If the same accident also triggers another reporting requirement (e.g. a specified injury under reg 4(1) or a fatality under reg 6), one report may serve, but the shortest applicable time limit must be met — which in practice means reporting immediately and not waiting for day 15.
(g) Regulations 14 and 15 (applied by reg 4(3)) restrict reporting where the incident is already covered by another statutory reporting regime. Where they apply, the reg 4(2) duty is displaced; where they do not, the 15-day period applies unchanged.
(h) Territorial scope. RIDDOR 2013 extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own regulations; do not apply the 15-day figure there without checking the NI instrument.
(i) Enforcing authority. 'Relevant enforcing authority' is HSE or the local authority in most premises; ORR for activities within the Health and Safety (Enforcing Authority for Railways and Other Guided Transport Systems) Regulations 2006. The identity of the authority does not change the 15-day period; the 'approved manner' (form) differs.

=====================================================================
7. OPERATIONAL PROCEDURE (what the responsible person actually does)
=====================================================================
1. On the day of the accident, open an incident record: date, time, injured person, injury, whether a specified injury, whether the person is likely to be absent from routine work.
2. If a specified injury is present, report immediately under reg 4(1) — do not wait for the seven-day question to resolve.
3. Diarise day 8 from the accident date. On day 8, confirm whether the person has been incapacitated for routine work for more than seven consecutive days (counting non-working days, excluding the day of the accident).
4. If yes: submit the over-seven-day report in the approved manner immediately (online form for HSE-enforced premises; ORR's approved route for rail/guided transport).
5. Record the submission date/time and retain a copy. Confirm submission is on or before day 15 from the accident; if the long-stop is at risk, escalate and submit what is available — a prompt incomplete report is better than a late one.
6. Open/keep the reg 12 record (including the over-three-day entry if applicable) for at least three years.
7. If the person subsequently dies within one year as a result of the accident, a fatality report under reg 6 is triggered separately — the over-seven-day report does not discharge it.

=====================================================================
8. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
=====================================================================
- Assumes the incident is in Great Britain and not within a reg 14/15 carve-out.
- Assumes the standard employer/responsible-person duty applies (regulation 3).
- The statutory quotation is taken from the 06/04/2026 point-in-time version of SI 2013/1471, which is the version in force on 2026-11-21 on the publisher's timeline; the publisher's general caveat about currency is noted and does not affect the conclusion, since the 2015 and 2026 texts are identical on this point.
- Nothing here varies the answer: **15 days from the accident, and in any event as soon as practicable.**
