For 10 CFR Part 431 Subpart K as in force on 2026-11-21, the two tables named in the request state the SAME manufacture-date window:

- Low-voltage dry-type distribution transformers, §431.196(a)(2): manufactured on or after January 1, 2016, but before April 23, 2029.
- Liquid-immersed distribution transformers (including submersible distribution transformers), §431.196(b)(2): manufactured on or after January 1, 2016, but before April 23, 2029.

Expressed as an interval: 2016-01-01 (inclusive) through 2029-04-23 (exclusive) for both transformer categories.

1. VERBATIM TEXT — §431.196(a)(2) (low-voltage dry-type)

Introductory text preceding the table:

"(2) The efficiency of a low-voltage, dry-type distribution transformer manufactured on or after January 1, 2016, but before April 23, 2029, shall be no less than that required for the applicable kVA rating in the following table. Low-voltage dry-type distribution transformers with kVA ratings not appearing in the table shall have their minimum efficiency level determined by linear interpolation of the kVA and efficiency values immediately above and below that kVA rating."

Table caption as printed in the CFR: "Table 2 to Paragraph (a)(1)" (see anomaly note in section 4).

Table note: "All efficiency values are at 35 percent of nameplate-rated load, determined according to the DOE Test Method for Measuring the Energy Consumption of Distribution Transformers under appendix A to this subpart K."

2. VERBATIM TEXT — §431.196(b)(2) (liquid-immersed)

Introductory text preceding the table:

"(2) The efficiency of a liquid-immersed distribution transformer, including submersible distribution transformers, manufactured on or after January 1, 2016, but before April 23, 2029, shall be no less than that required for their kVA rating in the following table. Liquid-immersed distribution transformers, including submersible distribution transformers, with kVA ratings not appearing in the table shall have their minimum efficiency level determined by linear interpolation of the kVA and efficiency values immediately above and below that kVA rating."

Table caption as printed in the CFR: "Table 5 to Paragraph (b)(2)".

3. WHERE THE WINDOW IS STATED

In both paragraphs the manufacture-date window is stated in the flush regulatory text that introduces the table, not in a column inside the table. The tables themselves carry only kVA ratings and efficiency percentages (single-phase and three-phase columns). A reader looking for a "date column" inside Table 2 or Table 5 will not find one; the operative date language is the sentence quoted above in each case.

For orientation only (not part of the answer): the same section contains earlier-vintage tables whose text states other windows — §431.196(a)(1) covers "on or after January 1, 2007, but before January 1, 2016" for low-voltage dry-type, and §431.196(b)(1) covers "on or after January 1, 2010, but before January 1, 2016" for liquid-immersed. Those are outside the two paragraphs the request names and are mentioned only so the (a)(2)/(b)(2) windows are not confused with them.

4. ANOMALIES AND CAVEATS THE READER SHOULD KNOW

(a) Table caption anomaly. The table that implements §431.196(a)(2) is captioned in the CFR as "Table 2 to Paragraph (a)(1)", not "(a)(2)". The date language, however, sits in paragraph (a)(2) itself, so the identification of the window is unaffected. This is a codification/caption artifact, not an ambiguity in the dates.

(b) Editorial note (version risk). The eCFR text carries an editorial note: "At 90 FR 43371, Sept. 9, 2025, as required by the Congressional Review Act and Pub. L. 119-8, the Department of Energy removed the amendments to several sections in part 431 made effective on Dec. 23, 2024, at 89 FR 91163, Oct. 9, 2024. As of Sept. 9, 2025, the affected sections reverted to the Dec. 22, 2024 version." The text quoted in sections 1 and 2 above is the text as it stands in both the eCFR and the 2026 annual CFR edition after that reversion, and it is what the regulation states on 2026-11-21. If the 2029 end-date is material to a compliance decision, confirm against the Federal Register documents cited in the authority line of §431.196; this answer reports the codified text, not the litigation/CRA history behind it.

(c) End-date consequence, stated only as the text reads. Because the window closes "before April 23, 2029," a transformer manufactured on or after April 23, 2029 is outside the (a)(2)/(b)(2) windows. What standard applies to such a transformer is not answered here; the section contains additional tables (e.g., "Table 3 to Paragraph (a)(3)" and "Table 7 to Paragraph (b)(4)") that are outside the scope of this request.

question: Y98
answer:
## Answer

**Provision:** regulation 28 of the Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002 (S.I. 2002/2665), headed *Information to be provided on request*, in the original (as made) version — made 24 October 2002, laid before Parliament 28 October 2002, coming into force 31 January 2003. Extent: E+W+S.

**Nature of the duty:** the distributor must provide a **written statement** of the five matters listed in reg 28(a)–(e), in respect of an existing or proposed consumer's installation connected or to be connected to his network, to any person who can show reasonable cause for requiring the information — being the matters "which apply, or will apply, to that installation".

### Verbatim text (as made)

> **Information to be provided on request**
>
> **28.** A distributor shall provide, in respect of any existing or proposed consumer's installation which is connected or is to be connected to his network, to any person who can show a reasonable cause for requiring the information, a written statement of—
>
> (a) the maximum prospective short circuit current at the supply terminals;
>
> (b) for low voltage connections, the maximum earth loop impedance of the earth fault path outside the installation;
>
> (c) the type and rating of the distributor's protective device or devices nearest to the supply terminals;
>
> (d) the type of earthing system applicable to the connection; and
>
> (e) the information specified in regulation 27(1),
>
> which apply, or will apply, to that installation.

### The four items asked about, mapped to the sub-paragraphs

| Item asked about | Sub-para | Exact statutory words | What the distributor must state in practice |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Supply terminals** | 28(a) | "the maximum prospective short circuit current at the supply terminals" | The maximum prospective short-circuit current (PSCC) at the point of supply — the three-phase (or single-phase) fault level in kA, as the maximum the network can deliver at those terminals. It is the *maximum* prospective value, not the measured or typical value. |
| **Earth fault path** | 28(b) | "for low voltage connections, the maximum earth loop impedance of the earth fault path outside the installation" | The maximum earth fault loop impedance (in ohms) of the return path **external to the consumer's installation** — i.e. the distributor's own contribution (Z_e / Z_s external), not the whole-installation loop impedance. Expressly confined to low voltage connections. |
| **Nearest protective devices** | 28(c) | "the type and rating of the distributor's protective device or devices nearest to the supply terminals" | Type (e.g. the standard/technology of the device — fuse or circuit breaker, and its standard/characteristic) **and** rating (current rating / setting) of the distributor's cut-out or other device nearest the supply terminals. "Or devices" covers more than one where the design uses several. |
| **Earthing system** | 28(d) | "the type of earthing system applicable to the connection" | The earthing arrangement type for that connection (e.g. TN-S, TN-C-S, TT), as the distributor's system applies to that connection. |

### Fifth item — do not omit it

The duty is not confined to the four matters in the question. Reg 28(e) additionally requires the written statement to include "the information specified in regulation 27(1)", namely the supply declaration — the number of phases, the frequency and the voltage at which it is proposed to supply electricity, and the extent of the permitted variations thereto. A statement answering only (a)–(d) would be an incomplete discharge of reg 28.

### Conditions and limits that attach to the duty

- **Who may ask:** "any person who can show a reasonable cause for requiring the information" — the beneficiary is not limited to the consumer or the installation's owner; the threshold is reasonable cause, which the question presupposes is met.
- **What it covers:** both an **existing** and a **proposed** consumer's installation, provided it is connected or is to be connected to the distributor's network. Reg 28 draws no distinction in content between the two; the closing words ("which apply, or will apply") accommodate a proposed connection.
- **Form:** a **written statement**. No prescribed form, template, certificate or drawing is required by the regulation.
- **No time limit** for provision and **no fee** is specified in reg 28 as made. (A distributor may have separate charging/timing arrangements, but they are not in this regulation and must not be presented as if they were.)
- **No unit prescription:** the regulation names the quantities, not the units; kA and ohms are the conventional engineering units for (a) and (b).
- **Only (b) is expressly limited to low voltage.** Paragraphs (a), (c), (d) and (e) are unqualified as to voltage. For a low-voltage connection all five apply.

### Version boundary — why this is the 'as made' answer

The 'Original (As made)' King's Printer version carries reg 28 in exactly the words above. The textual-amendment table for the instrument records amendments only to **regulation 1(5)** — by S.I. 2006/1521 (1.10.2006), S.I. 2009/639 (6.4.2009) and S.I. 2012/2400 (19.9.2012). Regulation 28 itself is unamended, and the text of reg 28 in the 2006, 2009 and 2012 snapshots is identical to the as-made text. So the answer does not turn on the version cutoff; relying on the as-made text is both required by the constraint and substantively safe.

### Caveats to record honestly

1. The **definition of 'low voltage'** in reg 2 was not among the passages retrieved, so it is not quoted here. It must be read from reg 2 of the as-made instrument before the answer is relied on for the boundary case (the conventional ESQCR definition is a band with an upper limit of 1,000 V a.c. / 1,500 V d.c., but that is stated here as recollection, **not** as verified text).
2. The text of **reg 27(1)** quoted in the project material is the supply-declaration provision (number of phases, frequency, voltage, permitted variations); its paragraph number is taken from the reg 28(e) cross-reference rather than from a numbered heading in the retrieved snippet.
3. Reg 28 creates no duty to supply a schematic, a network diagram, or plant ratings beyond those enumerated.

### Illustrative compliant statement (specimen structure — not statutory wording)

A distributor's response satisfying reg 28 for an LV connection would read, in substance:

1. Maximum prospective short-circuit current at the supply terminals: …… kA (three-phase/single-phase as applicable).
2. Maximum earth loop impedance of the earth fault path outside the installation: …… Ω.
3. Distributor's protective device nearest the supply terminals: type ……, rating …… A.
4. Type of earthing system applicable to the connection: …… (e.g. TN-C-S).
5. Supply declaration under reg 27(1): number of phases ……; frequency …… Hz; voltage …… V; permitted variations …….

The values in lines 1–4 are the distributor's own network characteristics for that connection; they are stated as maxima because reg 28 requires the maximum prospective short-circuit current and the maximum earth loop impedance.

question: Y99
answer:
ANSWER

Under 29 CFR 1910.110, the minimum rated working pressure for valves, fittings, and accessories connected directly to an LP-Gas container — expressly including primary shutoff valves — is 250 p.s.i.g. (about 1.72 MPa).

Controlling text (§ 1910.110(b)(7)(i), paragraph headed 'Container valves and container accessories'):

  '(i) Valves, fittings, and accessories connected directly to the container including primary shutoff valves, shall have a rated working pressure of at least 250 p.s.i.g. and shall be of material and design suitable for LP-Gas service. Cast iron shall not be used for container valves, fittings, and accessories. This does not prohibit the use of container valves made of malleable or nodular iron.'

250 psig is a FLOOR, not a target. 'At least 250 p.s.i.g.' means a component rated exactly 250 psig complies, but any component that may see more than 250 psig in service (high-vapor-pressure product, high ambient, pump discharge, regulator inlet manifold) must be rated for the maximum pressure to which it can be subjected.

1. WHAT THE REQUIREMENT COVERS (scope of (b)(7)(i))
- Every valve, fitting, and accessory whose pressure boundary is directly exposed to container contents: container/service valves, primary shutoff valves (liquid and vapor), filler valves and filling connections, excess-flow valves, back-pressure check valves, internal valves, liquid-level gauge bodies and rotogauge fittings, plugs, adapters, nipples, unions, bushings, elbows/tees at the container, and the first length of hose/pigtail where it is connected directly to the container valve (hose has its own additional burst requirement — see §5).
- It applies across the section: the same 250 psig floor is repeated for cylinder systems (container valves and accessories), for container fittings, for pumps and accessory equipment, for dispensing devices, and for manifolds/fittings connecting containers to regulator inlets. There is no container-size, liquid-vs-vapor, or occupancy-based exception to the 250 psig figure in the basic rule.

2. MATERIAL/DESIGN CONDITIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THE PRESSURE RATING
- 'Suitable for LP-Gas service' is a separate requirement from the pressure rating; both must be met.
- Gray cast iron is prohibited for container valves, fittings, and accessories. Malleable iron and nodular (ductile) iron container valves are permitted.
- Valve seats, packing, gaskets, and diaphragms must be resistant to LP-Gas.
- Fittings must be steel, malleable iron, or brass rated at least 250 psig; cast iron pipe fittings (ells, tees, unions) are prohibited.

3. THINGS THE FIGURE IS NOT
- It is not a hydrostatic test pressure and not a burst pressure. Test pressure (proof/leak test after assembly at not less than normal operating pressure) and burst requirements are separate provisions.
- It is not the container design pressure. Container design pressure and safety-relief start-to-discharge settings are governed by other provisions and Table H-26 (e.g., 110%/125% relationships for older ASME/API-ASME code containers); relief valves are excluded from the 'shutoff valve close to the container' rule but are not exempted from being suitable for LP-Gas service.
- It is not a substitute for the 'designed for not less than the maximum pressure to which they may be subjected' language that applies to shutoff valves generally.

4. WHY 250 psig IS THE RIGHT ORDER OF MAGNITUDE
Commercial propane's vapor pressure at 100 °F is on the order of 180–210 psig depending on product and grade, and rises further at higher ambient or for higher-vapor-pressure LP-Gas mixtures. 250 psig therefore gives margin at ordinary ambient temperatures while remaining a single, simple procurement floor; where the product or the installation can exceed it, the 'at least' language plus the 'maximum pressure to which subjected' language drives the rating higher.

5. ADJACENT 250 psig FLOORS IN THE SAME SECTION (do not confuse them with the container-connection rule, but they should be applied together)
- Container valves and accessories (cylinder systems): rated working pressure at least 250 psig, suitable for LP-Gas service.
- Shutoff valves (liquid or gas) that may be subjected to container pressure: rated working pressure at least 250 psig.
- Fittings: minimum working pressure 250 psig; steel, malleable iron, or brass; no cast iron pipe fittings.
- Pumps and accessory equipment: accessories minimum rated working pressure 250 psig; positive-displacement pumps need pressure-actuated bypass.
- Dispensing devices: meters, vapor separators, valves, and fittings designed for a minimum working pressure of 250 psig.
- Manifolds and fittings connecting containers to pressure-regulator inlets: designed for at least 250 psig service pressure.
- Hose subject to container pressure: working pressure at least 250 psig, and bursting pressure not less than 1,250 psig.
- Hose and hose connections on the low-pressure side of the regulator: bursting pressure not less than 125 psig or five times the set pressure of the protecting relief device, whichever is higher.

6. PROCUREMENT / SPECIFICATION LANGUAGE (drop-in)
'All valves, fittings, and accessories connected directly to the LP-Gas container, including primary shutoff valves, shall be rated for a minimum working pressure of 250 psig (1.72 MPa) LP-Gas service. Bodies: steel, brass, malleable iron, or nodular iron; gray cast iron prohibited. Seats, packing, gaskets, and diaphragms shall be resistant to LP-Gas. Fittings shall be steel, malleable iron, or brass, minimum 250 psig working pressure; cast iron pipe fittings (ells, tees, unions) prohibited. Components that can be subjected to pressures above 250 psig shall be rated for the maximum pressure to which they may be subjected. Where hose is subject to container pressure: minimum 250 psig working pressure and minimum 1,250 psig burst.'

7. CURRENCY CHECK FOR THE 2026-11-21 DATE
The quoted sentence is identical in the 2010, 2021, and 2025 printed CFR editions of 29 CFR 1910.110 and in the eCFR 'current' text retrieved 2026-11-23 (after the target date), so no intervening amendment changed the 250 psig figure between the editions checked and 2026-11-21. To re-verify at any future date: eCFR point-in-time query, Title 29, Subtitle B, Chapter XVII, Part 1910, Subpart H, § 1910.110, date 2026-11-21, read the paragraph headed 'Container valves and container accessories,' subparagraph (i). If a later amendment ever changes the number, the amended figure governs; nothing in the sources reviewed suggests one.

BOTTOM LINE: 250 psig (1.72 MPa) minimum rated working pressure, per 29 CFR 1910.110(b)(7)(i), with the accompanying prohibitions on cast iron and the requirement that materials and design be suitable for LP-Gas service.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 250 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title29-vol5/pdf/cfr-2025-title29-vol5-sec1910-110.pdf and 125 on ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-b/chapter-xvii/part-1910/subpart-h/section-1910.110. The first reads: "(g)(1) Hose shall be designed for a working pressure of at least 250 p.s.i.g."

question: Y100
answer:
## Answer

**500 psig** (500 p.s.i.g.; approximately 3,447 kPa gauge) is the maximum permitted start-to-discharge pressure setting for a hydrostatic relief valve installed between each pair of shut-off valves on LP-Gas liquid piping under 29 CFR 1910.110.

Governing provision: **29 CFR 1910.110(b)(10)(xii)** (Storage containers — safety relief devices — hydrostatic relief valves).

### Controlling text

> "(xii) A hydrostatic relief valve shall be installed between each pair of shut-off valves on liquefied petroleum gas liquid piping so as to relieve into a safe atmosphere. **The start-to-discharge pressure setting of such relief valves shall not be in excess of 500 p.s.i.g.** The minimum setting on relief valves installed in piping connected to other than DOT containers shall not be lower than 140 percent of the container relief valve setting and in piping connected to DOT containers not lower than 400 p.s.i.g. The start-to-discharge pressure setting of such a relief valve, if installed on the discharge side of a pump, shall be greater than the maximum pressure permitted by the recirculation device in the system."

### Basis for the 2026-11-21 in-force date

- The identical sentence appears in the eCFR current text of 29 CFR 1910.110 (retrieved 2026-11-23, i.e., two days after the cited in-force date), and verbatim in the bound CFR volumes for 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2025 (title 29, vol. 5, § 1910.110), plus the 2025 XML.
- The figure has therefore been textually unchanged across more than a decade of annual editions and across the cited date; no Federal Register amendment altering 1910.110(b)(10)(xii) is reflected in any edition examined.
- The requirement is stated directly in the OSHA rule text, not solely by incorporation by reference; the NFPA 58 editions referenced elsewhere in 1910.110 do not displace the 500 psig ceiling stated in (b)(10)(xii).

### The three-part setting envelope (apply all three)

1. **Ceiling (this ask): ≤ 500 psig** start-to-discharge, always.
2. **Floor, non-DOT container piping: ≥ 140% of the container relief valve setting.** Because the ceiling in item 1 is absolute, a non-DOT container relief setting above 500 ÷ 1.40 = **357.1 psig** would make the floor exceed the ceiling — such a combination is not achievable within 1910.110(b)(10)(xii) and requires redesign (e.g., lower container relief setting or a different isolation arrangement), not a setting above 500 psig.
3. **Floor, DOT-container piping: ≥ 400 psig.** A workable band of 400–500 psig exists for this case.
4. **Pump discharge special case:** if the valve is on the discharge side of a pump, its setting must also be **greater than the maximum pressure permitted by the recirculation device**. If that recirculation pressure exceeds 500 psig, the design must be changed (recirculation/bypass set lower); the 500 psig maximum is not waived by the pump clause.

### Practical selection guidance

- Select the lowest setting within the applicable band that satisfies the floors in items 2–4, since a lower setting gives earlier protection of the isolated liquid segment against thermal expansion.
- Verify the selected setting does not exceed the rated working pressure of any component in the isolated segment (valves subject to container pressure are required to be rated at least 250 psig; piping and fittings may be rated higher or lower).
- Discharge must terminate to a safe atmosphere; 1910.110(b)(10)(xiii) prohibits terminating in or beneath any building except for the enumerated relief devices.
- Unit conversion for SI documentation: 500 psig × 6.894757 = 3447.4 kPa gauge (≈ 3.45 MPa gauge). State the primary value in psig to match the rule text.

### Notes and limits of this answer

- This is the regulatory maximum, not a recommended setting; a system-specific value must satisfy all four conditions above and any stricter manufacturer or consensus-standard requirement.
- The answer addresses the liquid-piping hydrostatic relief valves of 1910.110(b)(10)(xii). It does not apply to vaporizer-section hydrostatic relief valves, which have a different rule (not less than 250 psig, set to protect the components involved), nor to container safety relief devices.

question: Y101
answer:
ANSWER

Under 29 CFR 1910.179, the rated load divided by the number of parts of rope shall not exceed 20 percent of the rope's nominal breaking strength.

GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim)

29 CFR 1910.179, "Ropes," subparagraph (2)(i) — the subparagraph immediately following "Sheaves" (1) in the hoisting-equipment paragraph:

  "In using hoisting ropes, the crane manufacturer's recommendation shall be followed. The rated load divided by the number of parts of rope shall not exceed 20 percent of the nominal breaking strength of the rope."

PROVENANCE AND AS-OF-DATE CHECK (as in force 2026-11-21)

- eCFR current text, 29 CFR subtitle B, ch. XVII, part 1910, subpart N, Sec. 1910.179 (retrieved 2026-11-23; sha256 3eb1ac03cbe8): "...shall not exceed 20 percent of the nominal breaking strength of the rope."
- GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 29 vol. 5, Sec. 1910.179, XML (sha256 c2f8a614b6bf) and PDF (sha256 85958c70e5f7): same sentence, 20 percent. The PDF carries the current annual-edition print stamp ("VerDate Sep<11>2014 14:18 Jan 15, 2026 ... 7-1-25 Edition"), i.e., this is the codified text in force on 2026-11-21 absent an intervening amendment.
- eCFR subpart-N page (sha256 7cd3410ef3d4): same sentence, 20 percent.
- The eCFR retrieval is two days after the 2026-11-21 as-of date, so it is corroborating rather than sole evidence; the 2025 annual edition supplies the same figure and no amendment altering this subparagraph appears in any rendering reviewed. Conclusion: 20 percent is the value in force on 2026-11-21.
- Citation-precision note: the operative sentence is quoted verbatim above so it can be located by text search. When transcribing into a compliance document, pin the lettered paragraph designator (the sheaves/ropes paragraph) against the current eCFR page rather than copying a secondary citation; the number 20 percent does not depend on that designator.

WHAT THE RULE MEANS ARITHMETICALLY

  rated load / (number of parts of rope) <= 0.20 x nominal breaking strength (NBS)
  => number of parts of rope >= 5 x rated load / NBS
  => equivalent design factor of 5 on nominal breaking strength.

Definitions that control the calculation (all from Sec. 1910.179(a)):
- "Rated load" = the maximum load for which the crane or individual hoist is designed and built by the manufacturer and shown on the equipment nameplate(s).
- "Rope" = wire rope, unless otherwise specified.
- "Parts of rope" = the number of rope lines (falls) supporting the load block as actually reeved.

WORKED EXAMPLE (check of the 20 percent ceiling)

Rated load 20,000 lb; 1/2 in, 6x19 IWRC, improved plow steel, NBS = 26,600 lb (from the rope certificate/catalog for that construction, diameter, grade and core).
  required parts = 5 x 20,000 / 26,600 = 3.76 -> use 4 parts.
  load per part at 4 parts = 20,000 / 4 = 5,000 lb.
  utilization = 5,000 / 26,600 = 18.8 percent <= 20 percent. OK.

APPLICATION PROCEDURE (what a safety engineer documents)

1. Record the crane/hoist rated load from the nameplate (1910.179(a) definition; nameplate marking requirement in the same section).
2. Record the reeving: number of parts of rope supporting the load block as installed, from the reeving drawing, not from the sales literature.
3. Record NBS for the exact rope: construction, diameter, grade, core, and lay, per the rope manufacturer's certificate. Do not substitute a generic table value for a different construction.
4. Compute load per part = rated load / parts; compare to 0.20 x NBS. If it exceeds 20 percent, add parts, increase rope size, or reduce the rated load — and confirm with the crane manufacturer, because the same subparagraph requires the manufacturer's recommendation to be followed in using hoisting ropes.
5. Re-verify after any reeving change, rope substitution, or rerate. The 20 percent figure is a ceiling, not a design target; a crane may be built to a higher factor.
6. Retain: rope certificate, reeving drawing, the calculation, and the nameplate rating. This is the evidence package for the 20 percent check.

BOUNDARIES AND CAVEATS (safety-engineering limits of this answer)

- Nominal vs. minimum breaking strength: the rule is written against NOMINAL breaking strength, a published catalog value. Minimum breaking strength (per the applicable rope specification) can be lower, so the realized factor on actual minimum strength can be below 5. Record which value the rope certificate reports.
- The formula assumes equal load sharing among parts. Sheave friction, fleet angle, and dead-end geometry mean some parts carry more; the 20 percent check is a floor, not a substitute for the manufacturer's reeving instructions.
- The provision is a design/application limit, not a rope-condemnation criterion; removal-from-service criteria for running ropes are in 1910.179(m) (monthly thorough inspection, deterioration causing appreciable loss of original strength).
- Scope: this is the overhead and gantry crane section. Mobile cranes (1910.180) and slings (1910.184) have their own, different strength provisions; do not cross-apply the 20 percent figure to them.
- Jurisdiction: OSHA state-plan states may adopt identical text or a stricter rule; verify the state plan for the specific worksite before relying on the federal figure alone.

FALSIFIERS (what would overturn this answer)

- A Federal Register amendment effective on or before 2026-11-21 changing "20 percent" in this subparagraph.
- An eCFR/CFR rendering in force on that date showing a different figure.
- A scope finding that the equipment at issue is not an overhead or gantry crane covered by 1910.179.
None of these was found in the reviewed text.

question: Y102
answer:
ANSWER

Under 29 CFR 1910.180(d)(2)(ii), as in force on 2026-11-21, the periodic inspection interval stated for crawler, locomotive, and truck cranes is 1 to 12 months, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.

GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim)

29 CFR 1910.180(d) Inspection classification
  (1) Initial inspection. Prior to initial use all new and altered cranes shall be inspected to insure compliance with provisions of this section.
  (2) Regular inspection. Inspection procedure for cranes in regular service is divided into two general classifications based upon the intervals at which inspection should be performed. The intervals in turn are dependent upon the nature of the critical components of the crane and the degree of their exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction. The two general classifications are herein designated as "frequent" and "periodic", with respective intervals between inspections as defined below:
    (i) Frequent inspection: Daily to monthly intervals.
    (ii) Periodic inspection: 1- to 12-month intervals, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.

CITATION: 29 CFR 1910.180(d)(2)(ii). Scope of the section is fixed by 1910.180(b)(1), which applies it to crawler cranes, locomotive cranes, and wheel-mounted cranes of both truck and self-propelled wheel type (plus variations retaining the same fundamental characteristics), powered by internal combustion engines or electric motors and using drums and ropes.

SOURCES CONSULTED AND DATE-STATUS CHECK

1. eCFR, 29 CFR 1910.180, current text, fetched 2026-11-23 — contains (d)(2)(ii) exactly as quoted. Because the fetch postdates 2026-11-21 by two days, the text shown is the text in force on the target date unless an amendment took effect in that 48-hour window; the print-edition comparison below rules that out.
2. GovInfo, CFR-2025-title29-vol5, sec. 1910.180 (revised as of 2025-07-01) — identical (d)(2)(ii) language.
3. GovInfo, CFR-2012-title29-vol5, sec. 1910.180 (7-1-12 edition) — identical (d)(2)(ii) language ("Periodic inspection: 1- to 12-month intervals, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.").
The provision has therefore read identically from at least the 2012 edition through the 2025 edition and the current eCFR text; no amendment between 2012 and 2026-11-21 alters it. The answer is not date-sensitive within that span.

WHAT THE PROVISION ACTUALLY REQUIRES (safety-engineer reading)

- The regulation states a range, not a single fixed interval. "1- to 12-month intervals" is a bounded window; the employer selects the specific interval within it. It is not a flat annual requirement, and it is not employer discretion unbounded — the outside limit is 12 months.
- The selection within the range is governed by the sentence in (d)(2): intervals "are dependent upon the nature of the critical components of the crane and the degree of their exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction." A crane in severe service (high duty cycle, corrosive or abrasive environment, heat, continuous use) is expected to be inspected on the short end (approaching monthly); a crane in infrequent, benign service may be placed on the long end (up to 12 months). The basis for the chosen interval should be documented per crane.
- The manufacturer carve-out is part of the same sentence: "or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer." Where the manufacturer specifically recommends a periodic-inspection interval, that recommendation defines the interval and replaces the default range for that machine. "Specifically" matters — a general manual statement is weaker support than a stated interval tied to the model or to service conditions; the recommendation should be identified in the equipment file by document and section.
- "Periodic" is the regulation's own defined term (1910.180(d)(2)(ii)), distinct from "frequent" inspection (daily to monthly, (d)(2)(i)) and from "initial" inspection ((d)(1)). The request's use of "periodic inspection" maps directly onto this provision; no translation is needed.
- Do not confuse this with other interval requirements in the same section that run in parallel and are not displaced by the periodic interval, notably 1910.180(g)(1) (thorough inspection of all running ropes in use at least once a month, with a certification record of date, inspector signature, and rope identifier). A 12-month periodic inspection does not satisfy the monthly rope inspection.

COMPLIANCE APPLICATION (how to use the answer)

1. For each crane in the 1910.180(b)(1) scope, record the periodic inspection interval in the equipment file as either (a) a fixed interval between 1 and 12 months, with the component-criticality/exposure basis stated, or (b) the manufacturer's specifically recommended interval, citing the manual and section.
2. Calendar the interval; the maximum permissible default is 12 months. Any interval exceeding 12 months is noncompliant unless it is the manufacturer's specific recommendation and is documented as such.
3. Keep the frequent-inspection program (daily to monthly, (d)(2)(i)) and the monthly running-rope inspection ((g)(1)) as separate line items; they are not subsumed by the periodic inspection.
4. Jurisdiction note: this is the federal text. Twenty-six states and two territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans that must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may differ in wording or in state-specific interpretive guidance; if the workplace is in a State Plan jurisdiction, verify the state counterpart of 1910.180(d)(2)(ii) before fixing the interval.

CAVEAT ON PRECISION

The honest answer to "what interval" is the range 1 to 12 months, qualified by the manufacturer's specific recommendation. Any single number asserted as "the" interval (e.g., "12 months" or "annually") would be a misstatement of the regulatory text.

question: Y103
answer:
ANSWER (29 CFR 1910.184, in force 2026-11-21):
- A sling hook must be removed from service if it has been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point.
- A sling hook must be removed from service if it has been twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook.
Both are 'more than' thresholds: a hook at exactly 15 percent opened or exactly 10 degrees twisted is at the limit and is not, by the terms of the text, required to be removed on that criterion alone.

1. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, as fetched from primary sources)

1.1 29 CFR 1910.184(e)(9)(ii) — alloy steel chain slings, deformed attachments:
"(ii) Slings shall be removed from service if hooks are cracked, have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook."

1.2 29 CFR 1910.184(f)(5)(vi) — wire-rope slings, removal from service:
"(vi) Hooks that have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook."

Both provisions are part of the removal-from-service criteria in section 1910.184 and are the provisions that state the numeric hook throat-opening and twist limits.

2. WHERE THE NUMBERS RESIDE (resolves the open question in the request analysis)
The 15 percent and 10 degree figures are express regulatory text in 1910.184 itself. They are not supplied by an incorporated-by-reference consensus standard (e.g., ASME B30.10), so no edition-of-the-consensus-standard question attaches to these two values. The answer does not change with any B30.10 edition.

3. EFFECTIVE-DATE VERIFICATION FOR 2026-11-21
Identical wording of both provisions was confirmed in every snapshot retrieved:
- eCFR current title 29, part 1910, section 1910.184 (fetched 2026-11-23T01:24:44Z, sha256 0b902b30fd4e)
- GovInfo CFR 2025, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910-184 (XHTML and XML; 2025 annual print, revised as of July 1, 2025)
- GovInfo CFR 2024, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910-184 (PDF)
- GovInfo CFR 2018, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910-184 (PDF)
- GovInfo CFR 2013, title 29 vol. 5, sec. 1910-184 (PDF)
Conclusion: the criteria have been unchanged across at least five annual prints spanning 2013 through the 2026 eCFR snapshot, so the values in force on 2026-11-21 are 15 percent and 10 degrees. Residual note for a records-grade citation: the nearest official snapshot to the target date is the eCFR 'current' point fetched 2026-11-23, two days after 2026-11-21; the fetched record shows no intervening amendment. If a point-in-time citation to 2026-11-21 is required for an enforcement file, re-run the eCFR point-in-time query for that date and confirm the same two sentences.

4. HOW TO APPLY THE CRITERIA (inspection procedure)

Step 1 — Establish the normal throat opening. Determine the throat opening of the hook in its normal (unopened) condition, measured at the narrowest point of the throat, i.e., the minimum distance across the throat between the hook point/tip and the inside of the bowl, measured in the plane of the hook. Use the hook manufacturer's published dimension for the same model and size, or measure an unused hook of the same model and size. Record the value as T_normal.

Step 2 — Measure the in-service throat. Measure the same dimension, at the same narrowest point, on the hook being inspected. Record as T_now.

Step 3 — Compute percent opened:
    percent opened = (T_now - T_normal) / T_normal x 100
Remove from service if percent opened > 15.
Worked example: T_normal = 2.000 in. 15 percent of 2.000 in = 0.300 in, so the 15 percent limit corresponds to T_now = 2.300 in. Removal is required when T_now is greater than 2.300 in; a hook measuring exactly 2.300 in is at, not beyond, the limit.

Step 4 — Measure twist. Establish the plane of the unbent hook — the plane containing the shank axis and the bowl of the hook, as it would lie on a flat reference surface with the shank straight. Measure the angular deviation of the hook point/tip out of that plane (a straightedge along the shank plus an angle gauge, or a surface plate and dial indicator with the chord/height converted to degrees). Remove from service if the deviation is more than 10 degrees.

Step 5 — Independent removal triggers. The throat and twist criteria are not the only hook triggers in the same provisions. Under (e)(9)(ii) a cracked hook on an alloy steel chain sling is removed regardless of throat opening or twist; under (f)(5)(v) end attachments that are cracked, deformed or worn require removal of the wire-rope sling. Do not let a passing 15 percent / 10 degree measurement override a crack or other listed condition.

5. SCOPE NOTES AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
- The two quoted provisions are written for alloy steel chain slings and wire-rope slings respectively. They are the provisions that state the hook throat-opening and twist numbers.
- Do not extend the 15 percent / 10 degree figures to metal-mesh sling handles. 1910.184(g)(9) sets handle-distortion criteria in different terms (slot depth increased more than 10 per cent, eye width decreased more than 10 per cent, distortion of either handle out of its plane) and states no throat-opening or twist percentage for hooks.
- The retrieved record did not include 1910.184(i)(9) (synthetic web slings). This answer does not assert its content; an inspector who needs the synthetic-web-sling hook criterion should read (i)(9) directly from the current eCFR text.
- These are the federal OSHA standards. State-plan states may adopt a different or additional rule; the request specifies 29 CFR 1910.184, so no state-plan variant is addressed here.
- The regulation does not define a latch as part of the throat; the measurement is of the load-bearing throat at its narrowest point. Latch presence does not alter the 15 percent / 10 degree criteria.

6. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE INSPECTION RECORD
Remove the sling hook from service when: throat opening exceeds 115 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point (i.e., more than 15 percent opened); or twist exceeds 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook; or the hook is cracked. Cite 29 CFR 1910.184(e)(9)(ii) for alloy steel chain slings and 29 CFR 1910.184(f)(5)(vi) for wire-rope slings.

question: Y104
answer:
ANSWER

0 °F. The permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings under 29 CFR 1910.184 and the maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings under the same section are the same number — 200 °F — so the fiber-core limit is 0 degrees Fahrenheit higher than the polypropylene limit.

1. GOVERNING TEXT (29 CFR 1910.184, in force 2026-11-21)

Source A — wire rope slings, § 1910.184(f)(3) 'Safe operating temperatures':
"Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F. When nonfiber core wire rope slings of any grade are used at temperatures above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F, recommendations of the sling manufacturer regarding use at that temperature shall be followed."
→ Fiber core wire rope sling permanent-removal temperature = 200 °F.

Source B — synthetic web slings, § 1910.184(i)(7) 'Safe operating temperatures':
"Synthetic web slings of polyester and nylon shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 180 °F. Polypropylene web slings shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 200 °F."
→ Polypropylene web sling maximum use temperature = 200 °F.

2. CALCULATION

Fiber core wire rope permanent-removal temperature:  200 °F
Polypropylene web maximum use temperature:          200 °F
Difference (fiber core − polypropylene):            200 − 200 = 0 °F

Units: both figures are stated in the regulation in degrees Fahrenheit ('°F'); no conversion is needed, and the difference is in °F. (In Celsius both limits are 93.3 °C and the difference is likewise 0 °C.)

3. VERSION CHECK FOR THE 2026-11-21 AS-OF DATE

The two provisions were compared across available editions and snapshots:
- eCFR 'current' snapshot, fetched 2026-11-23 (two days after the as-of date, therefore inclusive of any amendment with an effective date on or before 2026-11-21): both paragraphs read as quoted above.
- GovInfo, 29 CFR Ch. XVII, 7-1-25 edition (CFR-2025-title29-vol5), HTML/XML/PDF: identical wording.
- GovInfo, CFR 2024 edition (7-1-24): identical wording.
- GovInfo, CFR 2018 edition (7-1-18): identical wording.

Conclusion: the two temperature limits are textually identical in every version spanning the as-of date, so the result is insensitive to which of these snapshots is treated as controlling. Residual uncertainty is limited to an amendment published and effective in the narrow window between the eCFR snapshot and the as-of date; none is indicated, and the provisions have been stable across at least the 2018–2026 editions checked.

4. BOUNDARY SEMANTICS (why the answer is exactly 0)

Both provisions are phrased as 'in excess of 200 °F' — the same threshold with the same open-ended reading. Whether the 200 °F bound is read as open (prohibited only above 200 °F) or closed (prohibited at and above 200 °F), both limits move together, so the difference between the two stated limits is 0 °F under either reading. No interval convention can make the difference nonzero.

5. TRAPS CHECKED AND EXCLUDED

- 180 °F is the limit for polyester and nylon web slings, not polypropylene. Using it would wrongly give 20 °F.
- 400 °F and −60 °F in § 1910.184(f)(3) apply to nonfiber core wire rope slings and are manufacturer-recommendation triggers, not a removal temperature. Using 400 °F would wrongly give 200 °F.
- 1000 °F in § 1910.184(e) applies to alloy steel chain slings and is unrelated.
- −20 °F to +180 °F for natural and synthetic fiber rope slings (§ 1910.184(g)) is a working-load-limit temperature range, a different sling type and a different concept.

6. SAFETY-ENGINEERING NOTES ON USING THIS NUMBER

- A zero difference is a numerical coincidence of the rulemaking, not an equivalence of the two limits. They are different kinds of control: § 1910.184(f)(3) is a hard removal-from-service threshold (the sling must be permanently removed once exposed above 200 °F, with no manufacturer-engineering escape for fiber core), while § 1910.184(i)(7) is a maximum use temperature (the sling shall not be used above 200 °F).
- The failure modes differ. In fiber core wire rope, elevated temperature degrades the fiber core (strength and lubricant/cushioning function) with the wire outer strands masking the damage; in polypropylene web, the concern is softening, creep and eventual melting/charring of the web, which § 1910.184(i)(9)(ii) also captures as a removal-from-service condition.
- Because both limits sit at 200 °F, any workplace where slings see radiant heat, steam lines, preheated loads or hot-work adjacent operations should treat 200 °F as a common action level for both sling types: at or approaching 200 °F, fiber core wire rope is at its removal threshold and polypropylene web is at its no-use threshold simultaneously. There is no temperature band in which one of the two is permitted and the other is not.
- Ambient/contact temperature must be assessed at the sling, not at the furnace or process setpoint; the regulation gives no time-at-temperature allowance for either sling type.

7. HOW TO RE-VERIFY IN ONE PASS

Open 29 CFR 1910.184 on eCFR (or the GovInfo CFR volume covering the as-of date); go to paragraph (f)(3) and read the first sentence (fiber core = 200 °F); go to paragraph (i)(7) and read the second sentence (polypropylene = 200 °F); subtract. If either sentence no longer reads 'in excess of 200 °F', the answer changes and the computation must be redone with the amended figures and units as printed.

question: Y105
answer:
ANSWER (bottom line)

Under 29 CFR 1910.181 as in force on 2026-08-12, a derrick in regular service for five consecutive calendar months requires, at minimum:

  - 5 thorough rope inspections (one in each month of regular service), and
  - 5 certification records (one for each of those 5 inspections).

Minimum counts are 5 and 5. They are equal because each monthly thorough inspection carries its own certification record bearing that inspection's date. The count is per month of regular service, not per rope: one inspection event that covers all ropes in use satisfies the month, provided every rope is inspected and identified on the record. If ropes are inspected on different days, the number of records may exceed 5, but 5 is the regulatory minimum.

1. GOVERNING TEXT (quoted)

29 CFR 1910.181(g) Rope inspection:

  (g)(1) Running ropes. "A thorough inspection of all ropes in use shall be made at least once a month and a certification record which includes the date of inspection, the signature of the person who performed the inspection, and an identifier for the ropes which were inspected shall be prepared and kept on file where readily available. Any deterioration, resulting in appreciable loss of original strength shall be carefully observed and determination made as to whether further use of the rope would constitute a safety hazard. ..."

  (g)(2) Limited travel ropes. Particular care at equalizer sheaves, limited-travel sheaves, and saddles (inspection emphasis, not a separate interval).

  (g)(3) Idle ropes. "All rope which has been idle for a period of a month or more due to shutdown or storage of a derrick on which it is installed shall be given a thorough inspection before it is used. ... A certification record shall be prepared and kept readily available which includes the date of inspection, the signature of the person who performed the inspection, and an identifier for the ropes which were inspected."

  (g)(4) Nonrotating ropes. Particular care shall be taken in their inspection.

Related but distinct derrick provisions (do not change the 5/5 count on the stated facts):
  - (d)(1)(ii): frequent inspection (daily to monthly) and periodic inspection (1- to 12-month intervals or manufacturer's specification) for derricks in regular service.
  - (d)(4)(i)-(iii): derricks not in regular use — idle 1 month or more but less than 6 months: inspection per (d)(2) and (g)(3) before being placed in service; idle over 6 months: complete inspection per (d)(2) and (d)(3) and (g)(3); standby derricks: at least semiannual inspection per (d)(2) and (g)(3).

2. CALCULATION

Rule: one thorough inspection of all ropes in use per month, each with its own certification record (1910.181(g)(1)).

  Months in regular service:            5 (consecutive calendar months, per the stated facts)
  Minimum inspections per month:        1
  Minimum inspections over the period:  5 x 1 = 5
  Records per inspection:               1
  Minimum certification records:        5 x 1 = 5

Minimum monthly compliance schedule (each row is one inspection event and one record):

  Month of regular service | Inspection event (thorough, all ropes in use) | Certification record
  Month 1                  | 1                                                 | 1
  Month 2                  | 1                                                 | 1
  Month 3                  | 1                                                 | 1
  Month 4                  | 1                                                 | 1
  Month 5                  | 1                                                 | 1
  TOTAL                    | 5                                                 | 5

No month may be covered by the prior month's inspection: "at least once a month" is a recurring requirement, so an inspection performed in the month before the five-month window does not discharge any month inside the window. Conversely, if the derrick remains in regular service into a sixth month, a sixth inspection and sixth record become due; the figure of 5 is specific to a five-month service period.

3. MINIMUM CONTENT OF EACH CERTIFICATION RECORD (1910.181(g)(1))

Each of the 5 records must contain, at minimum:

  1. Date of inspection (the actual date the thorough inspection was performed).
  2. Signature of the person who performed the inspection.
  3. Identifier for the ropes inspected (e.g., rope ID/tag number, location on the derrick — hoist, boom, pendant, etc. — and the derrick/equipment identifier so the record is traceable).

The record must be "prepared and kept on file where readily available" — i.e., retrievable at the equipment/on site for review by the employer, the affected employees, and an OSHA compliance officer, not archived off-site. 1910.181(g)(1) sets no numeric retention period; do not represent any specific retention duration as a regulatory minimum. (The 2019 Federal Register document in the source set is an OMB Paperwork Reduction Act information-collection notice for the Derricks standard, OMB Control No. 1218-0222; it confirms the inspection/certification obligations and record disclosure on inspection but adds no interval or retention requirement.)

Minimum record template (repeat once per month):

  Equipment: Derrick ID ______   Location: ______
  Inspection type: Thorough rope inspection, 1910.181(g)(1) (monthly, running ropes in use)
  Date of inspection: ____/____/______
  Ropes inspected (identifier): Hoist rope ID ______; Boom/other ropes ID ______; ...
  Method/coverage: entire length of each rope in use, with particular care at limited-travel locations (g)(2) and on nonrotating rope (g)(4)
  Conditions observed (diameter reduction, broken wires and their distribution/concentration, worn outside wires, corrosion, core support loss, other): ______
  Determination: further use acceptable / restricted / rope removed from service (appreciable loss of original strength → safety-hazard determination recorded)
  Signature of person who performed the inspection: ____________________
  Record filed where readily available: ______ (date filed ____/____/______)

4. SCOPE CONDITIONS THAT WOULD CHANGE THE COUNT (state these when the facts differ)

  - Idle rope: any rope idle for a month or more because of derrick shutdown or storage must be given a thorough inspection before use, with its own certification record (g)(3). That adds inspections/records beyond the 5 and is triggered by the idle event, not by the monthly cycle.
  - Derrick idle 1 month or more but less than 6 months: inspection per (d)(2) and (g)(3) before being placed in service (d)(4)(i)); idle over 6 months: complete inspection per (d)(2) and (d)(3) plus (g)(3) (d)(4)(ii)); standby derricks: at least semiannual per (d)(2) and (g)(3) (d)(4)(iii)). None of these apply to a derrick in regular service throughout the five months.
  - Partial month of service: a month in which the derrick is in regular service for any part is treated as a month of service for scheduling purposes; the count remains one inspection per calendar month in which the derrick is in regular service.
  - Multiple ropes: the minimum stays at 5 inspection events and 5 records only if each event covers all ropes in use; splitting rope inspections across dates raises the record count (never lowers it below one per month).
  - Do not import crane requirements: 1910.180(g)(2)/(g)(3) and its 'appointed person' and semiannual standby-crane provisions, and 1910.180(g)(6)-style monthly certification of critical items by crane serial number, are crane provisions. 1910.181 is the derrick section; its rope rule is (g)(1) and it does not require an 'appointed person' for derrick rope inspection, only the signature of the person who performed it.

5. REGULATORY CURRENCY FOR 2026-08-12

The text of 1910.181(g)(1) quoted above is confirmed by the eCFR Title 29 snapshot of section 1910.181 (and the parallel Title 29 Subpart N page) retrieved 2026-11-23 — i.e., a snapshot taken after the 2026-08-12 date in force, showing the same wording as the 2020 printed CFR volume. The only other source in the set bearing on this section, the October 1, 2019 Federal Register document, is an information-collection (PRA) renewal notice that describes (g)(1) exactly as quoted and effects no change to the inspection interval or record content. No amendment effective between knowledge cutoff and 2026-08-12 that alters the monthly rope rule is evidenced; the analysis therefore applies 1910.181(g)(1) as quoted, and the answer of 5 inspections / 5 certification records holds.
cautions: The recompute vote compared nothing, so no figure in this answer was recomputed independently.
The answer gives 5 for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y106
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — 40 CFR § 82.156, technicians evacuating refrigerant from appliances with a full charge of more than 5 and less than 50 pounds for purposes of disposal; text as in force 2026-11-21.

HEADLINE ANSWER
- Start date: January 1, 2018.
- Record-retention period: three years.
- Governing text: § 82.156, the paragraph headed "Recordkeeping" numbered (3) within paragraph (a) (cited here as § 82.156(a)(3)); it sits immediately before Table 1 in the current text.

1. OPERATIVE TEXT (quoted verbatim from the sources below)
"(3) Recordkeeping. As of January 1, 2018, technicians evacuating refrigerant from appliances with a full charge of more than 5 and less than 50 pounds of refrigerant for purposes of disposal of that appliance must keep records documenting the following for three years:
(i) The company name, location of the appliance, date of recovery, and type of refrigerant recovered for each appliance;
(ii) The total quantity of refrigerant, by type, recovered from all disposed appliances in each calendar month; and
(iii) The quantity of refrigerant, by type, transferred for reclamation and/or destruction, the person to whom it was transferred, and the date of transfer."

ASK 1 — START DATE: January 1, 2018.
- The date is stated in the operative sentence itself ("As of January 1, 2018 ..."). It is a fixed calendar date, not a date computed from a rule's effective date and not the rule's publication date.
- It is corroborated by the section-wide applicability sentence, which uses the same date for the scope expansion: "Until January 1, 2018, this section applies only to evacuation of refrigerant from appliances containing class I or class II refrigerants. Starting on January 1, 2018, this section applies to evacuation of refrigerant from appliances containing any class I or class II refrigerant or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant, excluding paragraph (i) of this section which applies only to appliances containing class I or class II refrigerants until January 1, 2019. Starting January 1, 2019, the provisions in § 82.157 apply in lieu of paragraph (i) of this section."
- Compliance reading on 2026-11-21: the start date has long passed, so a technician performing a disposal evacuation on that date is subject to the duty and must create the records. There is no phase-in, delayed-compliance, or future applicability date attached to this paragraph.
- Provenance note: the CFR 2025 print edition carries the source note "[81 FR 82353, Nov. 18, 2016]" at § 82.156, i.e., the printed text derives from the 2016 Section 608 rulemaking, whose applicability date for this paragraph was January 1, 2018; the section's extension to non-exempt substitute refrigerants from January 1, 2018 is the change the request calls the post-2018 rule. The date quoted above is taken directly from the current text, so this provenance note is explanatory only and does not affect the answer.

ASK 2 — RECORD-RETENTION PERIOD: three years.
- Stated flatly as "for three years"; there is no charge-size or refrigerant-class variation inside the band, and no "until the appliance is retired" tail (that formulation belongs to a different record type — the >=50 lb full-charge/leak records, which run "until three years after the appliance is retired").
- Do not import the § 82.158 equipment-purchase rule ("All records must be kept for three years after each purchase"); that is a different record set. For the 5–50 lb disposal records the period is a plain three years.
- Clock trigger: the paragraph does not say when the three years starts. The defensible compliance rule is to retain each record three years from its creation (the date of recovery for the per-appliance record; the end of the calendar month for the monthly total; the transfer date for the transfer record). Where a single file holds several of these, retaining three years from the latest date documented satisfies every reading of the text. Record the retention basis in the facility's record-retention procedure so an inspector can see the clock.
- Records must be retained in a form the technician can produce on request; nothing in this paragraph prescribes paper vs. electronic, so either is acceptable provided it is retrievable for the full three years.

ASK 3 — THE POST-2018 RULE, AS AN APPLIED STEP SEQUENCE
Step 1. Identify the appliance and its full charge. Take the full charge from § 82.152 (amount of refrigerant the appliance holds when fully charged per the manufacturer, or the amount in it when last charged if that is unknown). Confirm the charge is strictly greater than 5 lb and strictly less than 50 lb.
Step 2. Confirm the purpose is disposal of that appliance (not merely service, repair, or maintenance). The paragraph is triggered by evacuation "for purposes of disposal of that appliance."
Step 3. Apply the post-2018 refrigerant scope: the evacuation and recordkeeping requirements of § 82.156 reach appliances containing any class I refrigerant, any class II refrigerant, or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant. Do not screen the job by refrigerant class; a non-exempt substitute refrigerant (e.g., an HFC or HFO blend) is in scope on the same terms as a class I or class II refrigerant.
Step 4. The duty-holder named in the text is the technician performing the evacuation. The technician (and, operationally, the technician's employer or the facility holding the records on the technician's behalf) must create and keep the three record elements:
  (i) company name, appliance location, date of recovery, and refrigerant type — per appliance;
  (ii) total quantity of refrigerant, by type, recovered from all disposed appliances in each calendar month;
  (iii) quantity, by type, transferred for reclamation and/or destruction, the transferee, and the transfer date.
Step 5. Retain all of it for three years (see Ask 2).
Step 6. Separately satisfy the evacuation level. The recordkeeping paragraph documents the evacuation; it does not set a vacuum level. For an appliance in this band that is not a small appliance, MVAC, or MVAC-like appliance, evacuation is to the levels in Table 1 under § 82.156(a). (Small appliances — 5 lb of refrigerant or less under the § 82.152 definition — are governed by § 82.156(b) and are outside this paragraph's charge band; MVACs and MVAC-like appliances by § 82.156(c)–(d).)

ASK 4 — CONSTRAINT: THIS IS NOT THE OLD CLASS I / CLASS II-ONLY SCOPE
- The pre-2018 sentence ("Until January 1, 2018, this section applies only to evacuation of refrigerant from appliances containing class I or class II refrigerants") is superseded text. It must not be used to answer a 2026-11-21 question.
- The recordkeeping paragraph itself contains no refrigerant-class limitation at all; its only qualifiers are the charge band (>5 and <50 lb) and the purpose (disposal). The section-wide applicability sentence supplies the refrigerant scope and, from January 1, 2018, that scope is class I + class II + any non-exempt substitute refrigerant.
- The only element of § 82.156 still tied to class I/class II is paragraph (i) (leak repair), which was class I/II-only until January 1, 2019, and from January 1, 2019 is superseded by § 82.157. Paragraph (i) is not the paragraph at issue here, so it must not be used to narrow the answer.
- Out of scope by the text's own terms: exempt substitute refrigerants (the applicability sentence reaches only non-exempt substitutes).

BOUNDARY AND INTERNAL-CONSISTENCY CHECK (values against the limits this memo states)
- Charge band is open at both ends: exactly 5 lb is outside (small-appliance regime) and exactly 50 lb is outside (the >=50 lb appliance regime). Only charges strictly between them are covered. Nothing in this memo places 5 lb or 50 lb inside the paragraph.
- The three-year retention is uniform across the whole >5–<50 lb band; no sub-threshold changes it.
- January 1, 2018 < 2026-11-21, so the requirement is operative on the as-of date; there is no pending-effective-date conflict with the answer.
- The retention figure (3 years) and the band (5, 50) are taken from the same quoted sentence, so no figure in this memo contradicts another.

SOURCES VERIFIED
- eCFR, 40 CFR § 82.156 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/part-82/section-82.156), fetched 2026-11-23T01:33:30Z, sha256 14ed35e228ee — contains the operative sentence verbatim.
- GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 40 vol. 21, § 82.156 PDF (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title40-vol21/pdf/CFR-2025-title40-vol21-sec82-156.pdf), fetched 2026-11-23T01:33:29Z, sha256 93d11d6e6440 — contains the same sentence verbatim, with source note [81 FR 82353, Nov. 18, 2016].
- eCFR Subpart F page and XML (sha256 c810faf83407, 3287a5298501) — same sentence; also confirms the separate "three years" and "until three years after the appliance is retired" formulations belong to other record sets.
Because the 'current' eCFR text (which covers 2026-11-21) and the 2025 print edition agree word for word, there is no indication that any 2020–2026 amendment changed either the January 1, 2018 start date or the three-year retention for this category.

DISCLOSED LIMITS OF THE VERIFICATION (do not affect the two values)
- Paragraph designation: the fetched text shows the sentence under a paragraph numbered "(3)" headed "Recordkeeping," positioned within paragraph (a) immediately before Table 1; it is cited here as § 82.156(a)(3) on that basis. The quoted sentence is reproduced verbatim so the citation can be confirmed against any print of the section regardless of numbering.
- The § 82.152 definitions of "small appliance," "full charge," and "exempt substitute" were not in the fetched passages; they are used only for the boundary discussion. Both requested values appear in the quoted operative sentence itself and do not depend on those definitions.
