question: Y108
answer:
COMPARISON OF 40 CFR 82.156 AND 40 CFR 82.158 RECOVERY/EVACUATION PERCENTAGES (AS IN FORCE 2026-11-21)

=====================================================================
1. SCOPE AND OPERATIVE PROVISIONS
=====================================================================
Authority: 40 CFR part 82, subpart F (Recycling and Emissions Reduction).

Two provisions contain the percentages keyed to compressor condition:

(A) 40 CFR 82.156(b) -- 'Small appliances.' Field recovery requirement. The
    relevant paragraph, (b)(2), reads:

    '(b) Small appliances. Before opening a small appliance or when disposing
    of a small appliance, persons must recover refrigerant, using a recovery
    and/or recycling machine certified pursuant to Sec. 82.158, according to
    the following conditions:
      (1) When using recovery equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993,
          recover 80 percent of the refrigerant in the small appliance; or
      (2) When using recovery equipment manufactured on or after November 15,
          1993, recover 90 percent of the refrigerant in the appliance when the
          compressor in the appliance is functioning, or 80 percent of the
          refrigerant in the appliance when the compressor in the appliance is
          not functioning; or
      (3) Evacuate the appliance to four inches of mercury vacuum.'

(B) 40 CFR 82.158(e) -- 'Small appliances.' Equipment certification
    requirement. The paragraph reads:

    '(e) Small appliances. Equipment used during the maintenance, service,
    repair, or disposal of small appliances must be certified by an approved
    equipment testing organization to be capable of recovering 90 percent of
    the refrigerant in the test stand when the compressor of the test stand is
    operational and 80 percent of the refrigerant when the compressor of the
    test stand is not operational, when used in accordance with the
    manufacturer's instructions under the conditions of appendix C, Method for
    Testing Recovery Devices for Use with Small Appliances.
      (1) Equipment manufactured or imported before November 15, 1993, will be
          considered certified if it is capable of either recovering 80 percent
          of the refrigerant in the system, whether or not the compressor of
          the test stand is operational, or achieving a four-inch vacuum when
          tested using a properly calibrated pressure gauge.
      (2) Equipment manufactured or imported on or after November 15, 1993, may
          also be certified if it is capable of achieving a four-inch vacuum
          under the conditions of appendix B1 of this subpart, based upon ARI
          Standard 740-1993.'

WHY THESE ARE THE CORRECT PAIRINGS (and not Table 1 / Table 2):
  - 40 CFR 82.156 Table 1 ('Required Levels of Evacuation for Appliances') and
    40 CFR 82.158 Table 2 ('Levels of Evacuation Which Must Be Achieved by
    Recovery and/or Recycling Equipment') express evacuation levels in INCHES
    OF Hg VACUUM, not percentages, and both tables are captioned 'Except for
    small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances.' They therefore cannot
    supply a 'recovery percentage' for either side of this comparison.
  - The only percentage figure in either section that varies with compressor
    condition is the 90/80 pair, appearing once as a field-recovery duty in
    82.156(b)(2) and once as a certification duty in 82.158(e).
  - The two sections are expressly linked: 82.156(b) requires use of a machine
    'certified pursuant to Sec. 82.158.' The certification figure in 82.158(e)
    is the bench-scale counterpart of the field figure in 82.156(b)(2).
  - Both sides therefore concern the same appliance class (small appliances)
    and the same equipment vintage (manufactured/imported on or after
    November 15, 1993), so the comparison is category-matched, not cross-class.

=====================================================================
2. THE FOUR FIGURES
=====================================================================
 Condition                          | 82.156(b)(2) field   | 82.158(e) cert.
                                    | recovery required    | test required
 -----------------------------------+----------------------+-----------------
 Compressor functioning /           |        90 %          |      90 %
 operational                        |                      |
 -----------------------------------+----------------------+-----------------
 Compressor not functioning /       |        80 %          |      80 %
 not operational                    |                      |

=====================================================================
3. ARITHMETIC
=====================================================================
Ask 3 -- functioning / operational:
   82.156(b)(2)  = 90 percent
   82.158(e)     = 90 percent
   Difference    = 90 - 90 = 0 percentage points

Ask 4 -- nonfunctioning / nonoperational:
   82.156(b)(2)  = 80 percent
   82.158(e)     = 80 percent
   Difference    = 80 - 80 = 0 percentage points

Signed convention used: (field requirement) minus (certification requirement).
Because the two are equal in both rows, sign convention is immaterial -- the
result is 0 under either ordering and under absolute difference.

=====================================================================
4. INTERPRETATION
=====================================================================
The zero result is structural, not coincidental. 82.158(e) was written to
certify equipment against the same performance that 82.156(b)(2) demands in the
field: a machine that cannot recover 90% of a test-stand charge with the
compressor running, and 80% with it stopped, is not certifiable, and an
uncertified machine may not lawfully be used on a small appliance. The two
sections are the test-method and field-obligation faces of a single 90/80
standard.

Two adjacent provisions do NOT change the answer but should be noted:
  - 82.156(b)(1) and 82.158(e)(1): pre-November 15, 1993 equipment carries a
    flat 80% (82.156(b)(1)) and an 80%-regardless-of-compressor-or-four-inch-
    vacuum alternative (82.158(e)(1)). These are outside the requested
    on/after-November 15, 1993 vintage and are not used.
  - 82.158(e)(2) permits post-1993 small-appliance equipment to be certified
    ALTERNATIVELY on a four-inch-vacuum performance basis. That is an
    alternative certification route, not a percentage, and does not displace
    the 90/80 figures in the opening text of 82.158(e). Likewise
    82.156(b)(3) allows evacuation to four inches of mercury vacuum as an
    alternative field method.

=====================================================================
5. VERSION CONTROL AND VERIFICATION PROCEDURE
=====================================================================
As-of date requested: 2026-11-21.

Sources relied on and their identifiers:
  S1  eCFR, 40 CFR 82.156 (current at fetch), fetched 2026-11-23T01:38:19Z,
      sha256 14ed35e228ee. Contains 82.156(b)(1)-(3) as quoted.
  S2  eCFR, 40 CFR 82.158 (current at fetch), fetched 2026-11-23T01:38:19Z,
      sha256 0ad41990e0f6. Contains 82.158(e), (e)(1), (e)(2) as quoted.
  S3  eCFR, 40 CFR part 82 subpart F (index), fetched 2026-11-23T01:38:19Z,
      sha256 c810faf83407. Duplicates the 82.156(b)(2) and 82.158(e) text.
  S4  GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 40 vol. 21, sec. 82.156 (7-1-25 edition),
      fetched 2026-11-23T01:38:18Z, sha256 93d11d6e6440. Prints 82.156(b)(1)-
      (2) identically.

Residual gap and how it is closed: S1-S3 are 'current' snapshots taken two days
after the requested as-of date. S4 is the 7-1-2025 annual edition, which
predates the as-of date. The two paragraphs at issue are identical in S1-S3 and
S4, and both trace to the 1993 rule; no amendment to 82.156(b) or 82.158(e)
between 2025-07-01 and 2026-11-23 is identified in the retrieved text. The
figures are therefore treated as the text in force on 2026-11-21, with the
following confirmation step recommended before any formal reliance:

  Confirmation step (5 minutes, eCFR point-in-time):
   1. Open https://www.ecfr.gov/on/2026-11-21/title-40/section-82.156 and
      .../section-82.158 (the eCFR 'on <date>' point-in-time URL form).
   2. Confirm 82.156(b)(2) still reads '90 percent ... functioning, or 80
      percent ... not functioning' and 82.158(e) still reads '90 percent ...
      operational and 80 percent ... not operational.'
   3. If either reads differently, substitute the point-in-time values and
      recompute: Ask 3 = 82.156 value minus 82.158 value (functioning row);
      Ask 4 = 82.156 value minus 82.158 value (nonfunctioning row).

=====================================================================
6. ANSWER STATEMENT
=====================================================================
For recovery equipment manufactured or imported on or after November 15, 1993:
  - 40 CFR 82.156(b)(2) requires recovery of 90% of the refrigerant from a
    small appliance when the appliance compressor is functioning and 80% when
    it is not functioning.
  - 40 CFR 82.158(e) requires small-appliance recovery equipment to be
    certified as capable of recovering 90% of the refrigerant in the test stand
    when the test-stand compressor is operational and 80% when it is not
    operational.

Differences:
  - Functioning / operational: 90% vs 90% = 0 percentage points.
  - Nonfunctioning / nonoperational: 80% vs 80% = 0 percentage points.

The two regulatory instruments impose numerically identical percentage
performance on the same equipment vintage and appliance class; the certification
test in 82.158(e) and the field obligation in 82.156(b)(2) differ in setting and
method (appendix C test stand vs. in-situ appliance) but not in the percentage
recovery demanded under either compressor condition.

question: Y109
answer:
## 1. Verdict

**No.** Under 10 CFR 431.97 as in force on 2026-11-21, the January 1, 2029 minimum efficiency standards for air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment do **not** apply to an air-cooled unit with a cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h. The 2029 tranche is expressly limited by its own scope language to air-cooled equipment at or above 65,000 Btu/h (and, separately, excludes double-duct air conditioners and heat pumps at any capacity).

## 2. The scope language that controls

Controlling text — 10 CFR 431.97(b), second sentence (verbatim; line-break hyphenation removed from the CFR page image):

> "Each air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment (excluding air-cooled equipment with cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h and double-duct air conditioners or heat pumps) manufactured on or after January 1, 2029, must meet the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in table 2 to this paragraph (b)."

Immediately preceding sentence, same paragraph (the 2023–2028 tranche, same exclusion):

> "Each air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment (excluding air-cooled equipment with cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h and double-duct air conditioners or heat pumps) manufactured on or after January 1, 2023, and before January 1, 2029, must meet the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in table 1 to this paragraph (b)."

Corroborating table caption and rows — Table 2 to paragraph (b):

> "Table 2 to Paragraph (b)—Updated Minimum Efficiency Standards for Air-Cooled Commercial Package Air Conditioning and Heating Equipment With a Cooling Capacity Greater Than or Equal to 65,000 Btu/h (Excluding Double-Duct Air Conditioners and Heat Pumps)"

with capacity bands and compliance dates:

| Cooling capacity | Subcategory | Supplementary heating type | Minimum efficiency | Compliance date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ≥65,000 Btu/h and <135,000 Btu/h | AC | Electric Resistance Heating or No Heating | IVEC = 14.3 | January 1, 2029 |
| ≥65,000 Btu/h and <135,000 Btu/h | AC | All Other Types of Heating | IVEC = 13.8 | January 1, 2029 |
| ≥65,000 Btu/h and <135,000 Btu/h | HP | All Types of Heating | IVEC = 13.4; IVHE = 6.2 | January 1, 2029 |
| ≥135,000 Btu/h and <240,000 Btu/h | AC | Electric Resistance Heating or No Heating | IVEC = 13.8 | January 1, 2029 |
| ≥135,000 Btu/h and <240,000 Btu/h | AC | All Other Types of Heating | IVEC = 13.3 | January 1, 2029 |
| ≥135,000 Btu/h and <240,000 Btu/h | HP | All Types of Heating | IVEC = 13.1; IVHE = 6.0 | January 1, 2029 |

Table 1 to paragraph (b) carries the same caption form ("Greater Than or Equal to 65,000 Btu/h") with January 1, 2023 dates and IEER/COP metrics.

## 3. Why this language controls

The operative sentence imposes three cumulative conditions, and the sub-65,000 Btu/h unit fails the first:

1. **Equipment scope.** The obligation attaches to "air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment" *as narrowed by the parenthetical*. The parenthetical is a definitional carve-out written into the duty-creating sentence itself, not a test-procedure or rating-condition caveat — equipment with cooling capacity below 65,000 Btu/h is outside the class to which table 2 is addressed.
2. **Manufacture date.** "manufactured on or after January 1, 2029."
3. **Standard level.** "the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in table 2 to this paragraph (b)."

The table independently confirms the same boundary: Table 2's caption states ">= 65,000 Btu/h," and no row of Table 2 has a capacity below 65,000 Btu/h — the lowest band is ≥65,000 and <135,000 Btu/h. There is therefore no "applicable" table 2 level that could be assigned to a sub-65,000 Btu/h unit; the exclusion in the sentence and the absence of any qualifying row in the table are mutually reinforcing, not alternative readings.

## 4. Where a sub-65,000 Btu/h air-cooled unit's standard actually sits

A sub-65,000 Btu/h air-cooled unit is not unregulated; it is regulated elsewhere in § 431.97 on a different compliance track. Two anchors in the same section:

- Paragraph (i): "Air-cooled, three-phase, commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment with a cooling capacity of less than 65,000 Btu/h and air-cooled, three-phase variable refrigerant flow multi-split air conditioning and heating equipment with a cooling capacity of less than 65,000 Btu/h manufactured on or after the compliance date listed in tables 18 and 19 to this paragraph (i) must meet the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in this paragraph (i)." (Table 18 rows run from June 16, 2008 and January 1, 2017; table 19 carries the updated SEER2/HSPF2 levels.)
- The <65,000 Btu/h entries in § 431.97 carrying **January 1, 2025** compliance dates at 13.4/14.3 SEER2 and 6.7/7.5 HSPF2 for Commercial Package Air Conditioning (and Heating) Equipment, split-system and single-package, plus the space-constrained (≤30,000 Btu/h) and small-duct, high-velocity (<65,000 Btu/h) classes.

So the practical consequence for the unit in question: its compliance date is **January 1, 2025** (or the earlier table 18 date, for the classes those tables govern), not January 1, 2029, and the metric is SEER2/HSPF2 (or SEER/HSPF under the legacy tables), not IVEC/IVHE.

## 5. Boundary and measurement notes

- **Exactly 65,000 Btu/h is inside, not outside, the 2029 tranche.** The bands read "≥65,000 Btu/h" and the exclusion reads "less than 65,000 Btu/h." A unit rated at exactly 65,000 Btu/h is therefore subject to the January 1, 2029 table 2 levels, not excluded. The answer above turns on "less than," so a unit at the boundary should be re-verified against its rated capacity, not assumed into the exclusion.
- **Capacity is the rated cooling capacity determined under the applicable test procedure** in subpart F (appendix A1 for the ≥65,000 Btu/h air-cooled classes per the compliance-certification/test-procedure table in § 431.96/431.97; appendices F/F1 for the <65,000 Btu/h three-phase classes). The 65,000 Btu/h comparison is made on that rated value, at the rating conditions those appendices specify — not on nominal or site-adjusted capacity.
- **Double-duct is a separate exclusion.** A double-duct air conditioner or heat pump is excluded from both table 1 and table 2 regardless of capacity; a double-duct unit at or above 65,000 Btu/h would still fall outside the 2029 sentence, but on the double-duct ground rather than the capacity ground.
- **Definitional check (§ 431.92).** If a particular sub-65,000 Btu/h product is not "commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment" within the § 431.92 definition at all, § 431.97 does not reach it and the 2029 question is moot. Either path yields the same answer — no 2029 obligation — but the reasoning differs, so the § 431.92 scope should be confirmed for the specific model family (particularly whether it is three-phase, space-constrained, small-duct high-velocity, or a VRF multi-split, each of which has its own paragraph and table).

## 6. Date-pinning of the text (ask 1)

The quoted language is taken from the eCFR text of 10 CFR 431.97 (fetched 2026-11-23T01:41:41Z, sha256 51a32539ebb1) and cross-checked against the GovInfo PDF of the **2026 edition of 10 CFR, volume 4 (1-1-26 Edition)**, § 431.97 (sha256 726075ed6cd1), which reproduces the same exclusion and the same Table 2 caption. The 2029 tranche derives from the DOE final rule at federalregister.gov/d/2024-08546. No amendment between 2026-11-21 and the 2026-11-23 fetch is reflected in the two sources; if a later-filed rule were to alter the sub-65,000 Btu/h carve-out, only that carve-out would be affected, and the answer would need re-running against the amended sentence — nothing in the sources retrieved suggests such a change.

## 7. Residual verification points

- Confirm the specific unit's rated cooling capacity is strictly below 65,000 Btu/h under the applicable appendix (the entire answer rests on that single comparison).
- Confirm the unit is not at exactly 65,000 Btu/h (which would flip it into the 2029 tranche).
- Confirm phase and product class, to identify the correct sub-65,000 Btu/h paragraph (paragraph (i) for three-phase; the January 1, 2025 SEER2/HSPF2 entries for the others) and therefore the correct compliance date to cite in lieu of January 1, 2029.

The first reads: "Table 8 to Paragraph (d)—Updated Minimum Efficiency Standards for PTAC Equipment type Category Cooling capacity Minimum efficiency Compliance date:"

question: Y110
answer:
DETERMINATION

No. Under 10 CFR 430.32 as in force on 2026-11-21, the energy conservation standards in that section do not apply to a refrigerator-freezer whose total refrigerated volume exceeds 39 cubic feet (1104 liters).

1. CONTROLLING SCOPE LANGUAGE

10 CFR 430.32, paragraph (a) heading and lead-in text (undesignated text preceding the paragraph (a)(1) table):

  "(a) Refrigerators/refrigerator-freezers/freezers. These standards do not apply to refrigerators and refrigerator-freezers with total refrigerated volume exceeding 39 cubic feet (1104 liters) or freezers with total refrigerated volume exceeding 30 cubic feet (850 liters). The energy standards as determined by the equations of the following table(s) shall be rounded off to the nearest kWh per year. If the equation calculation is halfway between the nearest two kWh per year values, the standard shall be rounded up to the higher of these values."

The operative clause, isolated:

  "These standards do not apply to refrigerators and refrigerator-freezers with total refrigerated volume exceeding 39 cubic feet (1104 liters) ..."

Text verification: this sentence appears identically in two independent retrievals — the eCFR current text of 10 CFR 430.32 (fetched 2026-11-23T01:44:49Z, sha256 0ac12a2943ec) and the GovInfo 2026 edition of the CFR, title 10, volume 3, sec. 430-32 (sha256 c513ae5fee1f). No divergence between the two sources on this sentence.

2. WHY THIS SENTENCE, AND NOT THE TABLES, CONTROLS

(a) Placement. The exclusion is in the lead-in text of paragraph (a), outside and ahead of the standards tables in paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(3). It therefore governs every product class and every compliance date within paragraph (a), including the January 31, 2030 standards codified at (a)(3). A unit above 39 cubic feet is outside the standards for all manufacture dates, not merely for the pre-2030 tables.

(b) Form. It is an express exclusion from "these standards," not a coverage or definitional provision. The class definitions in the tables (manual defrost, partial automatic defrost, automatic defrost with top/side/bottom-mounted freezer, through-the-door ice service, automatic icemaker, built-in) contain no upper volume limit; the only volume boundary in the class structure is the lower one separating compact from standard size (compact = less than 7.75 cubic feet). The single upper bound on volume in 430.32(a) is the 39 cubic foot sentence.

(c) Metric. The exclusion is measured on "total refrigerated volume," whereas the equations are computed on "AV = Total adjusted volume, expressed in ft3, as determined in appendices A and B to subpart B of this part" (and on "av = Total adjusted volume, expressed in Liters"). These are not interchangeable: adjusted volume adds a volumetric allowance for freezer compartments, so AV can exceed 39 ft3 on a unit whose total refrigerated volume is at or below 39 ft3. Applicability must be tested on total refrigerated volume determined under the applicable subpart B appendix (Appendix A for refrigerator-freezers), not on AV.

3. BOUNDARY TEST

- "Exceeding 39 cubic feet" is strict. A unit at exactly 39.0 ft3 is not excluded, and the standards apply to it. A unit at any value greater than 39 ft3 is excluded, and no standard in 430.32 applies to it.
- "1104 liters" is the regulation's own metric rendering of the same boundary (39 x 28.316846592 = 1104.36 L, rounded to 1104 L). It is a conversion, not a second or tighter limit; the two figures must not be applied cumulatively.
- The parallel 30 cubic feet (850 L) figure in the same sentence applies to freezers only and has no application to a refrigerator-freezer.

4. DECISION PROCEDURE FOR A SPECIFIC UNIT

Step 1 — Product type gate. Confirm the unit is a consumer refrigerator-freezer within the part 430 subpart A definitions and is not commercial refrigeration equipment regulated under 10 CFR part 431 subpart C. If it is part 431 equipment, 430.32 does not apply at all — an independent second ground for "no."
Step 2 — Volume determination. Determine total refrigerated volume in cubic feet using the applicable subpart B appendix (Appendix A for refrigerator-freezers). Do not substitute AV (total adjusted volume) for this step.
Step 3 — Apply the exclusion. If total refrigerated volume > 39 ft3 (1104 L), the paragraph (a) exclusion applies and no energy conservation standard in 430.32 governs the unit, at any manufacture date, including on or after 2030-01-31.
Step 4 — If not excluded (total refrigerated volume <= 39 ft3), the unit is subject to the equation for its product class: Table 1 to paragraph (a)(1) for units manufactured on or after 2014-09-15 and before the applicable 2029/2030 compliance date, or Table 4 to paragraph (a)(3) for units manufactured on or after 2030-01-31, with the applicable K-factors and I (icemaker) terms.

5. APPLICATION TO THE REQUEST

The described unit is a refrigerator-freezer (matches the first excluded category) with total refrigerated volume exceeding 39 cubic feet (matches the metric and the direction of the inequality). Both elements of the exclusion are satisfied on the face of the description. Result: excluded; the energy standards in 10 CFR 430.32 do not apply.

6. EFFECTIVE-DATE VERIFICATION FOR 2026-11-21

- Both the GovInfo 2026 CFR edition (title 10, vol. 3) and the eCFR current text carry the sentence in identical form. The eCFR snapshot was taken 2026-11-23, two days after the control date; its currency note reflects the 2030 standards already codified at (a)(3) and shows no pending amendment to paragraph (a).
- Nothing in the sources reviewed stays, vacates, or amends the 39 cubic foot exclusion. The severability language appearing in 430.32 is limited to paragraph (f)(2) (external power supplies) and has no bearing on paragraph (a).
- Residual risk, stated rather than resolved: the retrievals post-date the control date by two days, and no Federal Register search beyond the 2019 refrigerator/freezer RFI was performed. A document published 2026-11-21 through 2026-11-23 amending paragraph (a) would not appear in these snapshots. Before relying on this in a certification, confirm against the Federal Register listing of documents amending 10 CFR 430.32 with an effective date on or before 2026-11-21.

7. SCOPE OF THIS ANSWER

This answers only the applicability of the energy conservation standards in 10 CFR 430.32. It does not address certification and reporting under 10 CFR part 429, FTC EnergyGuide labeling under 16 CFR part 305, or state and provincial requirements. A unit excluded from the 430.32 standards is not thereby relieved of any of those obligations.

question: Y111
answer:
COMPLIANCE NOTE — PSSR 2000 (S.I. 2000/128), REGULATION 8, ORIGINAL VERSION AS MADE

1. Governing text (verbatim, original 'as made' version — no amendments applied)

'Written scheme of examination
8.—(1) The user of an installed system and owner of a mobile system shall not operate the system or allow it to be operated unless he has a written scheme for the periodic examination, by a competent person, of the following parts of the system, that is to say—
(a) all protective devices;
(b) every pressure vessel and every pipeline in which (in either case) a defect may give rise to danger; and
(c) those parts of the pipework in which a defect may give rise to danger,
and such parts of the system shall be identified in the scheme.
(2) The said user or owner shall—
(a) ensure that the scheme has been drawn up, or certified as being suitable, by a competent person;
(b) ensure that—
(i) the content of the scheme is reviewed at appropriate intervals by a competent person for the purpose of determining whether it is suitable in current conditions of use of the system; and
(ii) the content of the scheme is modified in accordance with any recommendations made by that competent person arising out of that review.
(3) No person shall draw up or certify a scheme of examination under paragraph (2)(a) unless the scheme is suitable and—
(a) specifies the nature and frequency of examination;
(b) specifies any measures necessary to prepare the pressure system for safe examination other than those it would be reasonable to expect the user (in the case of an installed system) or owner (in the case of a mobile system) to take without specialist advice; and
(c) where appropriate, provides for an examination to be carried out before the pressure system is used for the first time.
(4) References in paragraphs (2) and (3) to the suitability of the scheme are references to its suitability for the purposes of preventing danger from those parts of the pressure system included in the scheme.'

(Reg 8 came into force at 21.2.2000, see reg 1. Source: legislation.gov.uk uksi/2000/128/regulation/8/made and the King's Printer PDF of the whole instrument.)

2. Allocation of duties — the two layers that must not be confused

Every function in reg 8(2) has TWO persons attached to it: the person who PERFORMS the function, and the person on whom the statutory duty to ENSURE that it happens is imposed. The regulation is drafted as 'the said user or owner shall ... ensure that ...' throughout paragraph (2).

| Function | Performer of the function | Duty-holder (must ensure) | Provision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Draw up the written scheme | a competent person | user (installed system) / owner (mobile system) | reg 8(2)(a), first limb |
| Certify as suitable (where drawn up by someone else) | a competent person | user / owner | reg 8(2)(a), second limb |
| Review content at appropriate intervals for suitability in current conditions of use | a competent person | user / owner | reg 8(2)(b)(i) |
| Modify content per the reviewer's recommendations | user / owner (the modification itself) | user / owner | reg 8(2)(b)(ii) |
| Not to operate/allow operation without a scheme | — | user / owner | reg 8(1) |
| Not to draw up or certify unless scheme is suitable and meets 8(3)(a)-(c) | any person doing the drawing up/certifying | that person (direct 'no person shall' prohibition) | reg 8(3) |

3. Answers to the asks

ASK 2 — Who must draw up the written scheme of examination or certify it as suitable?
A COMPETENT PERSON. Reg 8(2)(a) gives two alternative routes, and they are alternatives, not cumulative: the scheme may be (i) drawn up by a competent person, OR (ii) certified as being suitable by a competent person. The second limb exists precisely because the scheme may be written by someone who is not a competent person (e.g. an in-house engineer or the user's own staff); in that case it is lawful only once a competent person has certified it as suitable. The user/owner is the duty-holder who must ensure one of those two routes has been followed. Reg 8(3) independently forbids ANY person from drawing up or certifying a scheme unless it is suitable and specifies (a) nature and frequency of examination, (b) special preparation measures, and (c) where appropriate, pre-first-use examination. 'Suitability' is defined in reg 8(4) as suitability for preventing danger from the parts of the system included in the scheme.

ASK 3 — Who must review its content at appropriate intervals for suitability in current conditions of use?
A COMPETENT PERSON must carry out the review (reg 8(2)(b)(i)); the user (installed system) or owner (mobile system) must ensure that the review takes place and must then ensure the content is modified in accordance with the reviewer's recommendations (reg 8(2)(b)(ii)). The regulation does not fix the interval — 'appropriate intervals' is determined case by case and will normally be set out in the scheme itself; there is no statutory maximum period in reg 8.

4. Practical points a duty-holder needs

- The drawer-up/certifier and the reviewer need not be the same individual, and the roles may be split between in-house and independent providers; HSE guidance L122 (paras 100–101) confirms the scheme may be written in-house and certified by an in-house compet individual, or written in-house and certified by an independent compet person. L122 is guidance, not the SI, and does not alter the reg 8 test.
- The compet person may be in-house or a third party; nothing in reg 8 requires independence. The choice is the user's/owner's, and so is the consequence of choosing badly.
- 'Written' is expanded by the instrument's writing provision: a form capable of being reproduced as a written copy when required and secure from loss or unauthorised interference.
- Reg 9 then carries the examination forward: the user/owner must ensure examination by a compet person at the intervals in the scheme (and before first use where the scheme so provides), and the compet person must examine properly and in accordance with the scheme.

5. Caveats and limits of this answer

- The passages retrieved for this answer do NOT include any definition of 'competent person' in reg 2 of the instrument. The ordinary meaning plus the L122 criteria (sufficient practical and theoretical knowledge and actual experience of the type of system) are what is available; I have not invented statutory wording for that definition. If a verbatim reg 2 definition is required, it must be read from the instrument's interpretation provision.
- The request specifies the original 'as made' text; later amendments and any consolidated version are out of scope by design. legislation.gov.uk shows an alternative version dated 21/02/2000 (the commencement date) and records no outstanding effects for section 8; the text quoted above is the 'as made' text.
- This note allocates statutory duties; it is not legal advice on any particular system, and it does not address exemptions, enforcement or offence provisions beyond reg 8.

question: Y112
answer:
Determination against the original version (as made) of the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/2307). The source version used is the legislation.gov.uk 'Original (As Enacted or Made)' text, not a later consolidated/amended version.

Operative provision: regulation 9(3)(a). The original text provides:

'Subject to paragraph (6), every employer shall ensure that lifting equipment which is exposed to conditions causing deterioration which is liable to result in dangerous situations is—
(a) thoroughly examined—
(i) in the case of lifting equipment for lifting persons or an accessory for lifting, at least every 6 months;
(ii) in the case of other lifting equipment, at least every 12 months; or
(iii) in either case, in accordance with an examination scheme; and
(iv) each time that exceptional circumstances which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the lifting equipment have occurred; and
(b) if appropriate for the purpose, is inspected by a competent person at suitable intervals between thorough examinations...'

Schedule 1, paragraph 7(a) does not set an independent interval; it prescribes what the report of thorough examination must record and cross-refers to regulation 9(3):

'...whether it is a thorough examination—
(i) within an interval of 6 months under regulation 9(3)(a)(i);
(ii) within an interval of 12 months under regulation 9(3)(a)(ii);
(iii) in accordance with an examination scheme under regulation 9(3)(a)(iii); or
(iv) after the occurrence of exceptional circumstances under regulation 9(3)(a)(iv);...'

Answers:
1. Lifting equipment for lifting persons, or an accessory for lifting: at least every 6 months — regulation 9(3)(a)(i), corroborated by Schedule 1 paragraph 7(a)(i). Under the original wording, all accessories for lifting fall within this 6-month limb.
2. Other lifting equipment: at least every 12 months — regulation 9(3)(a)(ii), corroborated by Schedule 1 paragraph 7(a)(ii).
3. Difference: 12 months - 6 months = 6 months. The first interval is 6 months shorter than the second.

Qualification: 'at least every' sets the maximum default interval. Regulation 9(3)(a)(iii) permits examination in accordance with an examination scheme, and regulation 9(3)(a)(iv) requires examination after exceptional circumstances. The separate inspection duty under regulation 9(3)(b) is not the thorough-examination interval. For compliance, the thorough examination should be scheduled at not more than 6 months for person-lifting equipment and lifting accessories, and not more than 12 months for other lifting equipment, unless a valid examination scheme provides otherwise; the report should record the interval basis required by Schedule 1 paragraph 7.

question: Y113
answer:
SOURCE AND DIRECT ANSWER

FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 4, Design of Roadside Channels (May 1965; author James K. Searcy, FHWA Bridge Division; Bureau of Public Roads publication, GPO Stock No. 050-001-00068-7), Section 1.2 'Factors in Design', states verbatim:

"Bureau of Public Roads policy requires that on Interstate System projects, all drainage facilities other than culverts and bridges be designed to keep the traveled ways usable during storms at least as great as that for a 10-year frequency, except that a 50-year frequency shall be used for underpass or other depressed roadways where ponded water can be removed only through the storm-drain system."

(The archived scan renders this passage with OCR artifacts — 'an drainage facilities' for 'all drainage facilities' and 'designedCto' for 'designed to'. The reading above is the evident intent and is confirmed by the parallel statement of the same policy elsewhere in the document.)

Therefore:

1. Drainage facilities other than culverts and bridges on Interstate System projects: 10-year frequency (10-year return period; 10 percent annual exceedance probability).

2. Higher frequency for underpass or other depressed roadways where ponded water can be removed only through the storm-drain system: 50-year frequency (50-year return period; 2 percent annual exceedance probability).

The performance standard attached to both numbers is that the traveled ways must be kept usable during the design storm — not merely that the facility not be overtopped.

HOW TO READ THE RULE

- Structure of the provision: a base requirement (10-year) for all Interstate drainage facilities except culverts and bridges, plus a single stated exception (50-year) that applies only where BOTH conditions hold: (a) the roadway is an underpass or other depressed roadway, and (b) ponded water can be removed only through the storm-drain system. If a depressed roadway can shed ponded water by gravity to an outlet other than the storm drain (e.g., a graded high point, an open channel outfall, a break in the profile), the 50-year exception is not triggered and the 10-year base applies.

- 'Other than culverts and bridges': the 10-year figure is a policy floor for the roadside and storm-drainage works within HDS-4's scope — gutters and shoulder gutters, chutes and downdrains, roadway channels, toe-of-slope channels, intercepting channels, median swales, paved and grass-lined channels, storm-drain inlets and conduits, and the storm-drain system serving depressed sections. Culverts and bridges are expressly carved out and are governed by their own criteria (HDS-5 for culverts, HDS-7 for bridges; the 1965-era companion reference HEC-19, Table 1, lists culverts and small bridges and river crossings at 50 years for Interstate and controlled-access highways).

- 'At least as great as': the 10-year is a minimum. A designer may and often should use a rarer storm where the consequence of overtopping is severe; HDS-4 itself says the frequency chosen 'depends somewhat upon the climate, the topography of the area, and the cost of the drainage system,' and that where shoulder gutters protect high fills highly susceptible to erosion, the design discharge 'might be greater than the class of the road would otherwise warrant.' The 50-year depressed-roadway figure is mandatory, not discretionary.

- Rationale given in the text for the depressed-roadway escalation: 'should water remain for a long time or collect in pavement sags or in underpass depressions, a traffic hazard will result.' A depressed roadway with no gravity escape holds water to a depth limited only by the pump or storm-drain capacity, so the consequence of underdesign is a closed facility rather than a wet pavement.

CORROBORATION (does not change the answer)

- HEC-19, Table 1, 'Design Frequencies for Highway Structures' (credited to the Texas Highway Department, 1970), for Interstate and controlled-access highways: Inlets and Sewers = 10 years; Inlets for Depressed Roadways = 50 years (other highways and frontage roads: 2 to 5 years and 2 to 50 years, respectively). Same two numbers, same pairing.

- The later edition of HDS-4, retitled Introduction to Highway Hydraulics (2nd ed. June 1997, FHWA-HI-97-028; reprinted as FHWA-NHI-01-019, 2001, and as the 2006 printing FHWA-NHI-05-xxx), retains the same design posture: 'Storm drains in sag locations are typically checked for the 50-year frequency storm,' and 'Most state highway agencies consider a 10-year frequency storm as the minimum for design of storm drains.' It does not restate the 10/50 Interstate policy as a directive, because that edition is expressly an introduction that provides 'detailed design criteria and standards ... primarily by reference.'

EDITION AND AUTHORITY CAVEATS THE USER MUST CARRY WITH THE ANSWER

- The 10-year/50-year statement is from the 1965 first edition, which is archived and listed by FHWA as superseded (superseded by later HDS-4 editions and by HEC-15 and HEC-22). The numbers answer the question 'what does HDS-4, Design of Roadside Channels, say' precisely. They are also still the conventional Interstate values in most state DOT drainage manuals, but they are no longer the controlling text for a current project.

- For a live project, the governing criteria are, in order: the state DOT drainage manual / design standards (which commonly restate 10-year for storm drains and 50-year for sag or depressed-roadway inlets, sometimes with a check storm such as the 100-year for spread or for pump-station sizing), AASHTO's Highway Drainage Guidelines, and FHWA's current hydraulic references — HEC-22 (Urban Drainage Design Manual) for pavement drainage, inlets and storm drains, HEC-15 for roadside channel linings (which uses 5- to 10-year return periods for permanent lining design, a separate lining-stability criterion and not the Interstate capacity requirement), HDS-5 for culverts, and HDS-7 for bridges. A state standard that is more restrictive than 10/50 governs; a less restrictive one does not relieve an Interstate project of the federal policy floor.

- Terminology: report the values as return periods ('10-year' and '50-year') unless the reviewing agency requires annual exceedance probability; the equivalents are 10 percent AEP and 2 percent AEP.

DESIGNER'S APPLICATION CHECKLIST

1. Classify the facility: culvert or bridge (go to HDS-5 / HDS-7, not this rule) versus other drainage facility (this rule applies).
2. If other drainage facility on an Interstate route: minimum design storm = 10-year, with the performance test that the traveled way remains usable.
3. Ask whether the site is an underpass or other depressed roadway and whether ponded water can be removed only through the storm drain. If both yes: design storm = 50-year. Document the basis for the 'only through the storm drain' determination, including the pumping or gravity storm-drain capacity assumed.
4. Check the state DOT manual for a more restrictive requirement or an additional check storm; adopt the more restrictive of the two.
5. Where the consequence of overtopping is unusually severe (high erodible fills, sole-access embankments), evaluate a rarer storm than the minimum and record the decision.

question: Y114
answer:
ANSWER (FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 4, citing AASHO Policy on Geometric Design of Rural Highways)

For roadside drainage channels built in earth, where terrain permits, the cited AASHO Policy recommends:

- Side slopes: not steeper than 4 horizontal to 1 vertical (4H:1V, written 4:1).
- Rounded bottom: at least 4 ft (1.2 m) wide.

Both are bounds, not fixed dimensions: 4:1 is the steepest side slope permitted and 4 ft is the narrowest bottom permitted. Flatter side slopes and wider bottoms are acceptable and, on channels beside low fills, flatter side slopes are stated to be desirable.

SOURCE TEXT (verbatim)

HDS-4, Section 1.6 'Roadway Channels' — the sentence that answers the question:
  "The AASHO (1) 'Policy on Geometric Design of Rural Highways' recommends that where terrain permits, roadside drainage channels built-in earth should have side slopes not steeper than 4 horizontal to 1 vertical, and a rounded bottom at least 4 feet wide. Flatter side slopes are desirable on channels beside low fills. The depth of channel should be sufficient to remove the water without saturating the pavement subgrade."

Same recommendation restated twice in HDS-4:
  Section 4.5 'Channel Section': "In general, open channels adjacent to the roadway should have a section with side slopes not steeper than 4:1 (horizontal to vertical) and a rounded bottom at least 4 feet wide (1). The rounding (vertical curves) at the junctions of the side slopes and the bottom do not appreciably affect the capacity, but they do add greatly to the safety and appearance of the channel."
  Section 7.3 'Effect of Channel Section': "Roadway channels built in earth (Section 1.6) should have side slopes not steeper than 4:1, and rounded bottoms at least 4 feet wide."
  Section 7.3 also identifies the reference section used in HDS-4's comparison table: "...ratios ... to those for the 4-foot bottom, 4:1 side slope channel."

CITATION / EDITION NOTES (needed to verify the lookup)

- Reference '(1)' in HDS-4 is AASHO, A Policy on Geometric Design of Rural Highways (American Association of State Highway Officials, 1954; 655 pp.; the drainage guidance appears in the chapter on Drainage Channels and Side Slopes, p. 209 ff.). HDS-4 quotes the policy; it does not derive the numbers.
- The quoted wording is from the original FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 4, 'Design of Roadside Channels' (the archived edition, reprinted as DOT/ROSA dot_75188), where the passage appears in Section 1.6, Section 4.5 and Section 7.3.
- The current edition, HDS-4 'Introduction to Highway Hydraulics' (FHWA-NHI-08-090), carries the same design intent but updated to AASHTO (2002) via its Figure 5.1, 'Preferred ditch cross section geometry', which is stated to be "applicable for rounded ditches with bottom widths of 2.4 m (8 ft) or more, and trapezoidal ditches with bottom widths equal to or greater than 1.2 m (4 ft)". The 1.2 m value is the metric equivalent of the same 4 ft minimum; the 2.4 m (8 ft) figure applies to the fully rounded (non-trapezoidal) ditch shape, not to the earth trapezoidal channel with rounded bottom asked about here. Do not report 8 ft as the answer to this question.
- HDS-4's companion circular on flexible linings (HEC-15, FHWA 05114) uses the same convention but states side slope as 1:Z (V:H), where Z is the horizontal run per unit rise; Z = 4 corresponds to the 4H:1V reported here. This is only a notation difference — the geometry is identical — but it is the most common source of a 4:1 vs 1:4 error when transcribing.

INTERPRETATION / APPLICATION

- Side slope convention: report as horizontal:vertical. 4:1 = 4 horizontal to 1 vertical = 1V:4H = Z = 4 in HEC-15 notation = 14.0 degrees from horizontal.
- 'Rounded bottom at least 4 feet wide': the bottom is a flat of not less than 4 ft width, with the junctions to the side slopes formed by vertical curves (fillets) rather than sharp breaks. HDS-4 §4.5 notes the rounding does not appreciably affect hydraulic capacity but adds greatly to safety and appearance, i.e., the rounding is a vehicle-recovery/appearance and maintenance feature, not a capacity feature.
- 'Where terrain permits': the qualifier is part of the AASHO recommendation itself; it licenses deviation only where terrain (or right-of-way) makes the 4:1 / 4 ft section impracticable. It does not license a steeper section for convenience.
- Depth is not part of the quoted recommendation: HDS-4 §4.5 gives the channel "deep enough to carry the flow with a freeboard of from 0.3 to 0.5 ft on flat slopes, except where subdrainage requires a deeper channel." Set depth by the hydraulic design (Manning / permissible shear), not by this geometric recommendation.
- Safety-based upgrade to be aware of: HDS-4 §4.5 also records Stonex (ref. 5, p. 26) as stating that for roads designed for speeds above 65 mph the minimum channel section required for safety is side slopes 6:1, a bottom width of 6.5 ft, and vertical curves 6.5 ft long connecting sides and bottom. This is a separate, higher-speed criterion quoted by HDS-4; it does not change the AASHO recommendation of 4:1 and 4 ft, but on high-speed rural facilities the 6:1 / 6.5 ft section should govern.

RESULTING SECTION TO DRAW

Trapezoid, earth, in cut: 4 ft minimum flat bottom; both side slopes 4H:1V or flatter; vertical-curve fillets at both bottom-to-side-slope junctions; depth = required flow depth + 0.3 to 0.5 ft freeboard on flat grades; side slopes blended to natural terrain at the top. Flatten side slopes (and widen bottom) where right-of-way and terrain allow, and where the adjacent fill is low.

question: Y115
answer:
HDS-4 RATIONAL METHOD — MINIMUM TIME OF CONCENTRATION AND MAXIMUM DRAINAGE AREA

1. DIRECT ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Minimum time of concentration used when finding rainfall intensity: 5 minutes.
  Source (verbatim): FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 4, Section 2.4-2, Time of Concentration:
  "A minimum time of concentration of 5 minutes is recommended for finding the intensity used for estimating the design discharge."
  Rule as applied: compute t_c by the normal procedure; if the computed t_c is less than 5 minutes, enter the IDF curve at 5 minutes. Do not use a shorter duration. The minimum exists because i → ∞ as duration → 0 on the IDF curve, so very small, steep, impervious areas would otherwise draw unrealistically high intensities and over-size the structure.

Ask 2 — Approximate maximum drainage area for which the method is recommended: about 200 acres (≈80 hectares).
  Sources (verbatim):
   - HDS-4 (original edition), Rational Method applicability: "The method is recommended for use in determining the design discharge for roadside drainage channels draining less than about 200 acres." and "For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 200 acres unless no other method is available to estimate the design discharge."
   - HDS-4, 2001 reprint (FHWA-NHI / hif02001), Section 5.3.1, Assumptions: "The drainage area should be smaller than 80 hectares (200 acres)."
   - HDS-4, 3rd ed., 2006 (FHWA-IF-06-034 / 08090), Section 2.5.1: "For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 80 hectares (200 acres)." Section 2.5: "...methods such as the Rational Method are commonly used for smaller areas, less than about 80 hectares or 200 acres."
  Unit consistency: 80 ha × 2.4711 ac/ha = 197.7 acres ≈ 200 acres. The SI and CU statements are the same limit; use 200 acres (80 ha).

2. EDITION TABLE (which number comes from where)

| Edition / document | Min. t_c for intensity | Area limit | Retrieval status |
|---|---|---|---|
| HDS-4, original (FHWA, "Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts/Introduction" series, Sec. 2.4-2, 2.4-5) | 5 min (explicit) | "less than about 200 acres" / "less than 200 acres unless no other method is available" | quoted verbatim |
| HDS-4, 2001 reprint (hif02001.pdf), Sec. 5.3.1 | not restated in retrieved text | "smaller than 80 hectares (200 acres)" | area quoted; no t_c minimum found |
| HDS-4, 3rd ed. 2006 (08090), Sec. 2.5, 2.5.1, 2.5.4 | not restated in retrieved text | "less than 80 hectares (200 acres)" | area quoted; no t_c minimum found |
| TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Ch. 4 §12 (companion, NOT HDS-4) | 10 min (explicit) | 200 acres (80 ha) | quoted verbatim |

Interpretation: the 5-minute minimum is HDS-4's own recommendation and is the answer to ask 1. The commonly cited 10-minute minimum is a state-DOT convention (TxDOT HDM Ch. 4 §12, and similarly many state hydrology manuals) adopted because 10 minutes is the shortest duration for which point-rainfall frequency estimates are broadly reliable. It is not an HDS-4 number. If the project is governed by a state manual that imposes 10 minutes, the governing document controls and 10 minutes should be used — but that is a manual-of-jurisdiction decision, not an HDS-4 citation.

3. WHY THE TWO NUMBERS ARE THE TWO NUMBERS (design basis)

Minimum t_c = 5 min
- The rational method requires the storm duration to equal t_c (HDS-4: peak discharge occurs when the whole watershed is contributing, and the storm of duration t_c gives the highest peak of that frequency).
- On the IDF curve, intensity rises without bound as duration falls toward zero, so a computed t_c of 2 or 3 minutes yields an intensity that is an extrapolation, not a measurement. The 5-minute floor keeps the lookup on the defensible part of the curve.
- Check against HDS-4's own worked examples: t_c values used are 7 min (Example, Figure 5 Kirpich), 10 min (combined areas above 5A), and 14 min (area above 5C). All exceed 5 min, i.e., the floor is a floor, not a typical value.

Maximum area = 200 acres (80 ha)
- Physical basis is the rational method's own assumption list: rainfall intensity uniform over a duration equal to t_c, and rainfall distributed uniformly over the drainage area. Both degrade as area grows — HDS-4 states "rainfall intensity is seldom the same over an area of appreciable size or for any substantial length of time during the same storm."
- Second basis: peak flow is assumed to occur when the entire watershed contributes, and the method has no storage term. Storage (detention, significant channel/floodplain volume) invalidates the steady inflow-outflow assumption.
- HDS-4 2006 §2.5 explicitly notes the boundary is not sharp: "there is no clearly defined line where one method should end and another method be used... they may disagree by 50 or more percent." For areas above ~200 acres (80 ha) HDS-4 directs the designer to regional regression equations, or to the methods of Potter, Dalrymple, or SCS (NRCS) as cited in the original edition.

4. APPLICATION PROCEDURE (as the designer would execute it)

Step 1. Delineate the tributary area A to the design point. If A > 200 acres (80 ha), stop and use a hydrograph/regression method instead.
Step 2. Compute t_c as the sum of travel times from the hydraulically most remote point (most remote in time, not distance) to the outlet.
Step 3. Set the intensity duration d = max(t_c, 5 min). If a state manual with a 10-minute floor governs, use d = max(t_c, 10 min).
Step 4. Read i for the design return period at duration d from the IDF curve (or state power-law IDF, e.g. TxDOT Eq. 4-21, i = b/(t_c + d)^e form).
Step 5. Q = C·i·A, with C the area-weighted runoff coefficient, i in in/hr, A in acres, Q in cfs. Unit check: 1 acre·in/hr = 43,560 ft² × (1/12 ft) / 3600 s = 1.008 cfs ≈ 1, which is why the coefficient is unity in CU units and 1/360 in SI (A in ha, i in mm/h, Q in m³/s).
Step 6. For complex/multiple-subarea systems, use the longest t_c to the design point with accumulated CA (ΣCA), and check the partial-area critical condition (short t_c, high i on the impervious subarea) per HDS-4 §2.5.6.

Illustrative numerical check (assumed values, for arithmetic consistency only): A = 200 acres, C = 0.35, 10-yr i at d = 5 min = 7.0 in/hr → Q = 0.35 × 7.0 × 200 = 490 cfs. At d = 14 min with i = 4.5 in/hr → Q = 0.35 × 4.5 × 200 = 315 cfs. Both are ordinary magnitudes for a 0.31 mi² basin; the arithmetic demonstrates the sensitivity to the duration floor and confirms the 5-minute floor does not produce an absurd intensity in a typical IDF.

5. CAVEATS THE REVIEWER SHOULD CARRY FORWARD
- Cite the edition. The 5-minute value is in the original HDS-4, Section 2.4-2. The 2001 and 2006 revisions restate the 200-acre/80-ha limit but, in the retrieved text, do not restate a minimum t_c; a designer working strictly from those reprints should take the minimum from the governing state manual.
- The 200-acre limit is a recommendation/restriction for highway drainage structures, stated as "about" 200 acres in the original edition and as a hard "less than 80 hectares (200 acres)" in the 2006 edition. Do not present it as an exact hydrologic threshold.
- Verify errata currency for the specific HDS-4 printing in use before quoting page numbers in a design document.

question: Y116
answer:
MANNING n DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE HDS-3 TRAPEZOIDAL AND RECTANGULAR CHANNEL CHART BASES

Publication identified. The governing document is FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 3, 'Design Charts for Open-Channel Flow' (1961; the FHWA-hosted PDF at fhwa.dot.gov/engineering/hydraulics/pubs/hds3.pdf). Note for the record: the project context assumed HDS-3 was 'Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts'; that title belongs to HDS-5. HDS-3 is the open-channel chart series, and it is the document that contains the rectangular and trapezoidal channel charts in question. Both chart families sit in the same chapter (Chapter 3, charts 1-29) of the same edition, so no cross-edition reconciliation is required.

Step 1 - Rectangular chart basis. HDS-3, Chapter 3, statement of chart bases (quoted verbatim):
  'The rectangular cross-section channel charts, Nos. 1-14, are prepared for an n of 0.015 (average value for concrete). A separate chart is provided for each foot of width from 2 feet to 10 feet and for each even foot of width from 10 feet to 20 feet.'
  => n_rect = 0.015

Step 2 - Trapezoidal chart basis. Same passage, next sentence (quoted verbatim):
  'The trapezoidal cross-section channel charts, Nos. 15-28, are prepared for an n of 0.03 and side slopes of 2:1 (horizontal to vertical). A separate chart is provided for each foot of bottom width from 2 feet to 10 feet and for each even foot of width from 10 feet to 20 feet.'
  => n_trap = 0.03 (with side slopes fixed at 2H:1V)

Step 3 - Independent confirmation within HDS-3. Section 3.2-1, 'Use of charts 1-28 with basic chart-design value of n,' restates the same two bases:
  'For a given slope and cross section of channel, when n is 0.015 for rectangular channels or 0.03 for trapezoidal channels, the depth and velocity of uniform flow may be read directly from the chart for that size channel.'
This is a second, independent statement of the identical pair of values, so the two bases are not a reading artifact of a single sentence.

Step 4 - Computation.
  Delta n = n_trap - n_rect = 0.03 - 0.015 = 0.015
  Ratio   = n_trap / n_rect = 0.03 / 0.015 = 2.0 (the trapezoidal chart base is exactly twice the rectangular chart base)
  Percent = (0.03 - 0.015)/0.015 x 100 = 100 percent larger

ANSWER (Ask 2): The Manning n used for the trapezoidal cross-section channel charts (0.03) exceeds the Manning n used for the rectangular cross-section channel charts (0.015) by 0.015.

ANSWER (Ask 3): The dimensionless difference is 0.015. It is a pure number - no units, no percent sign. (If a percent form is wanted for narrative use only: 100 percent. The requested dimensionless difference is 0.015.)

Consistency check on the reported numbers: 0.015 < 0.03; 0.015 = 0.03 - 0.015; 0.015 = 0.03/2; 0.03 = 2 x 0.015. All four statements agree, and the deliverable sets no threshold or bound that any of them could violate.

Scope discipline (Ask 1 constraint - stated chart bases only). The 0.015 and 0.03 values above are the chart-construction bases printed in HDS-3 for charts 1-14 and 15-28 respectively, restated in section 3.2-1. The following n values also appear in HDS-3 but are NOT chart bases for these two families and were deliberately excluded from the calculation:
  - n = 0.019 for 40-percent paved-invert pipe-arches (charts 66-68) - a pipe-arch chart basis, not a channel chart basis.
  - The grass-lined channel charts (charts 30-34) in Chapter 4, which are organized by retardance class (C, D) with n varying with depth and grass type rather than a single fixed n.
  - Chart 29, the triangular cross-section chart, for which the source text explicitly notes no single fixed n is the basis in the same manner (the 'except the triangular cross-section channel chart, No. 29' carve-out).
  - Table 2 (Appendix A) recommended roughness values and any site-specific n discussed in the text; these are design-selection aids, not chart bases.
  - The PPI Drainage Handbook's tabulated n ranges attributed to HDS-4/HDS-5; those are a secondary source and were not used.

Use note carried from the same source (does not change the answer, but a designer applying these charts should know it): the charts are not rigidly locked to the base n. HDS-3 states that each chart is 'prepared for a channel of given bottom width, and having a particular value of Manning's n, but auxiliary scales make the charts applicable to other values of n,' and HDS-4 describes the same mechanism: 'The channel charts can be used for values of n other than that for which the chart was constructed by using the Qn and Vn scales.' The question asked, however, is about the n used to construct the charts, and those construction values are 0.015 (rectangular, charts 1-14) and 0.03 (trapezoidal, charts 15-28).

Result: 0.03 - 0.015 = 0.015 (dimensionless).

question: Y117
answer:
ANSWER

Under 23 CFR 650 Subpart A, the minimum design flood for encroachments by through lanes of Interstate highways is the flood with a **2-percent chance of being exceeded in any given year** — i.e., an annual exceedance probability (AEP) of **0.02**, the **50-year** recurrence-interval flood.

GOVERNING CLAUSE

23 CFR § 650.115(a)(2) (Design standards), quoted verbatim from the eCFR:

> "The design flood for encroachments by through lanes of Interstate highways shall not be less than the flood with a 2-percent chance of being exceeded in any given year. No minimum design flood is specified for Interstate highway ramps and frontage roads or for other highways."

Source: https://www.eCFR.gov/current/title-23/part-650/section-650.115 (Subpart A — Location and Hydraulic Design of Encroachments on Flood Plains; fetched 2026-11-23, sha256 16b10ca8f480), corroborated by https://www.eCFR.gov/current/title-23/part-650 (sha256 8509bf1ac16d) and the GPO CFR-2025-title23-vol1 PDF, part 650 (sha256 e7516bda351e). The answer is taken from the fetched regulatory text itself, not from recall; the same sentence appears identically in all three fetches.

UNIT / FORMAT CONVERSION (ask 3)

| Expression | Value |
|---|---|
| Annual exceedance chance (regulatory wording) | 2 percent chance of being exceeded in any given year |
| Annual exceedance probability, dimensionless | 0.02 |
| Recurrence interval | 50 years (1 / 0.02) |
| Chance of at least one exceedance in a 30-year period | 1 − (1 − 0.02)^30 = 1 − 0.98^30 ≈ 0.45 (≈45%) |

The regulation states the standard directly as an annual exceedance chance, so no conversion is required to answer; the recurrence-interval and multi-year figures above are provided only as engineering equivalents and are not part of the regulatory requirement.

ENGINEERING READING (what the number does and does not mean)

1. It is a **floor**, not a target. § 650.115(a)(2) says the design flood "shall not be less than" the 2%-AEP flood. A design at exactly the 2%-AEP stage satisfies the minimum; a design at a rarer event also satisfies it.
2. The **base flood is a different number** and must not be substituted. § 650.105(b): "Base flood shall mean the flood or tide having a 1-percent chance of being exceeded in any given year" (the 100-year flood). The 2% minimum is not the base flood.
3. The risk analysis in § 650.115(a)(1) operates alongside the minimum: consideration of capital costs and risks shall include "(i) The overtopping flood or the base flood, whichever is greater, or (ii) The greatest flood which must flow through the highway drainage structure(s), where overtopping is not practicable." In practice, an Interstate through-lane encroachment is designed to the 2%-AEP flood as the minimum, and the documentation must still analyse the 1%-AEP base flood (or the greater overtopping flood) as part of the alternative/risk analysis. Do not read the 2% floor as capping the analysis at the 50-year event.
4. **Where the 2% minimum applies.** § 650.105(e): "Encroachment shall mean an action within the limits of the base flood plain," and § 650.105(c): the base flood plain is the area subject to flooding by the 1%-AEP base flood. So the 2% minimum attaches to Interstate through-lane actions that fall inside the 1%-AEP flood plain (§ 650.107(a) applicability).
5. **Where it does not apply.** The same sentence expressly states: "No minimum design flood is specified for Interstate highway ramps and frontage roads or for other highways." Ramps, frontage roads, and non-Interstate highways carry no Subpart A numeric minimum; the design flood for those is set by the alternative/risk analysis and by § 650.115(a)(5) NFIP consistency, not by a federal floor.
6. **Design-flood definition.** § 650.105(d): design flood is "the peak discharge, volume if appropriate, stage or wave crest elevation of the flood associated with the probability of exceedance selected for the design of a highway encroachment. By definition, the highway will not be inundated from the stage of the design flood." Thus the controlling deliverable at a specific site is the water-surface elevation (and discharge) of the 2%-AEP flood, and the through lanes must be protected from inundation to that stage; freebord is separately required where practicable under § 650.115(a)(3), and the effect of existing flood-control channels, levees, and reservoirs must be reflected in the 2%-AEP peak discharge and stage under § 650.115(a)(4).
7. **Version caveat.** The figure above is from the current eCFR edition as fetched (and matches the CFR-2025 bound volume). If a project is grandfathered under approvals predating the rule's effective date, § 650.107(b) preserves those prior approvals; verify the edition in force for the specific action. The 2% figure has been stable in the text as published (44 FR 67580, Nov. 26, 1979, as amended 48 FR 29274, June 24, 1983).

ONE-LINE CITABLE STATEMENT

"Per 23 CFR 650.115(a)(2), the design flood for encroachments by through lanes of Interstate highways shall not be less than the flood with a 2-percent chance of being exceeded in any given year (annual exceedance probability 0.02; the 50-year flood); no minimum design flood is specified for Interstate ramps and frontage roads or for other highways."
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.
The answer gives 0.02 for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y118
answer:
ANSWER (23 CFR 650.105(m), Subpart A — Policies and Procedures for the Location and Hydraulic Design of Encroachments on Flood Plains)

Maximum designated cumulative increase in base-flood water surface elevation allowed in the definition of 'regulatory floodway': 1 foot (0.3048 m).

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

23 CFR 650.105(m) — Definitions — reads verbatim (as fetched from ecfr.gov, § 650.105 and the Subpart A page; identical on all mirrors fetched, sha256 640cc1276fd5 / 4a9294c5d38d / 8509bf1ac16d):

"(m) Regulatory floodway shall mean the flood-plain area that is reserved in an open manner by Federal, State or local requirements, i.e., unconfined or unobstructed either horizontally or vertically, to provide for the discharge of the base flood so that the cumulative increase in water surface elevation is no more than a designated amount (not to exceed 1 foot as established by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) for administering the National Flood Insurance Program)."

The parenthetical is the operative cap: the designated amount chosen by the Federal, State or local requirement may not exceed 1 foot. One foot is thus the maximum designated cumulative increase; it is a ceiling, not a default — a stricter (smaller) designated amount is permitted and common.

2. HOW THE NUMBER IS BOUNDED (why 1 foot and not another figure)

- "cumulative" — the limit applies to the total, combined rise in base-flood (1-percent-annual-chance) water surface elevation caused by all encroachments within the floodway, not to each encroachment individually.
- "designated amount" — the actual number is fixed by the Federal/State/local requirement reserving the floodway; 23 CFR 650 sets only the outer bound.
- "not to exceed 1 foot" — the bound. FEMA's NFIP floodway standard (44 CFR 60.3(d)(3), the criterion 23 CFR 650.117(b)(3) points to via 44 CFR 60.3) uses the same 1-foot surcharge figure.

3. FIGURES DELIBERATELY NOT CONFUSED WITH THE ANSWER (all appear in the same subpart)

- 1-percent chance of exceedance — definition of "base flood," § 650.105(b). A probability, not an elevation increase.
- 2-percent chance of exceedance — minimum design flood for encroachments by through lanes of Interstate highways, § 650.115(a). A design-flood frequency, not a surcharge.
- Freeboard — § 650.105(g), vertical clearance of the lowest structural member of the bridge superstructure above the overtopping-flood water surface. A separate vertical clearance requirement, not a floodway surcharge.
- Overtopping flood — § 650.105(j). The flood at which flow passes over the highway or through emergency relief structures.

4. CITATION FORM FOR USE IN A DESIGN OR COMPLIANCE DOCUMENT

"23 CFR 650.105(m) (definition of 'regulatory floodway'): cumulative increase in base-flood water surface elevation shall be no more than a designated amount, not to exceed 1 foot, as established by FEMA for administering the NFIP."

Caveat to carry forward: the CFR text is current as of the eCFR revision in effect on the fetch date (2026-11-23); re-verify the revision date if the citation is going into a permanent design document or permit application.

question: Y119
answer:
GOVERNING PROVISION (Ask 1)
44 CFR 65.10(b)(1)(i) — Freeboard, riverine levees — under 44 CFR Part 65, Subpart B ("Map Changes" / levee recognition), section 65.10 "Mapping of areas protected by levee systems," paragraph (b) "Design criteria," subparagraph (1) "Freeboard." This is the provision the supplied eCFR page displays and the only one in Part 65 that sets riverine levee freeboard.

CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, eCFR current as fetched, sha256 3eba11c683bd; identical wording in the govinfo CFR-2025-title44-vol1-part65 PDF, sha256 ed6da6ac59fd):
"(b) Design criteria. For levees to be recognized by FEMA, evidence that adequate design and operation and maintenance systems are in place to provide reasonable assurance that protection from the base flood exists must be provided. The following requirements must be met:
(1) Freeboard.
(i) Riverine levees must provide a minimum freeboard of three feet above the water-surface level of the base flood. An additional one foot above the minimum is required within 100 feet in either side of structures (such as bridges) riverward of the levee or wherever the flow is constricted. An additional one-half foot above the minimum at the upstream end of the levee, tapering to not less than the minimum at the downstream end of the levee, is also required."

ANSWER — RIVERINE FREEBOARD WITHIN 100 FT OF A RIVERWARD STRUCTURE OR CONSTRICTED FLOW
- Base minimum freeboard (Ask 3): 3.0 ft above the base-flood water-surface level.
- Added amount (Ask 4): 1.0 ft, applied within 100 ft on either side of structures (such as bridges) riverward of the levee, or wherever the flow is constricted.
- Total minimum freeboard (Ask 2): 3.0 + 1.0 = 4.0 ft above the base-flood water-surface level (i.e., top of levee at or above BFE + 4.0 ft).

CALCULATION
  F_total = F_base + F_structure
          = 3.0 ft + 1.0 ft
          = 4.0 ft above the base-flood water surface.
The increment is additive to the base minimum, not a substitute for it; the regulation phrases it as "an additional one foot above the minimum."

APPLICATION NOTES AN ENGINEER MUST CARRY WITH THE 4.0 FT
1. Datum/basis: freeboard is measured from the water-surface level of the base flood (the 1%-annual-chance flood, the BFE where adopted on the FIRM), vertically to the levee crest. It is not a depth over ground and not a height above a datum such as NAVD 88 directly.
2. Extent of the 100 ft: per FEMA Guidance for Flood Risk Analysis and Mapping — Levees (Guidance Document No. 95, Nov. 2021), the 100 ft is measured from the furthest upstream and downstream point of the structure that influences flow — not from the center of the structure.
3. Non-cumulative with the upstream-end increment: the separate (b)(1)(i) requirement adds 0.5 ft at the upstream end of the levee, tapering to not less than the minimum at the downstream end. Where a constricting structure sits at the upstream end of the levee system, the required freeboard is 4.0 ft, not 4.5 ft (FEMA GD No. 95: "the required freeboard shall be 4.0 feet (not a cumulative 4.5 feet)"). Away from structures, the profile is 3.5 ft at the upstream end tapering to 3.0 ft at the downstream end.
4. Waiver of the +1.0 ft: FEMA GD No. 95 allows the additional structure freeboard to be waived where the certifying engineer demonstrates the structure does not influence the base-flood flow pattern; the regulation itself (b)(1)(ii) permits exceptions to the minimum riverine freeboard only on submitted engineering analysis of BFE uncertainty (confidence limits on the 100-year discharge, stage-discharge changes, debris/sediment/ice) plus structural stability under those loadings, and states: "Under no circumstances will freeboard of less than two feet be accepted." 2.0 ft is therefore an absolute floor, never a design target, and never available by simple election.
5. Not the coastal rule: (b)(1)(iii) sets coastal freeboard at 1 ft above the 1% wave height or maximum wave runup (whichever greater) at the 100-year stillwater surge elevation, with a 2.0 ft floor under (b)(1)(iv). Inapplicable to the riverine case posed; do not blend the two.
6. These are FEMA minimums for levee recognition/accreditation and for removal of the levee-protected area from the SFHA. State, local, or agency sponsor criteria (e.g., USACE design freeboard) may be stricter, and the more restrictive governs the design. Settlement must also be analyzed under 65.10(b)(?) so that freeboard is maintained within these minimums over time; erosion/constriction analyses are required and must expressly address "expected flow velocities (especially in constricted areas)."

BOTTOM LINE
Base minimum: 3 ft. Added within 100 ft of a riverward structure or constricted flow: 1 ft. Total minimum required there: 4 ft above the base-flood water surface.

question: Y120
answer:
# Flood Opening Requirements — 44 CFR 60.3(c)(5)

## 1. Controlling text

44 CFR 60.3(c)(5) (eCFR current; identical in the CFR 2025 print edition and Cornell LII):

> "(5) Require, for all new construction and substantial improvements, that fully enclosed areas below the lowest floor that are usable solely for parking of vehicles, building access or storage in an area other than a basement and which are subject to flooding shall be designed to automatically equalize hydrostatic flood forces on exterior walls by allowing for the entry and exit of floodwaters. Designs for meeting this requirement must either be certified by a registered professional engineer or architect or meet or exceed the following minimum criteria: **A minimum of two openings having a total net area of not less than one square inch for every square foot of enclosed area subject to flooding shall be provided. The bottom of all openings shall be no higher than one foot above grade.** Openings may be equipped with screens, louvers, valves, or other coverings or devices provided that they permit the automatic entry and exit of floodwaters."

## 2. The three requested values (federal baseline, prescriptive path)

| # | Requirement | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum number of openings | **2** | openings |
| 2 | Total net area of openings, per unit enclosed area subject to flooding | **1** | square inch per square foot of enclosed area subject to flooding (1 in²/ft²) |
| 3 | Maximum height of the bottom of all openings above grade | **1** | foot (12 in) above grade |

Equivalent forms of value 2: 1 in² per 1 ft² = 144 in² per 144 ft² = 0.00694 ft² of net opening per ft² of enclosed area. Value 3 = 12 inches = 0.3048 m.

## 3. Scope and applicability (read before applying the numbers)

- **Trigger.** These criteria apply to *fully enclosed areas below the lowest floor* that are (a) usable **solely** for parking of vehicles, building access, or storage, (b) **not** a basement, and (c) **subject to flooding**. New construction and substantial improvements only, in the A zones covered by 60.3(c).
- **Two compliance paths.** The regulation states designs "must either be certified by a registered professional engineer or architect **or** meet or exceed the following minimum criteria." The three values above are the **prescriptive (non-engineered) minimum criteria**. A PE/RA-certified design is an alternative path and may depart from them, but it must still equalize hydrostatic forces automatically. Where no certification is obtained, the three values are mandatory floors/ceilings.
- **"Minimum" and "no higher than" are one-sided.** 2 openings is a floor — more are permitted and often required by the area ratio. 1 in²/ft² is a floor — provide ≥ that amount. 1 ft above grade is a ceiling — bottoms must be at or below it.
- **"All openings."** The 1-ft cap attaches to *all* openings, not just the two minimum. If the area calculation drives you to 6 openings, all 6 bottoms must be ≤ 1 ft above grade.
- **"Grade" is not further defined in the text.** The regulation says "grade" without specifying interior vs. exterior grade. Measurement convention should be fixed on the drawings and confirmed with the local floodplain administrator; FEMA technical guidance and most community permits address interior-grade measurement. The numeric cap (1 ft) does not change with the convention.
- **Net vs. gross.** "Total net area" is the clear, unobstructed area that actually passes water — not the rough framed opening. Screens, louvers, valves, and other coverings are expressly allowed **provided they permit automatic entry and exit of floodwaters**; the net area credited must be the free area after accounting for the device, frame, and any mullions. Do not credit gross opening dimensions.
- **State/local amendments.** This is the FEMA/NFIP federal minimum. States and communities may adopt stricter criteria (e.g., larger ratio, more openings, lower height cap). The values here are the federal baseline only; verify the adopted local ordinance before design.
- **Not in the quoted text.** 60.3(c)(5) does not itself state that the openings must be on two different walls. That is FEMA technical guidance and common local permit practice (needed for actual flow-through and to avoid a single-wall piston effect); treat it as a design requirement imposed by guidance/permit, not as part of the numeric answer to asks 1–3.

## 4. Design procedure

1. Confirm the enclosure qualifies: below lowest floor, solely parking/access/storage, not a basement, subject to flooding.
2. Compute **A_e** = enclosed area subject to flooding, in ft², measured on the enclosed footprint (the area that will be inundated), from the permit drawings — not the building's gross floor area.
3. Required total net area: **A_net,req = 1 in²/ft² × A_e (ft²)**, expressed in in². Round up.
4. Distribute A_net,req over **N ≥ 2** openings (place on at least two walls per guidance). Each opening's credited net area is its free area after louvers/screens.
5. Set every opening bottom at or below **12 in above grade**. Keep the top of each opening below the lowest floor.
6. Check: Σ net areas ≥ A_net,req; N ≥ 2; max(bottom elevation) ≤ 1 ft. If any check fails, resize or add openings and re-check.
7. Record the ratio calculation, opening schedule (location, width, height, free-area factor), and bottom elevations on the plans for the floodplain permit; if using the engineered path instead, obtain the PE/RA certification in lieu of steps 3–6.

## 5. Worked example (illustrative only)

Given A_e = 2,400 ft² enclosed area subject to flooding:

- A_net,req = 2,400 in² (≈ 16.67 ft²) total net area.
- Provide N = 8 openings at 300 in² net each = 2,400 in² provided. 2,400 ≥ 2,400 ✔ (exactly at the floor — the ratio is a minimum, so do not design below it; add margin if the louver free-area factor is uncertain).
- 300 in² net each ≈ 20 in × 15 in clear free area (verify louver free-area percentage; a 40% free-area louver needs ≈ 750 in² gross to credit 300 in² net).
- Bottom of every opening ≤ 12 in above grade (example: 6 in and 12 in above grade) ✔; tops stay below the lowest floor.
