- N = 8 ≥ 2 ✔; openings distributed on at least two walls per guidance ✔.

## 6. Source

44 CFR 60.3(c)(5), eCFR current (ecfr.gov/current/title-44/part-60/section-60.3), corroborated by the CFR 2025 print edition (GPO) and Cornell LII. Language is quoted verbatim; the three values are read directly from that sentence and require no interpretation.

question: Y121
shape: bridge inspection interval and training score
answer:
SOURCE AND EDITION
Text is the eCFR/govinfo text of 23 CFR Part 650, Subpart C (National Bridge Inspection Standards), as amended by the June 6, 2022 final rule (the '2022 NBIS final rule'), matching the 2025 print edition (23 CFR Ch. I, 4-1-25 Edition). The two provisions at issue live in different sections:
- Inspection interval: § 650.311 Inspection interval.
- Personnel qualifications / training: § 650.309 Personnel qualifications (with the training-course definitions in § 650.309(h) and the defined term 'End-of-course assessment' in § 650.305).

ASK 2 — BASIC-RULE REGULAR INSPECTION INTERVAL = 24 MONTHS
Operative text, § 650.311(a)(1)(i) ('Regular intervals'):
  "Each bridge must be inspected at regular intervals not to exceed 24 months, except as required in paragraph (a)(1)(ii) of this section and allowed in paragraphs (a)(1)(iii) of this section."

Derivation:
1. § 650.311(a) is headed 'Routine inspections' and directs that each bridge be inspected at regular intervals not to exceed the interval established by one of two risk-based methods — Method 1, § 650.311(a)(1), or Method 2, § 650.311(a)(2).
2. Method 1, paragraph (a)(1)(i), states the baseline ('regular intervals') maximum as 24 months. Paragraph (a)(1)(ii) is 'Reduced intervals'; paragraph (a)(1)(iii) is the extended-interval allowance (Method 1 categories not to exceed 12, 24, or 48 months; Method 2, § 650.311(a)(2)(vi), four risk categories with a routine inspection interval not to exceed 12, 24, 48, or 72 months).
3. The ask is expressly limited to bridges 'not subject to reduced or extended intervals.' That removes (a)(1)(ii) and (a)(1)(iii) from consideration and leaves the unqualified baseline sentence in (a)(1)(i):
  BASIC RULE = 24 MONTHS (interval must not exceed 24 months).

Answer: 24 months.

Notes that bound the answer (stated so the number is not misapplied):
- 'Not to exceed' is a ceiling, not a fixed period; a shorter interval is compliant.
- Interval tolerance, § 650.311(e)(2): for intervals of 24 months or greater, up to three (3) months after the month in which the inspection was due. This is an inspection-timing tolerance, not an extension of the 24-month rule.
- The 24-month figure is the routine-inspection baseline only. It does not govern other inspection types: underwater inspections under § 650.311(b)(1)(i) have a regular-interval ceiling of 60 months (risk categories up to 24, 60, or 72 months under Method 2, § 650.311(b)(2)); NSTM inspections under § 650.311(c)(1)(i) have a regular-interval ceiling of 24 months (risk categories 12, 24, or 48 months under Method 1; up to 48 months for certain NSTMs meeting all listed criteria).
- § 650.311(a)(4) eligibility gate: a new, rehabilitated, or structurally modified bridge must receive an initial inspection, be in service 24 months, and receive its next routine inspection before it is eligible for intervals greater than 24 months — consistent with 24 months as the baseline.
- § 650.311(a)(3): a service inspection is required at the midpoint month when a risk-based routine interval exceeds 48 months — relevant only to the extended-interval population excluded by this ask.

ASK 3 — END-OF-COURSE ASSESSMENT SCORE FOR THE FHWA-APPROVED COMPREHENSIVE BRIDGE INSPECTION TRAINING COURSE = 70 PERCENT
Operative text, § 650.309(a)(2) (program manager):
  "Complete an FHWA-approved comprehensive bridge inspection training course as described in paragraph (h) of this section and score 70 percent or greater on an end-of-course assessment (completion of FHWA-approved comprehensive bridge inspection training under FHWA regulations in this subpart in effect before June 6, 2022, satisfies the intent of the requirement in this paragraph (a));"

Identical requirement for the team leader, § 650.309(b)(2):
  "Complete an FHWA-approved comprehensive bridge inspection training course as described in paragraph (h) of this section and score 70 percent or greater on an end-of-course assessment (completion of FHWA-approved comprehensive bridge inspection training under FHWA regulations in this subpart in effect before June 6, 2022, satisfies the intent of the requirement in this paragraph (b));"

Derivation:
1. 'End-of-course assessment' is defined in § 650.305 as 'A comprehensive examination given to students after the completion of the delivery of a training course.' The score attaches to that examination.
2. The stated passing score in both places where the comprehensive course is required is 70 percent or greater. There is one number: 70.
3. Per the constraint, the parenthetical '(completion of FHWA-approved comprehensive bridge inspection training under FHWA regulations in this subpart in effect before June 6, 2022, satisfies the intent of the requirement ...)' is NOT treated as a separate score requirement. It contains no numeric score; it is a compliance-equivalency provision stating that pre-June 6, 2022 completion of the prior comprehensive course satisfies the intent of the paragraph. It therefore neither adds nor lowers a score — the required score remains 70 percent.

Answer: 70 percent (a score of 70 percent or greater).

Corroboration elsewhere in the same section (same 70 percent figure; not additional requirements for the comprehensive course):
- § 650.309(c)(2), NSTM team leaders: 'Complete an FHWA-approved training course on the inspection of NSTMs ... and score 70 percent or greater on an end-of-course assessment ...'.
- § 650.309(e), Underwater Bridge Inspection Diver: '... score 70 percent or greater on an end-of-course assessment ...'.
- § 650.309(h)(2), FHWA approval of alternate training: 'FHWA must approve alternate course materials and end-of-course assessments for national consistency and certification purposes.' (Alternates are held to the same assessment standard; the section does not state a different numeric cut score.)

CONSOLIDATED ANSWER
- Ask 2 (basic-rule regular routine inspection interval, bridges not subject to reduced or extended intervals): 24 months, maximum, per § 650.311(a)(1)(i).
- Ask 3 (end-of-course assessment score, FHWA-approved comprehensive bridge inspection training course): 70 percent or greater, per § 650.309(a)(2) and § 650.309(b)(2); the pre-June 6, 2022 completion parenthetical is an equivalency clause carrying no separate score.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 3 on ecfr.gov/current/title-23/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-650/subpart-c/section-650.311 and 2 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title23-vol1/pdf/cfr-2025-title23-vol1-part650-subpartc.pdf. The first reads: "(2) The acceptable tolerance for intervals of 24 months or greater for the next inspection is up to three (3) months after the month in which the inspection was due."

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 24 on ecfr.gov/current/title-23/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-650/subpart-c/section-650.311 and 60 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title23-vol1/pdf/cfr-2025-title23-vol1-part650-subpartc.pdf. The first reads: "Each bridge must be inspected at regular intervals not to exceed 24 months, except as required in paragraph (a)(1)(ii) of this section and allowed in paragraphs (a)(1)(iii) of this section."

question: Y122
answer:
SOURCE AND VERSION
Text is taken from 23 CFR Part 650, Subpart C (National Bridge Inspection Standards), current eCFR text at §§ 650.303 and 650.305, cross-checked against the 2025 print edition (CFR-2025-title23-vol1, §§ 650.303/650.305). Subpart C source note: 87 FR 27429, May 6, 2022. The two sources are word-for-word identical on the two provisions relied on here, so the answer is not edition-sensitive for these asks.

ASK 2 — OPENING THRESHOLD IN THE DEFINITION OF 'BRIDGE'
23 CFR 650.305 (Definitions) reads, verbatim:

"Bridge. A structure including supports erected over a depression or an obstruction, such as water, highway, or railway, and having a track or passageway for carrying traffic or other moving loads, and having an opening measured along the center of the roadway of more than 20 feet between under copings of abutments or spring lines of arches, or extreme ends of openings for multiple boxes; it includes multiple pipes, where the clear distance between openings is less than half of the smaller contiguous opening."

Answer: the threshold is an opening of MORE THAN 20 FEET, measured along the center of the roadway.

Engineering reading of the definition (all four elements must be satisfied for a structure to be an NBIS 'bridge'):
1. Structure with supports erected over a depression or obstruction (water, highway, railway, etc.).
2. It carries a track or passageway for traffic or other moving loads.
3. It has an opening of more than 20 feet — the governing dimension.
4. That opening is measured along the center of the roadway.

Measurement conventions fixed by the text:
- Direction of measurement: along the center of the roadway carried by the structure (i.e., along the roadway centerline), not along the waterway centerline, not along the skew-normal, and not the square (perpendicular) span. On a skewed crossing this deliberately yields the longer, along-centerline dimension.
- Termini of the measurement, by structure type:
  • Abutment-supported spans: between under copings of abutments (the underside of the bearing seat/coping, not the top of the backwall and not the clear face-to-face of the substructure units).
  • Arches: between spring lines of arches.
  • Multiple boxes: between the extreme ends of the openings (outside opening to outside opening across the group), not the individual cell.
  • Multiple pipes: pipes are included within a single 'bridge' where the clear distance between adjacent openings is less than half of the smaller contiguous opening. Where that inclusion test is met, the group is treated as one structure measured between the extreme ends of the openings along the roadway centerline. Note honestly: the regulation states only the inclusion test for multiple pipes; it does not separately spell out the tape-line convention for the grouped case, so the extreme-ends convention used for multiple boxes is the consistent reading.

Threshold strictness: the text is 'more than 20 feet,' not '20 feet or more.' A structure whose opening measures exactly 20.00 ft does not meet the definition; 20 ft 0+ in. does. Practical cut-points: 19 ft 11 in. → not a bridge; 20 ft 0 in. → not a bridge; 20 ft 1 in. → bridge. Where the as-built opening is within an inch or two of 20 ft, resolve it by field measurement along the roadway centerline and document the measurement; do not round up to capture or exclude a structure.

Consequence of failing the threshold: structures with an opening of 20 ft or less (short culverts, small pipes, minor arches) are outside the Subpart C definition and therefore outside the NBIS inventory, inspection-interval, team-leader, load-rating and NBI-reporting requirements — they may still be subject to State or owner inspection policy, but not to the NBIS by force of this definition.

ASK 3 — EXPRESS COVERAGE OF TEMPORARY BRIDGES AND BRIDGES UNDER CONSTRUCTION WITH PORTIONS OPEN TO TRAFFIC
Answer: YES — both are expressly covered, by name, in the applicability section.

23 CFR 650.303 (Applicability) reads, verbatim:

"The National Bridge Inspection Standards (NBIS) in this subpart apply to all structures defined as highway bridges located on all public roads, on and off Federal-aid highways, including tribally-owned and federally-owned bridges, private bridges that are connected to a public road on both ends of the bridge, temporary bridges, and bridges under construction with portions open to traffic."

Points that matter to the verdict:
- The coverage is express, not implied: 'temporary bridges' and 'bridges under construction with portions open to traffic' appear as named items in the same inclusive list, introduced by 'including,' so they are within scope rather than left to case-by-case reading.
- Location of the coverage: it sits in § 650.303 (applicability), not in the § 650.305 definition of 'Bridge.' The definition of 'Bridge' itself contains no reference to temporary or under-construction status; the express coverage comes from the applicability section. This is the precise answer to 'expressly cover' — yes, but cite § 650.303, not § 650.305, when making the point.
- 'Temporary bridge' is itself a defined term at § 650.305: 'A bridge which is constructed to carry highway traffic until the permanent facility is built, repaired, rehabilitated, or replaced.' A temporary structure that meets the >20 ft definition is therefore both a 'bridge' and a 'temporary bridge,' and is squarely in scope.
- The 'portions open to traffic' qualifier is the operative trigger for structures under construction: the NBIS attach once part of the structure is carrying traffic, not only at final completion. A structure under construction with no portion open to traffic is not captured by that clause.
- The coverage is reinforced operationally elsewhere in Subpart C, which requires an initial inspection 'for each new, replaced, rehabilitated, and temporary bridge as soon as practical, but within 3 months of the bridge opening to traffic' (inspection-procedures section of Subpart C, § 650.313), confirming that temporary bridges are not a carve-out but an inspected population. (Subsection lettering is not quoted here to avoid mis-citation; the quoted operative sentence is verbatim from Subpart C.)

SCOPE OF THE APPLICABILITY LIST, FOR COMPLETENESS
Structures covered: all structures defined as highway bridges, on all public roads, on and off Federal-aid highways — tribally-owned, federally-owned, private bridges connected to a public road on both ends, temporary bridges, and bridges under construction with portions open to traffic. Jurisdictional responsibility is then allocated by § 650.307 (State transportation departments, Federal agencies, Tribal governments, and joint written agreements for border crossings).

BOTTOM LINE
1. Threshold in the 'Bridge' definition: opening of more than 20 feet, measured along the center of the roadway, between under copings of abutments or spring lines of arches (or extreme ends of openings for multiple boxes). [§ 650.305]
2. Temporary bridges: expressly covered. Bridges under construction with portions open to traffic: expressly covered. [§ 650.303]

question: Y123
answer:
## 1. Answer in brief

**Ask 1 — Does HDS 3 cover the subject (uniform-flow velocity in a meandering natural channel with varying cross section and roughness, for certification)?**

**No.** FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 3 (*Design Charts for Open-Channel Flow*) does not cover that subject. Its charts are constructed for channels of uniform slope, cross section and roughness, free of backwater, and long enough to establish uniform flow; their stated accuracy is for "highway drainage channels of fairly uniform cross section and slope." The only allowance HDS 3 makes for natural channels is for "rough approximations" in channels "of nearly the nominal cross section." A meandering natural channel with varying cross section and varying roughness does not meet the chart's stated premise, and HDS 3 contains no method, chart, or correction for meander, non-prismatic geometry, or longitudinal roughness variability. It therefore cannot support a *certification* of uniform-flow velocity for that channel.

**Ask 2 — The condition HDS 3 states for the Manning equation to give a reliable velocity estimate (verbatim, Section 2.3, Uniform flow):**

> "The Manning equation will give a reliable estimate of velocity only if the discharge, channel cross section, roughness, and slope are constant over a sufficient distance to establish uniform flow conditions."

HDS 3 immediately adds:

> "Strictly speaking, uniform flow conditions seldom, if ever, occur in nature."

---

## 2. Ask 1 in detail — what HDS 3 actually covers, in its own words

Source quoted: the FHWA-published HDS 3 PDF (Hydraulic Design Series No. 3, archived edition; sha256 ef510f3b…). Section designations below (2.3, 3.2, 3.2-1, 4.2) are those of the quoted text; if the engineer is working from a different printing, re-verify these sentences before citing them.

### 2.1 The governing premise of the charts

Section 2.3 defines the flow class the charts serve:

> "Steady flow is further classified as uniform when the channel cross section, roughness, and slope are constant; and as non-uniform or varied when the channel properties vary from section to section. Depth of flow and the mean velocity will be constant for steady flow in a uniform channel."

Section 3.2 (general instructions for Charts 1–28, the principal open-channel charts):

> "Charts 1-28 provide a solution of the Manning equation for flow in open channels of uniform slope, cross section, and roughness, provided the flow is not affected by back-water and the channel has a length sufficient to establish uniform flow. The charts provide accuracy sufficient for the design of highway drainage channels of fairly uniform cross section and slope."

The same premise is repeated for the grassed-channel charts and the pipe charts:

> "Charts 30-34 provide a solution of the Manning equation for flow in open grassed channels of uniform slope and cross section, provided the flow is not affected by backwater and the channel has a length sufficient to establish uniform flow."

> "Charts 61-73 are designed for use in the solution of the Manning equation for pipe-arch channels which have sufficient length, on constant slope, to establish uniform flow at normal depth without backwater or pressure head."

> "Charts 74-82 are designed for use in the solution of the Manning equation for flow in oval concrete-pipe channels which have sufficient length, on constant slope, to establish uniform flow at normal depth without backwater or pressure head."

Four premises recur in every chart family: **uniform slope, uniform cross section, uniform roughness, no backwater, sufficient length.**

### 2.2 The one allowance for natural channels — and its limits

Section 3.2 does contain a limited concession, and it should be quoted in full so the scope answer is not overstated:

> "The charts may also be used to obtain rough approximations for depths and velocities in natural channels of nearly the nominal cross section. For such channels, a straight line drawn through irregularities in the bed profile may be used to define the slope."

Read strictly, this permits:
- **"rough approximations"** — not design-grade or certifiable values;
- **"depths and velocities"** — a normal-depth/normal-velocity screening number;
- **"natural channels of nearly the nominal cross section"** — i.e., a channel that reasonably matches one of the chart's prismatic templates (trapezoidal, rectangular, triangular);
- with slope taken as a straight line through the bed-profile irregularities — an averaging device, not a substitute for a water-surface-profile computation.

It does **not** permit a channel whose cross section varies materially from section to section, whose roughness varies along or across the section, or whose alignment meanders. HDS 3 offers no meander adjustment, no composite-n procedure, no subdivision rule, and no conveyance-weighted or divided-channel method. Those live elsewhere: the companion roughness guide (WSP 2339 / FHWA *Guide for Selecting Manning's Roughness Coefficients for Natural Channels and Flood Plains*) supplies the meander adjustment and the composite-n procedure, and HDS 4 and HEC-16 supply the varied-flow and channel-modification context. Citing HDS 3 alone for a meandering, variable-section, variable-roughness channel is a scope error.

### 2.3 Why the described channel fails the chart premise

| HDS 3 premise (Section 2.3, 3.2) | Condition in a meandering natural channel with varying cross section and roughness | Satisfied? |
|---|---|---|
| Cross section constant | Section varies through pools, riffles, crossings and bends; width and area change section to section | **No** |
| Roughness constant | n varies with bed material, bank vegetation, bed forms and local slope; meander adds up to 30 percent to n where flow is confined to the channel (Chow 1959, via WSP 2339) | **No** |
| Slope constant | Energy slope varies through the pool–riffle sequence; bed slope ≠ friction slope locally | **No** |
| Discharge constant (steady) | Acceptable only if the design discharge is treated as steady | Conditionally |
| No backwater | Must be demonstrated; a natural channel is routinely backwater-affected | Not demonstrated |
| Length sufficient to establish uniform flow | Requires a reach long enough for the profile to become parallel to the bed; usually not attainable in a meandering reach | **No** |

Four of six premises fail. The chart is being used outside its stated basis.

### 2.4 What "certify" can and cannot mean here

HDS 3 is a chart solution of the Manning equation, not a standard of care and not a certification instrument. It states its own limitation ("seldom, if ever, occur in nature"). An engineer can certify that a computation was performed and what it assumed; an engineer cannot certify a *uniform-flow velocity* for a reach that does not satisfy the constancy conditions, because the certified quantity would not exist as defined.

**Defensible certification language (recommended):**

> "Velocity in the study reach was estimated by the Manning equation using HDS 3 Charts 1–28 with n selected per WSP 2339 and slope defined as a straight line through the bed-profile irregularities, in accordance with the HDS 3 allowance for rough approximations in natural channels of nearly the nominal cross section. This value is a screening-level estimate only. It is not a uniform-flow velocity in the sense of HDS 3 Section 2.3, because the discharge, cross section, roughness and slope are not constant over a sufficient distance to establish uniform flow in this reach. Design velocities for the reach were computed by one-dimensional step-backwater analysis of the surveyed sections and are reported in Section ___ with the sensitivity range."

**Indefensible statement (do not sign):** "Uniform-flow velocity certified per FHWA HDS 3." That assertion contradicts the document's own stated condition and would not survive technical review.

---

## 3. Ask 2 in detail — the stated condition, decomposed

HDS 3 Section 2.3 states one sentence with five conjunctive requirements. All five must hold; failure of any one voids the reliability claim.

1. **Discharge constant** — steady flow at the design rate (Section 2.3 assumes "steady at the discharge rate for which the channel is to be designed").
2. **Channel cross section constant** — prismatic geometry.
3. **Roughness constant** — a single representative n, uniform along and across the section.
4. **Slope constant** — a single energy/bed slope through the reach.
5. **Constant over a sufficient distance to establish uniform flow conditions** — the reach must be long enough for the depth and mean velocity to become constant, i.e., water surface parallel to the streambed.

HDS 3 also embeds the backwater exclusion in the chart instructions ("provided the flow is not affected by back-water").

**Corroborating statement in HDS 4** (a different document — cite it as corroboration, not as HDS 3):

> "If the channel cross section, roughness, and slope are fairly constant over a sufficient distance to establish essentially uniform flow, equations such as that of Manning give reliable results."

and

> "Uniform flow conditions are rarely attained in drainage channels, but the error in assuming uniform flow in a channel of fairly constant slope and cross section is small in comparison to the error in determining the design discharge."

That second sentence is the honest basis for using Manning at all on a natural channel: the error is tolerable *relative to* discharge uncertainty, not because uniform flow exists.

---

## 4. What to do instead — procedure for the actual channel

Use HDS 3 as a screening check only; compute the design velocities by step-backwater analysis.

**Step 1 — Delineate the study reach.** Extend the reach upstream and downstream of the site of interest far enough that the profile at the site is not controlled by the reach boundaries (a backwater-free boundary condition at the downstream end is essential; otherwise the whole computation is invalid for the purpose).

**Step 2 — Survey cross sections.** Sections normal to the flow at each break in geometry, plus at bends, crossings, pools and riffles. Enough sections that interpolation between them does not smooth out the variability you are trying to capture.

**Step 3 — Subdivide each section.** Split at major roughness or geometric breaks (main channel / flood plain, vegetated / bare bank, dense brush / pasture). HDS 4: "When a channel cross section is irregular in shape such as one with a relatively narrow deep main channel and a wide shallow overbank channel, the cross section must be subdivided and the flow computed separately for the main channel and for the overbank channel."

**Step 4 — Assign n per WSP 2339, Steps 1–13 (channel) and 14–23 (flood plain).** Key elements:
- Step 1: the reach to which an n applies extends halfway to the next section; if roughness is not uniform through the reach, assign n for average conditions.
- Step 2/5/10: if roughness is not uniform across the width, subdivide and derive a composite n weighted by wetted perimeter or area.
- Step 11: add the Table 2 adjustment factors to the weighted base n; if base n came from Limerinos or Benson & Dalrymple rather than Chow, use one-half to three-fourths of the Table 2 increments.
- **Meander adjustment (m):** applied after the other adjustments, as a multiplier on the base n, and **only where flow is confined to the channel**. Degree of meandering is set by the ratio of meandering-channel length to straight reach length: **1.0–1.2 minor, 1.2–1.5 appreciable, 1.5 and greater severe**. Per Chow (1959), meanders can increase n by **as much as 30 percent** where flow is confined within the stream channel. This correction is in WSP 2339, **not** in HDS 3 — which is precisely why HDS 3 cannot carry the case alone.
- Note also WSP 2339's caution that the effects of sharp bends, constrictions and side-to-side shifting of the low-water channel may extend several hundred feet downstream, and that the usual amount of channel curvature in designed and natural channels produces a **maximum increase in n of 0.003** (Benson and Dalrymple, 1967).
- Step 13 (sand-bed channels only): the assigned n is not reliable unless stream power is sufficient to cause upper-regime flow — check the flow regime before using the n.

**Step 5 — Run the step-backwater analysis** (HEC-RAS or equivalent) with the surveyed geometry, subdivided sections, and the WSP 2339 n values. Use the standard-step energy method; the friction slope is computed section to section rather than assumed equal to the bed slope. This is the computation that produces a defensible velocity at each section, including the velocity distribution across the section.

**Step 6 — Bound the answer with an n sensitivity band.** Per FHWA NHI-01-004 guidance, carry a range of about **±10 percent** on the base n: use the **minimum** n to determine peak anticipated velocity (the governing case for riprap and scour) and the **maximum** n to determine peak depth and shear stress (the governing case for stage and conveyance). HEC-16 states the same principle in limit-value form: use the maximum n when estimating maximum stage and evaluating conveyance, and the minimum n where velocity is critical (riprap design, scour).

**Step 7 — Report.** Give the velocity at each section as a range from the n band, state the backwater boundary condition, state the n values with their derivation, and state explicitly that the HDS 3 chart value is a screening check and not the certified result.

**Step 8 — If an HDS 3 check is still wanted** (for the record): take the representative section nearest the chart's nominal geometry, take slope as a straight line through the bed-profile irregularities per Section 3.2, take n from WSP 2339 Step 11, and solve Charts 1–28. Report the result labeled "rough approximation per HDS 3 Section 3.2" and show its deviation from the step-backwater answer. Expect the chart to under-predict velocity where the reach is constricted and over-predict where it is pooled.

---

## 5. Two cautions before this goes in a report

1. **Edition.** Coverage and caveat wording can differ between printings of HDS 3. The sentences quoted here are from the FHWA-hosted HDS 3 PDF (archived edition, sha256 ef510f3b…). Re-verify the Section 2.3 and Section 3.2 sentences verbatim in whatever printing is being cited, and cite section numbers as they appear in that printing.
2. **Attribution.** Do not attribute the meander adjustment, composite-n weighting, or subdivision rules to HDS 3. They come from WSP 2339 (roughness selection) and HDS 4 / HEC-16 (varied flow, irregular and compound sections). Mixing the attributions is the most likely way this answer gets challenged in review.

---

## 6. Bottom line

- **Does HDS 3 cover it? No.** HDS 3's charts presuppose uniform slope, cross section and roughness, no backwater, and sufficient length for uniform flow; they are stated to be accurate for highway drainage channels of fairly uniform cross section and slope. The only natural-channel use permitted is "rough approximations" for channels "of nearly the nominal cross section." Meander, variable section and variable roughness are outside the document, and HDS 3 provides no method to handle them.
- **The stated condition:** "The Manning equation will give a reliable estimate of velocity only if the discharge, channel cross section, roughness, and slope are constant over a sufficient distance to establish uniform flow conditions" — with HDS 3's own qualifier that "strictly speaking, uniform flow conditions seldom, if ever, occur in nature."
- **Consequence:** compute by step-backwater with WSP 2339 roughness and a ±10 percent n band; use HDS 3 only as a labeled screening approximation; certify the method and its assumptions, not a "uniform-flow velocity" the reach does not have.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 23 on fhwa.dot.gov/bridge/wsp2339.pdf and 1 on nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2023-01/wsp2339.pdf. The first reads: "For example in figure 23, the n value for section 1 represents the roughness in reach A, and the n value for section 2 represents the roughness in reach B."

question: Y124
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION MEMO
Subject: Citation review — NBS Technical Note 904 (NBS TN 904), J. R. Shaver, "Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response" (National Bureau of Standards, May 1976), cited in the compliance file as the source of a design basic wind speed.
Basis of review: only the supplied page passages from the TN 904 document, the NIST publication record, and the code/standard material quoted in the grounding set. Full-document or external knowledge is not used to broaden the finding.

1. VERDICT (ask 2)
No. NBS TN 904 cannot be used as the source for a design basic wind speed.

2. WHY THE CITATION FAILS
(a) Subject-matter mismatch. Every supplied TN 904 passage is about perceptible floor vibration produced by human activity and human response to that vibration. The document describes a random-process treatment: "human activity which produces vibration and occupant response to vibration of a floor system are random variables"; the functional statement "F(t) + G(t) -> Y(t) -> D(t)" where F(t) is the random forcing function (human activity), G(t) the deterministic floor-system characteristics, Y(t) the random floor response, and D(t) the random human response; Fourier/spectral data reduction, mean-square values, probability density functions, pseudovelocity modulus; ISO/DIS 2631 whole-body-vibration exposure criteria (1 Hz to 80 Hz); and one field test on a wood-joist floor. None of this is wind climatology, wind load mapping, or design load specification.
(b) Absence of the cited content. Not one of the supplied passages contains a wind speed value, a wind speed map or contour, an annual exceedance probability or mean recurrence interval for wind, a velocity pressure, or any statement that TN 904 establishes or recommends a design basic wind speed. A citation cannot supply a design parameter that the cited source does not contain.
(c) The governing code names a different source. Under the code family represented in the grounding (IBC/TWIA 2024 §1609.3, "Basic Wind Speed", and the parallel Washington State amendment to §1609.3), "The basic wind speed, V, in mph, for the determination of the wind loads shall be determined by Figures 1609.3(1) through 1609.3(4)" — one figure per Risk Category — with location-specific values from the ASCE Wind Design Geodatabase (https://asce7hazardtool.online) or approved equivalent, and with Hawaii, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico taken from that geodatabase. The figure notes define the mapped values as 3-second gust speeds at 33 ft (10 m) above ground in Exposure Category C, corresponding for the Risk Category I figure to approximately a 7 percent probability of exceedance in 50 years (AEP = 0.00143, MRI = 700 years), with higher Risk Categories using longer mean recurrence intervals. ASCE 7-22 Chapter 26 (Figures 26.5-1A through 26.5-1D) is the underlying mapped source. A 1976 floor-vibration research note appears nowhere in that source chain.
(d) Robustness to the open variables. The specific jurisdiction and code edition are not stated in the project record. This does not change the verdict: in every edition and jurisdiction represented (IBC-derived §1609.3, ASCE 7 Chapter 26), V is obtained from mapped figures or the ASCE Wind Design Geodatabase, and no such code designates NBS TN 904 as a wind speed source. The verdict therefore stands regardless of jurisdiction.
(e) No fallback as an indirect wind source. TN 904 concerns floors under occupant activity, i.e. a serviceability/vibration-perception problem, not wind loading. Even if the compliance file meant to cite it indirectly (for dynamic response), it supplies no wind speed, no wind speed-up, no aeroelastic criterion, and no wind load parameter. It may legitimately support a floor-vibration serviceability discussion; it cannot support any element of design basic wind speed.

3. THE 25 Hz PASSAGE — WHAT IT ACTUALLY SAYS (ask 3)
Exact text of the relevant sentence, from the Appendix A field-test instrumentation description:
"The range of the accelerometer is from 10 mg to 0.001 mg. Figure 6 shows the location of this instrumentation. The LVDT was positively attached to the joist at mid-point of the clear span and the accelerometer set on the floor directly above the LVDT. Output from the LVDT and accelerometer were recorded as analog signals. While the frequency response of the electronic equipment was adequate to reproduce the time histories, the signal conditioning equipment for the accelerometer has a cut-off frequency of 25 Hz. This is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems."

Interpretation, stated precisely:
- The quantity is 25 Hz: the cut-off frequency of the accelerometer signal-conditioning equipment, i.e. the high-frequency roll-off of the measurement chain.
- The author's justification is adequacy for the test article: 25 Hz "is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems" — a statement about instrument bandwidth versus the response content expected in a wood-joist floor test, made in the same breath as "the frequency response of the electronic equipment was adequate to reproduce the time histories."
- It is NOT a floor natural frequency criterion, NOT a design limit, NOT a resonance or tuning requirement, and NOT a human perception or comfort threshold. The only human-response frequency range in the passages is the separate statement that ISO/DIS 2631 is "primarily intended for periodic (sinusoidal) vibrations in the frequency range from 1 Hz to 80 Hz but does cover narrow-band or wide-band vibration within this frequency range"; 25 Hz merely falls inside that 1 Hz to 80 Hz band and is unrelated to the cut-off statement.
- It has no wind-loading significance whatsoever. It is a property of the data-acquisition hardware used in one appendix field test on a wood-joist floor. It cannot be read as a structural dynamic characteristic, so it carries no bearing on wind-induced vibration or on a design basic wind speed.

4. NATURE OF THE ERROR AND CORRECTIVE ACTION
This is a citation error in the compliance file, not a defensible engineering judgment. Two plausible causes, both to be recorded in the file:
- Mis-copied note number: the companion 1976 NBS publication TN 909 (Yokel, Yancey, Cattaneo, Marshall, "Investigation of wind damage in the Metropolitan Washington, D.C. area, April 3-4, 1975") is wind-related and could be what a drafter reached for. Note that even TN 909 is a post-event wind-damage investigation and would not, by itself, be an acceptable source of a design basic wind speed either.
- Template citation drift: a vibration/serviceability reference left in a wind-load calculation reference block.

Required correction to the compliance file:
(a) Strike the citation to NBS TN 904 wherever it is offered as the source of the design basic wind speed. TN 904 may be re-cited only where the file genuinely addresses floor-vibration serviceability or human response to floor vibration.
(b) Replace it with the governing source: the adopted building code provision on basic wind speed (e.g., IBC §1609.3 "Basic Wind Speed", Figures 1609.3(1)–(4) by Risk Category) and, behind it, ASCE 7 Chapter 26 (ASCE 7-22 Figures 26.5-1A through 26.5-1D), with the location-specific value taken from the ASCE Wind Design Geodatabase / ASCE 7 Hazard Tool (https://asce7hazardtool.online) or the jurisdiction's approved equivalent. Where the jurisdiction amends §1609.3 (e.g., Washington State special wind regions per Table 1609.3.2 and local jurisdiction values near mountainous terrain and gorges), cite the amended section instead.
(c) Record the derived wind speed basis explicitly in the file: Risk Category, mapped or geodatabase value, units mph (3-second gust), reference height 33 ft (10 m), Exposure Category C basis, and the mean recurrence interval / annual exceedance probability applicable to that Risk Category. Where allowable stress design is used, apply the code's conversion (IBC Table 1609.3.1 or Equation 16-18, V_asd from V) — this conversion operates on code-mapped V, confirming again that V must come from the code source, not from TN 904.
(d) Note for the file: TN 904 is a 1976 NBS Technical Note (report number NBS TN 904, DOI 10.6028/NBS.TN.904) on floor vibration and human response; it contains no wind speed data in the reviewed passages.

5. LIMITATIONS OF THIS DETERMINATION
- The review is confined to the supplied page passages. If the compliance file's intent was something other than sourcing a wind speed value from TN 904 (e.g., citing it for floor-vibration acceptance criteria adjacent to a wind calculation), that narrower use must be re-stated and reviewed separately; it does not rescue the wind-speed citation.
- The adopting jurisdiction and code edition are not identified in the project record. The replacement citation in item 4(b) must be conformed to the jurisdiction's adopted edition before the file is closed. This does not affect the verdict.

6. VALUES STATED
- Verdict on whether TN 904 can serve as the source for a design basic wind speed: no.
- The 25 Hz passage value: 25 Hz — the cut-off frequency of the accelerometer signal-conditioning equipment in the TN 904 appendix field test, described as generally satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems; not a natural frequency, not a perception threshold, not a wind parameter.
- No design basic wind speed value is stated anywhere in this memo, because none can be derived from the supplied TN 904 passages.

question: Y125
answer:
Determination: Yes. For a proposed subdivision within a designated special flood hazard area (A zone) of a participating NFIP community, the federal minimum floodplain-management rule quoted in the supplied eCFR page requires base flood elevation (BFE) data to be included in the subdivision proposal. The applicable quoted provision is 44 CFR §60.3(b)(3): 'Require that all new subdivision proposals and other proposed developments (including proposals for manufactured home parks and subdivisions) greater than 50 lots or 5 acres, whichever is the lesser, include within such proposals base flood elevation data.'

Threshold: The rule's threshold is greater than 50 lots or 5 acres, whichever is the lesser. It is a disjunctive size test: a proposal that exceeds the 50-lot prong or the 5-acre prong, as limited by the 'whichever is the lesser' language, must include BFE data. The proposal is 60 lots and 4 acres. Numeric comparison: 60 lots > 50 lots — the lot-count prong is met; 4 acres < 5 acres — the acreage prong is not met. Because the lot-count prong is met, the 4-acre figure does not avoid the requirement. The proposal must include BFE data.

Why the answer is not 'No' based on 4 acres: The 5-acre figure is not the sole threshold. The rule independently uses 50 lots, and 60 lots exceeds it. The phrase 'whichever is the lesser' selects the lower applicable threshold; it does not require the proposal to exceed both 50 lots and 5 acres. Here the 50-lot threshold is the controlling prong because it is exceeded.

Supporting community duty: The provision is addressed to the community ('the community shall'), not directly to the developer. The practical effect is that the community must require the subdivision proposal to include BFE data before approving it. If FEMA has not produced water surface elevation data, §60.3(b)(4) also requires the community to 'Obtain, review and reasonably utilize any base flood elevation and floodway data available from a Federal, State, or other source, including data developed pursuant to paragraph (b)(3) of this section...' That allows BFE data developed by the applicant's engineer to be used, but the data must be in the proposal.

Applicability notes: (1) This answers the federal minimum standard shown in the supplied page. It applies where the subdivision is in a designated A zone on the community's FHBM or FIRM and the community is a participating NFIP community subject to 44 CFR Part 60. If the site is outside the SFHA, this particular BFE-data requirement is not triggered. (2) The quoted provision is §60.3(b)(3), which applies where FEMA has designated A zones but has not produced water surface elevation data or identified a floodway/coastal high hazard area. If the community's FIRM already provides BFEs and a regulatory floodway, the parallel subdivision provision is in §60.3(c); the same 50-lot/5-acre trigger should be confirmed. The conclusion for a 60-lot proposal remains yes. (3) State or local floodplain ordinances may be stricter and may require BFE data for smaller subdivisions; the stricter requirement controls. (4) Using the stated figures, the 4-acre area is below 5 acres but is not controlling because the 60-lot count exceeds 50 lots. If the 4-acre figure is only the total site area and the actual subdivision area is smaller, the 60-lot count still triggers the requirement. (5) The rule uses 'greater than,' so exactly 50 lots or exactly 5 acres would not trigger this provision; 60 lots is above 50.

Conclusion: Yes — BFE data is required in the proposal. The threshold is greater than 50 lots or 5 acres, whichever is the lesser; the 60-lot count exceeds the 50-lot threshold. The 4-acre area is below 5 acres but is not controlling because the lot-count prong is met.

Recommended submittal action: Include BFE data in the subdivision proposal. If FEMA BFE data are not available, have a qualified engineer develop BFE data for the site and submit it with the proposal; the community should review and reasonably utilize it under §60.3(b)(4). Document the 60-lot count and the threshold determination in the floodplain permit file.

question: Y126
answer:
MANNING n FOR DUNE BED AND PLANE BED — FHWA HEC-20, STREAM STABILITY AT HIGHWAY STRUCTURES, FOURTH EDITION

SOURCE
FHWA Hydraulic Engineering Circular No. 20, Stream Stability at Highway Structures, Fourth Edition, Publication No. FHWA-HIF-12-004, April 2012 (Lagasse, P.F.; Zevenbergen, L.W.; Spitz, W.J.; Arneson, L.A.; Ayres Associates for FHWA). Passage located in Chapter 3 (geomorphic/hydraulic factors), in the bed-form discussion immediately preceding the heading "3.4.4 Resistance to Flow," with cross-references to Section 3.4.4 (Resistance to Flow) and Section 3.3.3 (Manning n).

VERBATIM PASSAGE (HEC-20, 4th ed.)
"Care must be used in analyzing crossings of sand-bed streams in order to anticipate changes that may occur in bed forms and the impact of these changes on the resistance to flow, sediment transport, and the stability of the reach and highway structures. As described in Section 3.4.4, with a dune bed, the Manning n (see Section 3.3.3) could be as large as 0.040. Whereas, with a plane bed, the n value could be as low as 0.010. A change from a dune bed to a plane bed, or the reverse, can have an appreciable effect on depth and velocity. In the design of a bridge or a stream stability or scour countermeasure, it is good engineering practice to assume a dune bed (large n value) when establishing the water surface elevations, and a plane bed (low n value) for calculations involving velocity."

ANSWER (qualifiers preserved as the manual states them)
1. Dune bed — the Manning n could be AS LARGE AS 0.040.
2. Plane bed — the n value could be AS LOW AS 0.010.

Manning n is dimensionless; the manual gives no SI/English distinction for these two numbers (n is dimensionless in both unit systems), and the identical pair appears in the SI-format printing of the circular.

QUALIFIER HANDLING — CRITICAL
These are bounding statements, not typical or recommended design values. Do not restate them as "n = 0.040 for dunes" or "n = 0.010 for plane bed." The manual's own wording is "could be as large as 0.040" (upper bound for a dune bed) and "could be as low as 0.010" (lower bound for a plane bed). The spread between the two bounds — a factor of four — is the point of the passage: a dune-to-plane (or plane-to-dune) change produces an appreciable change in depth and velocity at a crossing.

ASSOCIATED DESIGN GUIDANCE (same passage, for context in application)
The circular directs that it is good engineering practice to:
- assume a dune bed (large n value, up to the 0.040 bound) when establishing water surface elevations; and
- assume a plane bed (low n value, down to the 0.010 bound) for calculations involving velocity.
This pairing is the conservative envelope for bridge/stream-stability/countermeasure design: high n raises stage, low n raises velocity.
